articles.title: Google Russie fait saisir 1,9 milliard d'euros chez Google France
articles.text:
Un commissaire de justice s’est rendu ce mercredi 25 novembre au siège de Google France pour y signifier une saisie conservatoire de 1,9 milliard d’euros. Elle est réclamée par le liquidateur de Google Russie, qui veut récupérer une partie des recettes publicitaires encaissées par Google Ireland.
Le cabinet WJ Associés, qui défend Google Russie en France, nous a confirmé la démarche. Elle vise à faire appliquer ici une condamnation prononcée à Moscou, au sujet de recettes perçues entre 2018 et 2022.
De la marge rabotée en 2018 à la saisie parisienne
Depuis 2009, Google Russie vendait les espaces publicitaires de Google Ireland et gardait 20 % du chiffre d’affaires. En 2018, cette part tombe à 3 % pour les grands comptes et à 1,5 % pour les autres clients. Selon le cabinet, ni le coût des services de Google Ireland ni la répartition du travail ne justifiaient cette baisse. Les salariés russes assuraient le même niveau de prestation. Le chiffre d’affaires de la filiale progressait, mais ses bénéfices et sa trésorerie reculaient. Elle versait aussi chaque mois à l’avance l’essentiel des sommes encaissées, sans attendre l’échéance trimestrielle. Pour WJ Associés, Google Ireland aurait cherché à fragiliser sa filiale.
Google a suspendu ses ventes publicitaires en Russie en mars 2022. Google Russie a été déclarée en faillite en 2023 et a fermé son bureau de Moscou, où travaillaient 224 personnes. En octobre 2023, nous rapportions que la justice russe avait officialisé cette faillite, notamment à cause d’amendes supérieures aux liquidités de la filiale et au gel de ses comptes bancaires. Pour le cabinet, la baisse de 2018 y a aussi contribué.
Le liquidateur de Google Russie a saisi le tribunal de commerce de Moscou en octobre 2024. Le 3 mars 2026, le tribunal a annulé le contrat de 2018 et condamné Google Ireland à restituer 101,7 milliards de roubles (environ 1,12 milliard d’euros). La décision a été confirmée en appel le 16 juin, puis en cassation le 1er septembre. Google Ireland a saisi la Cour suprême de Russie en octobre.
Pour faire appliquer ce jugement en France, le liquidateur passe par l’exequatur. Cette procédure permet de rendre une décision étrangère applicable en France. Google Russie, qui a obtenu gain de cause à Moscou, demande au juge français d’autoriser l’exécution de la condamnation de Google Ireland. Le juge ne rejuge pas l’affaire. Il vérifie notamment que Google Ireland a pu défendre sa position devant les tribunaux russes. En attendant, la saisie conservatoire sert à préserver des avoirs sur lesquels les créanciers de Google Russie pourraient être payés, explique Me William Julié, l’avocat de Google Russie en France.

articles.title: Tidal: Warum der Streaming-Dienst 27 Millionen Songs löschen will
articles.text:
Tidal verbannt vollständig KI-generierte Musik von seiner Plattform. Ab dem 9. Dezember lehnt der Streamingdienst solche Titel ab und entfernt sie aus dem Katalog. Erlaubt bleibt Musik, bei der Künstler KI „als Hilfsmittel“ einsetzen – sie darf aber nicht mehr ausschließlich von einem KI-Tool stammen.
Angekündigt hat Tidal den Schritt in einem Posting auf X und in seiner aktualisierten KI‑Richtlinie. Bislang hatte der Dienst Titel, die er als komplett von Werkzeugen wie Suno oder Lyria erzeugt einstufte, nur gekennzeichnet und von Tantiemen ausgeschlossen. „Aber das reicht nicht. Wir halten eine drastischere Änderung für nötig“, schreibt das Unternehmen. Vertriebspartner sollen solche Tracks künftig gar nicht mehr einliefern dürfen. Musik, deren Begleitdaten reine KI-Produktionen ausweisen, wird Tidal zurückweisen.
27 Millionen Titel werden verschwinden
In den vergangenen 90 Tagen entdeckte der Streamingdienst nach eigenen Angaben 43 Prozent aller angelieferten Tracks als „vollständig KI-generiert“. Am 6. November lag der Anteil mit über 60 Prozent sogar noch höher. Insgesamt sind rund 27 Millionen Titel im Katalog derzeit als KI-Musik markiert, das entspricht 6,3 Prozent des verfügbaren Angebots. Bis Anfang 2027 sollen diese Songs von der Plattform verschwinden.
Gehört wurden sie eh kaum: 96 Prozent kamen in den vergangenen drei Monaten auf null Streams. Das größere Problem sind für Tidal KI-Songs, die echte Künstler nachahmen und ihnen Streams und Tantiemen wegnehmen. Mehr als 65.000 Tracks hat der Dienst eigenen Angaben zufolge bereits entfernt, weil sie unter fremdem Namen liefen.
Die Richtlinie von Juni reicht nicht mehr
Mit dem Verbot verschärft Tidal seine erst Ende Juni vorgestellte KI-Richtlinie deutlich. Damals hatte der Dienst noch ausdrücklich erklärt, KI-generierte Musik weiter zu akzeptieren.
Komplett maschinell erzeugte Stücke bekamen ein sichtbares KI-Symbol und verdienten kein Geld mehr. Titel, die Hörer täuschen oder Künstler imitieren, wollte Tidal schon damals löschen. Doch offenbar reicht das nicht.

articles.title: L'enceinte portable Beats Pill (2024) passe à 99,00 € pour le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : L'enceinte Bluetooth portable Beats Pill (2024) à 99,00 € (-19%)
Actuellement notée 4/5 par notre rédaction, l'enceinte Bluetooth portable Beats Pill (2024) délivre un rendu sonore puissant tout en assurant une excellente autonomie. Le Black Friday 2026 est l'occasion de se l'offrir moins cher : elle passe à 99,00 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit une baisse d'environ 19 % et 23,65 € d'économie.
Beats remet au goût du jour son format emblématique avec la Beats Pill (2024), une enceinte Bluetooth portable pensée pour diffuser un son dynamique en déplacement. Ce modèle modernise l'architecture audio de la marque tout en conservant une ligne compacte facile à transporter. Lors de son passage dans notre labo, l'appareil s'est distingué par sa conception soignée et son endurance.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, l'enceinte descend à 99,00 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit environ 19 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (122,65 €). Cela représente une économie de 23,65 € sur cette référence.
Une signature dynamique et une autonomie solide
Sur le plan acoustique, l'enceinte délivre une restitution énergique qui met en avant les basses fréquences et le haut du spectre sonore, idéale pour animer une pièce ou une sortie en extérieur. Sa connectique USB-C assure la recharge mais autorise aussi la lecture audio directe par câble ainsi que la recharge inversée pour alimenter un téléphone. Comme détaillé dans notre test complet, l'appareil brille particulièrement sur la durée d'utilisation avec 28 heures d'autonomie mesurées par nos soins, ce qui évite de chercher une prise après quelques sessions d'écoute.
Beats Pill (2024)
Points forts
- Rendu sonore puissant et dynamique.
- Belle présence dans les graves et les aigus.
- Design et fabrication réussis.
- Excellente autonomie.
- Charge inversée et écoute musicale via l'USB-C.
Points faibles
- Quelques boursouflures dans les graves.
- Médiums trop en retrait.
- App pauvre en fonctionnalités.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Conception étanche et limites sur les voix
Certifiée IP67, la Beats Pill (2024) résiste à l'eau et à la poussière pour vous accompagner au bord d'une piscine ou sous la pluie. L'application mobile propose en revanche peu de réglages personnalisés, et le profil sonore laisse les voix en retrait au profit des rythmiques percutantes. Cette particularité sonore conviendra parfaitement aux amateurs de musiques rythmées, mais demandera un temps d'adaptation aux personnes qui recherchent avant tout des dialogues précis sur les podcasts.
Bose SoundLink Flex (2ème génération) : l'autre option face au Beats Pill (2024)
La Bose SoundLink Flex (2ème génération) adopte une approche différente en intégrant un égaliseur dédié et une prise en charge du codec aptX, ce qui assure une signature sonore plus équilibrée dès les premiers morceaux. Elle se montre également plus résistante face aux manipulations rugueuses, là où la Pill (2024) mise sur une meilleure endurance globale et une puissance supérieure dans les graves.
Actuellement notée 3,5/5 par notre rédaction, la SoundLink Flex (2ème génération) s'affiche à 89,99 €, soit un tarif inférieur de 9,01 € à celui du modèle Beats. La Beats Pill (2024) conserve l'avantage d'une note actuelle de 4/5 grâce à sa très grande autonomie, mais la Bose SoundLink Flex (2ème génération) reste un choix plus économique pour ceux qui privilégient la justesse des timbres vocaux.
Bose SoundLink Flex (2ème génération)
Points forts
- Restitution sonore homogène, précision des médiums.
- Extension et équilibre dans les basses.
- Construction robuste et étanche (IP67).
- Connectivité complète (codec aptX, multipoint…).
- App riche et prise en main facile.
Points faibles
- Extrêmes aigus un peu trop artificiels.
- Dynamique écrasée à volume élevé.
- Absence de connectique filaire (USB-C audio, mini-jack…).

articles.title: « La plus grande collection d’identifiants que j’ai découverte » : 2 milliards de mots de passe Gmail, Facebook et Netflix ont été exposés sur Internet
articles.text:
Jeremiah Fowler, un chercheur en cybersécurité réputé, vient de mettre la main sur une base de données exposée sur Internet. Celle-ci n’était « ni protégée par un mot de passe, ni chiffrée ». Autrement dit, n’importe qui pouvait la consulter sans avoir besoin d’un mot de passe ou d’un identifiant. Dans ce répertoire, il a découvert environ 2 milliards d’identifiants, à savoir des adresses e-mail, des noms d’utilisateur et des mots de passe.
 I discovered 2 Billion Usernames, Logins, and Passwords exposed in a suspected data breach of a criminal marketplace. Millions of individuals, businesses, organizations, and government account credentials exposed. Read my full report here: https://t.co/9uf3S4w6ns https://t.co/VAEI3yx6IE
— Jeremiah Fowler Security Researcher (@yoda69) November 24, 2026
« Par son volume et son ampleur, c’est la plus grande collection d’identifiants que j’ai découverte en toutes mes années de chercheur en sécurité », souligne le chercheur dans son rapport, publié par ExpressVPN ce 24 novembre 2026.
C’est plus de 13 fois la base de 149 millions de mots de passe, dénichée en janvier par le même expert. Jeremiah Fowler n’en est en effet pas à son coup d’essai. En 2025, le chercheur avait déjà mis au jour 2,7 milliards de mots de passe Wi-Fi et d’adresses IP. Quelques mois plus tard, il avait aussi repéré 184 millions de mots de passe piratés.
Gmail, Netflix, Facebook… Quels services sont touchés ?
Presque tous les services en ligne sont répertoriés dans la base de données. Le chercheur a comptabilisé environ 608 millions d’identifiants Gmail, 114 millions liés à d’autres services Google, 88 millions d’identifiants Facebook, 41,7 millions liés à des comptes Roblox, 36,6 millions pour Amazon, 32,9 millions pour X et 31 millions pour Instagram.
Près de 20 millions d’identifiants Netflix, plus de 15 millions d’identifiants PayPal et près de deux millions d’identifiants Binance ont aussi été recensés. Enfin, plus de 61 millions d’identifiants sont associés à des adresses gouvernementales en .gov. Notez que des internautes français sont concernés. En effet, certains dossiers sont classés par pays, avec des abréviations comme US, UK, DE ou encore FR.
Le chercheur précise bien que les chiffres avancés par ses soins ne sont que des estimations. En effet, un même compte peut apparaître plusieurs fois, ce qui tend à gonfler le nombre de victimes potentielles. Par ailleurs, le répertoire contient sans doute des mots de passe périmés.
« La présence d’environ 2 milliards d’enregistrements d’identifiants ne doit pas être interprétée comme représentant 2 milliards de victimes individuelles », précise le chercheur à la suite de ses investigations.
Bien plus que des mots de passe
La base de données ne contient pas que des identifiants et des mots de passe. Le chercheur a aussi découvert des cookies et des jetons de session, des petits fichiers qui permettent de rester connecté à un site sans devoir retaper son mot de passe à chaque fois. Ces fichiers sont déposés par un site sur votre navigateur. Un pirate qui le récupère peut s’en servir pour se connecter à votre place, sans connaître votre mot de passe et sans passer par la double authentification. Entre de mauvaises mains, ils peuvent offrir aux pirates « plus de moyens d’entrer qu’un simple mot de passe », rappelle le chercheur.
Dans 400 000 documents, l’expert a repéré des listes d’applications installées, des mots de passe enregistrés, le contenu du presse-papiers ou encore des informations techniques sur l’ordinateur de la victime. Ces données permettent de dresser un « profil détaillé de chaque victime ». Le chercheur a aussi trouvé des milliers de comptes associés à des sites du dark web. Dans les documents, il a en effet déniché des milliers d’adresses en « .onion », accompagnées de noms d’utilisateur et de mots de passe.
« C’est la première fois que je vois un grand nombre de comptes du dark web dans des identifiants piratés », s’étonne Jeremiah Fowler.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaques en cours dans le « monde entier » – le FBI alerte sur une vague d’intrusions menées par ARTEX, une redoutable IA
Des virus voleurs de données
Selon Jeremiah Fowler, ces identifiants ont vraisemblablement été dérobés par des « infostealers », des logiciels malveillants spécialisés dans le vol de données. Une fois installés sur un appareil, ils aspirent tout ce qui est enregistré dans le navigateur et les applications installées, ou enregistrent ce que vous tapez sur le clavier. C’est pourquoi on trouve énormément de données différentes dans le répertoire. Selon les estimations les plus récentes de Flashpoint, les infostealers infectent chaque année plus de 10 millions d’appareils.
Pour le moment, on ignore qui est à l’origine de la base de données. Celle-ci pourrait bien appartenir à une plateforme criminelle qui revend des identifiants volés, ou à un revendeur, théorise Jeremiah Fowler. Le chercheur a alerté l’hébergeur de la base, qui a coupé l’accès quelques jours plus tard par mesure de sécurité.
Si votre appareil est infecté par un infostealer, le fait de changer vos mots de passe ne suffira pas à vous protéger. Si « le logiciel malveillant reste actif », il pourra revenir à la charge et s’emparer de vos nouveaux mots de passe, prévient le chercheur. Il vaut mieux analyser votre appareil avec un antivirus pour tenter de débusquer un éventuel virus. Ce n’est qu’une fois que vous êtes certain que votre PC n’a pas été infecté que vous pouvez créer un nouveau mot de passe. Dans la foulée, prenez la peine d’activer la double authentification, de préférence avec une application dédiée ou une clé de sécurité.

articles.title: Cavó un estanque de 60 cm en el jardín y en pocas semanas aparecieron puestas de huevos de rana: de césped inútil a vivero
articles.text:
Cada primavera, el agua de deshielo recorría un trozo de césped de la finca de Stefano Ianiro y seguía su camino hacia la cuneta de la carretera. En 2024 aprovechó esta situación para crear una charca. En la parte baja de la finca cavó una depresión (que tiene unos 60 cm de profundidad en el punto más bajo) que se llenaba de agua. Quería ofrecer un espacio para la reproducción de anfibios.
En las primeras semanas (la orilla aún estaba casi pelada) llegaron las ranas de bosque. En el vídeo de la creación de la charca, comenta cómo en los primeros días en que llegaron las primeras ranas, él se alejó. Al volver a acercarse, calculó que había unas cinco puestas. También había puesto algunas ramas en el agua para que pudieran adherir los huevos y había tirado hojas secas para que tuvieran algún refugio.
Una charca pensada para secarse
Hay algunas diferencias entre esta charca y el estanque de truchas. Bajo el agua está la diferencia. En el estanque superior había truchas. Podían comerse a los renacuajos. El inferior ofrecía un espacio sin peces para que las ranas pudieran criar.
Las charcas temporales de primavera suelen llenarse con agua de lluvia y deshielo. Durante parte del año están secas. Como el agua desaparece de manera periódica, no pueden establecerse peces. Los anfibios sí precisan que la charca permanezca cierto tiempo.
El objetivo de Ianiro era que durase hasta agosto. Además, en primavera se calienta antes el agua poco profunda. Esto puede favorecer el desarrollo de las larvas. Al repasar ese primer verano, comentó cómo hubo momentos en que la charca estuvo a punto de secarse totalmente. Sin embargo, como hubo fuertes lluvias, se volvió a llenar.
Lo que aporta una charca pequeña
El potencial de estos espacios se ha visto en otro caso. En 2017 se publicó un estudio sobre 54 charcas formadas en cráteres de un bombardeo (de la Segunda Guerra Mundial) en Hungría. Juntas ofrecían un refugio para especies que también habitan en humedales naturales amenazados. A veces, el trabajo de recuperación de hábitats para la fauna pasa por aprovechar elementos que están presentes en el terreno, como hizo en su finca Ianiro aprovechando la escorrentía.
Entre las amenazas que recoge la evaluación global de anfibios (publicada en 2023) están la pérdida de hábitat, las enfermedades y el cambio climático. En este estudio se estimó que un 40,7 % de las especies de anfibios están amenazadas de extinción. En una red de pequeños humedales, cada charca puede suponer un espacio adicional de cría. En el caso de la finca de Ianiro, fue un trozo de césped por el que antes pasaba el agua hacia la cuneta.

articles.title: Hackers now exploit critical Drupal RCE flaw to hijack sites
articles.text:
The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical vulnerability that lets attackers hijack unpatched sites has been actively exploited since at least Thursday.
Drupal is a content management system (CMS) commonly used by large organizations, including government entities, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.
The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner and can be exploited by anonymous users to gain remote code execution or take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.
"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal security team warned last Wednesday. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."
While it wasn't initially flagged as abused in the wild, in an update to the original security advisory, Drupal warned that this flaw has been "exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."
Websites using the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but admins are still advised to upgrade to the latest available Drupal version in case other attack vectors are discovered.
Those who can't immediately upgrade should block access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root to secure the Drupal installer.
On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has also added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure their systems against ongoing attacks by Friday, November 27.
"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," the agency warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities."
Since November 2021, CISA has tagged five Drupal vulnerabilities as abused in the wild, two of which have also been exploited by ransomware groups.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

articles.title: Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents
articles.text:
Vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.
Each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.
A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.
Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.
Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.
Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to
Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,
then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol
For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.
Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:
Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.
Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.
Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation

articles.title: 9 startups picked for 1st Africa Ignite climate adaptation cohort
articles.text:
The United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) and BFA Global have selected nine climate adaptation startups from eight African countries for the first cohort of the Africa Ignite programme.
Funded by the Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA) and run under the Adaptation SME Innovation Facility (ASIF), Ignite targets early-stage startups that have built a working prototype but are yet to validate it with users. The nine were chosen from 453 applications.
Over eight weeks, founders will test their solutions with farmers, cooperatives and agribusinesses. Weekly live sessions, specialist office hours, AI training and real-world user testing will help them gather evidence of demand and impact, sharpen their business models, and prepare to land customers and raise investment.
“Every founder in this cohort has a working prototype. The next step is often the hardest: putting it in front of a cassava farmer, a coffee cooperative or a poultry producer and learning what they will use and pay for,” said Rasima Swarup, ASIF lead at BFA Global.
The cohort includes Benin’s ALLO VETO, which helps poultry farmers formulate affordable feed from local ingredients when drought disrupts supply; Angolan biodigester maker EcoBioGás; and Tanzania’s GeoVLUP Adaptation Services, which turns farm and climate data into practical guidance for coffee farmers.
Also selected are Ugandan circular savings platform Ghala Circular Solutions; Zimbabwe’s Global Vision Impact, which captures and stores runoff water for households during dry spells; and Kenyan agritech Kilimora, whose AgriKonnekt platform delivers localised climate intelligence to cooperatives.
Rounding out the cohort are Zambia’s LinkBridge, which builds shared solar-powered irrigation for clusters of smallholder farmers; Malawian food traceability startup MTENGO wa Mizu; and Kenya’s North Coast Innovators, which cuts post-harvest losses for cassava farmers through solar drying and milling.
More than half of the startups are founded or co-founded by women, and seven of the nine have a woman in a leadership position.
The programme kicked off on November 11, pauses in December and resumes in January, with the startups set to present their results at a Founder Showcase and Feedback Forum in late February 2027.

articles.title: Chizzy Nnamchi's plan for African builders to work globally
articles.text:
After more than three decades in a career, what keeps someone going? Is it the money, the excitement of the work, or the desire to see what else they can achieve?
For Chizzy Nnamchi, it is the excitement of imagining what is possible and helping others realise their potential. At 61, after decades of working across continents and holding senior positions at multinationals—including 3M and DHL—retirement is still not on his agenda.
“The way people go ‘wow’ sometimes when I say things. It’s the way I go ‘wow’ when I imagine certain things,” he says. “Especially working with young people who are just so brilliant and grounded. And that I can help them see better, and they will go and kill it.”
Today, Nnamchi is building Simvo Africa, an edtech platform that teaches people with little or no prior exposure to technology how to code through structured, project-based training. His broader ambition is to equip young Africans with the skills to compete in the global digital economy.
“It’s really about helping the next generation equip themselves with skills so that they can compete,” he says.
Choosing engineering
But Nnamchi’s interest in technology did not begin with a business idea. It began one afternoon in 1980 while he was walking across the field at the College of the Immaculate Conception in Enugu, south-east Nigeria. An aircraft was flying overhead; he could hear it, but could not see it.
He was in Class Three, and his physics class had just begun studying radar systems.
“I said to myself, if I had a radar, I would be able to tell without seeing this aircraft the type of aircraft it is, the direction it’s going and how fast,” he says.
“Right there at that spot, I decided I was going to study electronic and electrical engineering,” he adds.
His father wanted him to study chemical engineering or medicine, but Nnamchi had made up his mind.
He enrolled at the University of Ife—now Obafemi Awolowo University—in Osun State, south-west Nigeria, in 1982 and graduated with a first-class degree.
Despite the university’s limited resources, Nnamchi remembers his time at Ife as formative. Students learned computer programming in machine language and transferred their code onto punched cards for computers to read, with each card representing a line of code.
“In those days, I tried to write code using as few lines as possible to avoid errors,” he says.
Beyond academics, the university taught students to approach difficult engineering problems with confidence, even when resources were constrained.
“When we were at Ife, we developed the mindset that I can design pretty much anything that I want to if I have access to certain resources. We believed we could compete with anybody anywhere,” he says.
By the time he graduated in 1987, Nnamchi had decided to work rather than pursue postgraduate studies. He set his sights on Schlumberger, now known as SLB, an oilfield services company.
“I had chosen to join Schlumberger because that was one of the very few jobs that would put you on a dollar income track right away,” he says. “Instead of going to do a master’s and doctorate, I felt I needed to go earn money to support the family.”
Finding his way into Schlumberger
By the time he was due for the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in 1987, Nnamchi had already decided where he wanted to serve: Schlumberger’s Warri base in what was then Bendel State.
“I pushed to get assigned to Bendel State, as it was called before it was split up. I wanted either Bendel or Rivers State, where I could be in one of Schlumberger’s locations,” he says.
At orientation camp, Nnamchi says he discovered that the commandant’s girlfriend and his own girlfriend were best friends. He used the connection to approach the commandant.
“I convinced him to write a letter to Schlumberger, stating that NYSC would assign me to the company if they agreed to take me,” he says.
Armed with the letter, Nnamchi travelled to Warri and walked into Schlumberger without an appointment, asking to see the location manager. When he noticed the receptionist struggling with calls and visitors, he remarked that her job was not easy.
“She just melted,” he recalls. The receptionist eventually ushered him into the office of the location manager. He says the location manager noticed that Nnamchi had attended the University of Ife, which he had also attended, and asked whether he knew some of his former lecturers and colleagues. The shared alma mater helped open the door, and Nnamchi secured a place at Schlumberger for his service year.
Initially assigned routine tasks usually given to corps members, Nnamchi wanted more challenging engineering work. Within his first week, he approached the manager to ask for the opportunity to work on engineering projects or shadow the field engineers.
He says the manager challenged him: “Who gave you the guts to think you can shadow the field engineers?”
Instead, the manager assigned Nnamchi a project to build an alarm that would alert staff when public electricity was restored, so they could switch off their generators. Nnamchi completed it within a week.
“You hear it everywhere now when NEPA brings light, but then, I did the first one in Warri,” he says.
Impressed, Faiga gave him another assignment to automate the office gate, which Nnamchi also completed.
After finishing his service year in 1988, Schlumberger retained him alongside two other corps members.
“That was how I started my career fully,” he says.
From oilfields to Singapore
Nnamchi says his full-time career at Schlumberger began with a transfer to Egypt, where he spent six months before moving to Pakistan as a field engineer. There, he worked on wireline logging, using specialised tools and computing equipment to take scientific measurements inside drilled wells.
“It was seriously challenging work,” he says.
He was subsequently transferred to Oman, where Schlumberger field-tested new equipment and technologies. Nnamchi says the experience exposed him to some of the company’s most advanced technical work.
His time in Oman, however, was not without difficulties. He clashed with his Thai location manager over equipment allocation and maintenance, a disagreement he later acknowledged was partly due to his own attitude.
“I honestly had an attitude problem. I didn’t know better. I could have managed it differently,” he says.
After just over a year in Oman, Nnamchi moved to India in 1991, where he was promoted to senior field engineer. His responsibilities expanded to include a wider range of technical services, as well as planning and mobilising equipment and teams for remote projects.
By 1993, he was ready for a change. Although he enjoyed the technical challenges of oilfield work, he felt the industry offered limited exposure to the wider business world.
“If I want to be in the company for the long term, then I would stay and fight for promotions. But I wanted to be much more rounded,” he says. “As much as you do such high-tech work, and you’re dealing a lot with oil money, your exposure is very narrow. You don’t know much else going on in the real world.”
Having decided with his wife to settle in Singapore, he saw Asia’s rapid economic growth as an opportunity to broaden his experience and eventually bring some of what he learned back to Nigeria.
“Asia was growing so fast. So it would be ideal to live there, participate in that growth, learn a lot and see what we can bring back to Nigeria later on in life,” he says.
He left Schlumberger for Singapore, taking with him a key lesson: technical expertise alone was not enough.
“It’s not enough to be very good technically; one also has to be very good at dealing with people,” he says.
Taking 3M into oil and gas
Nnamchi settled in Singapore, where he says he provided business-development support to small technology companies supplying components to the hard disk drive industry. He helped get their components specified in new product designs, potentially opening up significant orders.
“We would spec components into new designs. And then if those components get accepted, tested, and work for the small company in the US or in Europe, it would be like massive sales for them,” he says.
He spent about a decade in that line of work, later extending it to mobile phone manufacturers and exploring the emerging internet economy. By 2002, following the dot-com bust, he was ready for something bigger.
In 2003, he joined American industrial company 3M to develop its oil and gas business in Southeast Asia. Despite the company’s extensive technology portfolio, Nnamchi saw an opportunity to bring its products into an industry where it had little presence.
During a presentation to 3M’s CEO in South Korea, he was asked why the company had not entered the oil and gas market.
“I told him point blank, ‘You’ve not hired people like me yet.’ I was born in the industry. I have relationships and contacts. I understand their pain points. I understand how they do business. So I can translate that to how different technologies within 3M can be applied within the industry. Technology doesn’t sell itself. You have to apply it,” he recalls.
After the presentation, Nnamchi says 3M committed resources to the opportunity, which became a global emerging-business initiative. He built technical teams, developed industry applications and helped expand manufacturing capacity, including helping to establish the company’s first factory in India.
“We built that business from less than $20 million to over $750 million in eight years,” he says.
Although his official position was director of oil and gas for Asia-Pacific, Nnamchi says he effectively ran the global business. Despite the growth, however, he felt his career had stalled.
“I was grinding hard, but I was not really flying career-wise,” he says.
When 3M offered him an opportunity to relocate to the United States, he declined, citing the financial and tax implications. He eventually left in 2011 without another job lined up.
“I actually left without another job, which is something I will not advise, but I left because I needed to just step out,” he says.
Nnamchi says his time at 3M taught him the value of a strong global brand and the resources that come with it. It also shaped his thinking about innovation, particularly the need for companies to look beyond developing new products and rethink how existing ones are taken to market.
Turning around DHL’s African operations
After 3M, Nnamchi says an opportunity to return to Africa came through global logistics firm DHL, which he joined as CEO for Central Africa, overseeing its air and ocean freight business. According to Nnamchi, some of the operations were losing money when he took over, and his task was to turn them around and address other challenges facing the business.
One of the opportunities he pursued was in Angola, where customs had seized three of Schlumberger’s warehouses, holding equipment for almost four years and demanding about $18 million in fines. Nnamchi saw a chance to resolve the dispute and secure a contract for DHL.
“One of my local guys in Angola had been the one training customs officers for quite some time. So I asked him, let’s go make a deal with these guys,” he says.
The negotiations brought the fine down to $3 million. Schlumberger agreed to pay the reduced sum, while DHL secured a contract to manage the movement of its equipment and warehouse operations.
Beyond turning around the business financially, Nnamchi also had to address staff morale, which he says was low when he arrived. He made a point of having lunch with employees to understand their concerns and the challenges they faced.
“People would tell me where they were having difficulties, why they were unhappy and what they thought could be done,” he says. “A lot of it came down to how people were being treated. I had to change that.”
After two and a half years at DHL, Nnamchi decided it was time to move on. The company’s regional headquarters had relocated from Singapore to Basel, Switzerland, complicating his travel arrangements. More importantly, the heavy travel schedule meant he was spending less time with his family.
“I wanted to be a bit more present,” he says.
Returning home and building Simvo Africa
After leaving DHL, Nnamchi began building businesses in West Africa, starting with a franchise from Bata, the global shoe company, covering Angola, Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire.
“I just needed to build up something so that I could move back home,” he says.
The three-country operation proved challenging, and after four years, he shut down the business in Angola and established his own brands in Nigeria and Côte d’Ivoire.
He also started Simvo Africa in Nigeria, an edtech company built around a coding course developed by his first son, John. Although John initially wanted to introduce the course in the US and Canada, Nnamchi saw an opportunity to bring it to Nigeria.
“I told him, I will start it here in Nigeria,” he says. “I want to train young people, allow them to learn how to code at a level that is not expensive.”
For Nnamchi, the goal goes beyond producing software developers. He sees digital literacy as an increasingly essential skill across professions, from medicine and engineering to finance and law.
“Digital literacy today is currency. It will help you in any field,” he says.
He also sees the venture as part of a wider effort to prepare young Africans for the global economy. With Africans expected to account for one in four young people worldwide by 2050, he believes the continent’s potential will depend partly on how well it equips its young population.
“If we can equip them well enough to compete, you will see amazing things happen in Nigeria and on this continent. I have no doubt about that,” he says.
Building a new generation of coders
Simvo’s training programme is entirely online, combining video lessons, structured chapters and practical projects. Nnamchi says it is designed to take learners from little or no prior exposure to technology to being able to code.
“You can come in with zero exposure to tech, and you will learn to code by the time you’re done,” he says.
The programme’s first student enrolled in March 2025 after approaching Nnamchi for a youth service job. With a background in chemical engineering, she was offered the opportunity to complete the course in three months, with a job at Simvo if she succeeded.
“If you can finish it, learn how to code in three months, I’ll give you a job. And she did,” he says.
She subsequently helped build the company’s website and backend systems. Nnamchi says some other graduates have also joined Simvo, while the company has helped others secure jobs elsewhere.
The platform now has about 105 people studying. Beyond training, Nnamchi says the company also helps graduates find employment.
“It’s not just skills. Oh, we charge you, you study, and we say bye-bye. No, we help you to get a job,” he says.
Over the next year, he hopes to strengthen the platform and expand into other English-speaking African countries before eventually reaching French-speaking markets.
For Nnamchi, however, the bigger ambition is the impact the venture can have on people’s lives and how they see their own potential.
“It’s almost never about me. It’s about the impact I have on people, their careers, their growth and their mindset,” he says. “If I can get somebody to imagine they can do far more than they thought possible, for me, that’s a big deal.”

articles.title: GTA 6 launch slashed Call of Duty's daily player count by 42%
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Three of the biggest live-service games lost players when Grand Theft Auto 6 launched this month, but Call of Duty was the slowest to get them back. Alinea Analytics estimates that Call of Duty HQ's daily player count fell 42% on launch day and barely improved over the next four days. The release also coincided with a shorter disruption outside gaming: Pornhub said its US traffic was 15.5% below normal an hour after GTA 6 went live.
Alinea estimated that Call of Duty HQ had 4.4 million daily active users on launch day, down from an average of 7.5 million across PlayStation, Xbox, and Steam. On PlayStation, which Alinea analyst Rhys Elliott identified as Call of Duty's main platform, the decline was 44%. GTA 6 launched only on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, so the overall Call of Duty figure includes a PC storefront where the new game was not available. The combined count does not show how much of the decline came from Steam.
Call of Duty's slow recovery stands out because it had less audience overlap with GTA 6 than Fortnite did. Of the people who played GTA 6 by the end of the launch weekend, 29% had also played Fortnite that month, compared with 16% for Call of Duty HQ and 11% for FC 27. Those figures identify shared audiences, not which game someone stopped playing to make time for GTA 6.
 – Rhys Elliott (@superhys) November 23, 2026
Fortnite's daily active users on PlayStation and Xbox fell from 17.8 million to 12.8 million on launch day, a 28% decline. By the end of the weekend, its daily player count was 19% below its usual level. FC 27 fell from 5.9 million to 4.3 million daily players, a decline of about 27%, before getting back to within 20% of its baseline. Call of Duty HQ was still 41% below its baseline after four days.
The competition for players' time came from GTA 6's single-player campaign, not an online service of its own. Alinea estimates the game has already sold 44.9 million copies and generated more than $4 billion. Elliott expects both an online mode and a PC version next year. The PC release would extend GTA 6 beyond its initial console audience, while the online mode could give players a reason to keep returning after they finish the campaign.
Pornhub's numbers tracked visits by the hour rather than players by the day. US traffic went from 16.5% above normal at 10 pm ET ahead of the release to 7.5% below normal by midnight. The drop deepened after launch, but by 8 am Thursday traffic was only 6.4% below average, and it edged above average later that day.
Pornhub's search data showed the game drawing interest on the site even as overall traffic fell. Searches for GTA-related terms rose 16,196% on launch day, and Pornhub reported 15 million such searches the following day. The most popular query was "gta 6," followed by "gta 6 lucia" and "gta 6 strip club / tacon." The timing of the traffic dip does not establish where visitors went, but the searches show what many of those who stayed or returned were looking for.

articles.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
articles.text:
AI is straining America’s open records systems
Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.
In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.
Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”
Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.
At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.
As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized
The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.
This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”
Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.
SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.
The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.
Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.” 
While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.
But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.
The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices. 
In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.
In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem
It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.
In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.
While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.
On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”
As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table
Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.
Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”
Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.
Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.
Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.
As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

articles.title: Two Newly Disclosed GeoServer Vulnerabilities Under Attack
articles.text:
Threat actors are targeting two recently disclosed GeoServer vulnerabilities that can be chained with other flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).
Cybersecurity firm WatchTowr has observed attempts to exploit two high-severity GeoServer vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243. The activity appears to be aimed at identifying vulnerable servers.
“Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries,” WatchTowr noted.
WatchTowr has not reported any instances of attackers successfully achieving remote code execution. At the time of writing there do not appear to be any other reports of exploitation attempts.
GeoServer is an open source application for publishing and sharing geospatial data. Government agencies widely use it, and utilities also deploy it. Cybersecurity company Eye Security has identified more than 3,000 internet-accessible GeoServer instances.
CVE-2026-120705 is an XML injection vulnerability that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to obtain sensitive files or conduct server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks. CVE-2026-129243 can enable attackers to bypass access controls and perform operations typically reserved for administrators.
The two security holes are part of a five-bug exploit chain discovered by Rapid7 researcher Jonah Burgess, aka CryptoCat, who reported his findings to GeoServer developers in early August.
Burgess also reported CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-129242. He showed how an attacker can gain admin access and execute arbitrary commands with the GeoServer process’s privileges.
The researcher disclosed technical details this week and published PoC exploit code.
Eye Security has independently found some of the vulnerabilities. It demonstrated unauthenticated RCE on Linux and Windows by combining three weaknesses: CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-120704. The security firm said it reported its findings to the vendor in late September.
GeoServer released patches several weeks ago, and it published advisories in recent days. Organizations are advised to upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6, or 2.27.7.
GeoServer vulnerabilities have been targeted in the past. In August 2026, hackers exploited a vulnerability as a zero-day, and in 2025 it came to light that a US government agency had been breached through the exploitation of a GeoServer flaw.

articles.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
articles.text:
Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store.
The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out.
According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement.
One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents.
Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers.
Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter.
Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported.
Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment.

articles.title: Motorola Signature (256 GB) fica mais barato com cupom da Black Week
articles.text:
Motorola Signature (256 GB) fica mais barato com cupom da Black Week
Motorola Signature com tela de 165 Hz, câmeras de 50 MP e chipset premium recebe ótimo desconto ao combinar cupom e pagamento via Pix
O Motorola Signature (256 GB) entrou em oferta por R$ 4.199 no Pix com o cupom MENOSPRATECH no Mercado Livre. O primeiro smartphone ultra-premium da Motorola com tela AMOLED e câmeras de 50 MP, lançado por R$ 5.999, atinge o menor preço já visto pelo Achados do TB nesta promoção de Black Week 2026.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Motorola Signature 5G 256 GB. Nas outras 1 ofertas publicadas desde novembro de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 4.498,20 (Magalu, 6/11/2026).
O Motorola Signature se destaca pela tela Extreme AMOLED de 6,8 polegadas, igual ao recente Signature 27, reproduzindo imagens na resolução Super 1.5K e taxa de atualização de 165 Hz. Além dos recursos Dolby Vision e HDR10+, o painel atua com brilho máximo de até 6.200 nits.
A câmera tripla traseira é composta por sensores de 50 MP, que fazem fotos com zoom híbrido de até 100x e registram vídeos em até 8K. A câmera frontal também adota um sensor de 50 MP, entregando selfies detalhadas com recurso de Foco Automático.
Com foco em alto desempenho, o Motorola Signature é equipado com o chip Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 e 12 GB de RAM. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno oferecem um espaço equilibrado para mídias, aplicativos e outros arquivos.
A bateria de silício-carbono de 5.200 mAh do smartphone da Motorola tem autonomia de até 39 horas de uso moderado. O modelo ainda possui carregamento rápido de até 90 W, indo de 0 a 50% em apenas 15 minutos.
O dispositivo é fabricado com estrutura de alumínio e acabamento traseiro em silicone imitando sarja ou linho. Os certificados IP68/IP69 de resistência à poeira e à água e militar MIL-STD-810H garantem ampla proteção contra mergulhos, quedas e condições extremas.
Na parte de conexões, o Motorola Signatura (R$ 4.199 no Pix com o cupom MENOSPRATECH) tem 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra WideBand (UWB) e NFC. O modelo sai da caixa com o Android 16 e, segundo a marca, receberá ao menos 7 grandes atualizações do sistema operacional.
A Black Friday 2026 acontece no próximo dia 27 de novembro, mas diversas lojas estão antecipando promoções e cupons de desconto desde o início do mês. Então, siga o Achados do TB para não perder nenhuma oferta.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Aunque suena a abuso, algunas cafeterías están cobrando 3 euros por estar una hora teletrabajando. Lo que dice la ley es más complicado
articles.text:
El portátil abierto, los auriculares puestos y un único café que lleva dos horas enfriándose, con el dibujito de la espuma disuelto por completo. Esta escena forma parte del paisaje de cualquier ciudad española y es, a partes iguales, el sueño del teletrabajador y la pesadilla del hostelero. Esta semana, El Español ha puesto cifras a la que parece ser la solución radical: 3 euros por hora y 22 euros por un bono diario.
¿Qué ha pasado exactamente?
La noticia proviene de un solo local: ‘Con·tempo’, recién abierto en la calle Montesa, en el barrio de Salamanca de Madrid, se presenta como un café de todo el día con espacio de trabajo flexible (All Day Café & Flexible Workspace) y la cuota ya mencionada: 3 euros por hora y silla. Sin membresía ni reserva previa.
También vende un Pase Diario de 22 euros que incluye 15 de consumo, así que el sitio en sí sale por apenas unos 7 (un cowork bastante rentable para freelances). La zona de trabajo ofrece puestos individuales, mesas compartidas, cabinas para llamadas y una sala para reuniones de hasta cuatro personas, tal y como indican en su nota de prensa. En la nota de prensa figura el resto de datos.
No es, por tanto, un bar que de repente te cronometra la tostada. Es un híbrido de café y coworking de zonas separadas. Su lema es "Less rush, more rhythm". Menos prisa pero con brío, lo que la separa del modelo Starbucks y la emparenta con el modelo de del Café Perfetto (o Coco Coffice, más bien), en plena Barceloneta, donde un café con leche cuesta 1,60 euros pero pasa a 2,50 si superas los 30 minutos y a 4 si pasas de una hora.
Fuera de España ya hay muchos modelos así: Anticafé en Francia (el que sobrevive en Estrasburgo, porque el de Lyon cerró) o el mítico Ziferblat, donde pagas por el tiempo, no por el café. Y también destacan los Bake Bros y Mama Shelter en Lisboa, que parten del modelo Desk Amigo: compartes mesa pero no café. En resumen, mucho brunch de bagel de salmón con queso crema y alcaparras, mucho diseño y conceptos heredados de la arqueología holandesa, pero pagas o te vas.
¿Te puede echar una cafetería por abrir el portátil?
Depende de lo que el local haya dejado por escrito. El derecho de admisión existe, pero no es un cheque en blanco. En la Comunidad de Madrid lo regula la Ley 17/1997 de Espectáculos Públicos, y cada comunidad tiene la suya.
El portal de consumo madrileño recuerda que el derecho sirve para frenar la violencia y las alteraciones del normal funcionamiento, nunca como excusa para la arbitrariedad o la discriminación en locales abiertos, por definición, a todo el público. Las condiciones tienen que estar a la vista en la entrada, eso siempre.
Sin embargo, entre juristas no hay unanimidad. El abogado Ignacio Palomar, de Servilegal, explicaba en Confilegal que una cafetería no alquila estancias, sino que vende consumiciones, así que puede ampararse en el derecho de admisión si tiene un protocolo claro y criterios objetivos. Su colega Laura Sierra replicaba en Consumidor Global que la norma no dice nada sobre usar dispositivos y solo prohíbe restringir el acceso de forma arbitraria o discriminatoria.
Quien sea expulsado por sacar el portátil podría reclamar ante Consumo o llamar a la policía. Lo que sí parece aceptado, como recogíamos en Genbeta, es la fórmula intermedia: limitar el portátil en horas punta, como ya hacen cafeterías de Valencia o Barcelona, y permitirlo cuando el local está vacío. El abogado Manuel Martínez Mercado lo avalaba en El Español siempre que no sea discriminatorio.
¿Y cobrar por el tiempo, es legal?
En principio, sí, si se avisa antes. El caso más sonado es el que citábamos más arriba, el Café Perfetto, en la Barceloneta, que se hizo viral en 2025 porque su café subía a 2,5 euros a los 30 minutos. Según VilaWeb, la Agència Catalana de Consum explicó que no existe una norma específica y que se aplica el código de consumo: es lícito tener precios distintos según dónde te sientes, siempre que se muestren de forma visible y clara.
Un análisis publicado entonces lo resumía así: no compras un café, contratas un servicio, y las condiciones deben conocerse de antemano. La OCU va en la misma línea: por el mismo refresco te pueden cobrar 2 euros o 10, siempre que el precio conste en la lista del establecimiento. Si la hostelería pierde mesas, este "tercer lugar" se convertirá en negocio con tarifa. La ley protege más contra la arbitrariedad que contra el cobro, pero mientras vayan de cara, legal sí es.
