articles.title: Ce que disent les paramètres graphiques de GTA 6 sur PS5 et Xbox
articles.text:
GTA 6 est un jeu vidéo visuellement sublime. Rockstar Games a bâti un monde ouvert vivant, avec une densité impressionnante et un niveau de détails à tomber à la renverse. Les développeurs ont certes sacrifié la fluidité, avec un affichage limité à 30 images par seconde, mais la prouesse reste immense.
La version PC de GTA 6, qui n’a pas encore été officialisée mais finira par arriver selon la tradition de Rockstar Games, devrait offrir un rendu encore plus incroyable. C’est en tout cas ce que l’on devine à la découverte des paramètres graphiques des différentes versions console, révélés par le dataminer Tex2 dans un message supprimé depuis (via MP1st, ce mercredi 25 novembre).
Comment Rockstar Games a peaufiné les différentes versions de GTA 6
Comme on peut le deviner, la PS5 Pro dispose des paramètres graphiques les plus poussés, notamment du côté des ombres en ray tracing (un argument mis en avant par Rockstar Games, qui réserve ces ombres à la PS5 Pro). La Xbox Series X et la PS5 standard sont réglées de la même façon. La console de Microsoft garde pourtant l’avantage sur la fluidité : dans son comparatif publié le 24 novembre, Digital Foundry relève nettement moins de chutes sous les 30 images par seconde sur Xbox Series X, aidée par la prise en charge du VRR en 120 Hz sur les téléviseurs compatibles. La Xbox Series S, la moins puissante du quatuor, doit faire plus de concessions.
La plupart des paramètres sont réglés sur moyen ou élevé, preuve que Rockstar Games a bel et bien misé sur la fidélité graphique. Des options comme la qualité du moteur physique, la densité des piétons et des véhicules, l’intelligence artificielle, la simulation de l’eau, la qualité des textures ou encore la modélisation des cheveux sont toutes réglées sur « Élevé » sur PS5, PS5 Pro et Xbox Series X. Rockstar Games aurait sans doute pu proposer un mode Performance qui dépasse les 30 fps, en réduisant ces éléments. Le studio a privilégié un rendu plus précis et détaillé qu’une expérience plus fluide.
Une version PC de GTA 6 aurait en revanche une carte à jouer sur les ombres de la végétation, l’éclairage volumétrique ou encore la qualité maximale des textures des armes, qui ne dépassent pas « Moyen » sur les consoles. Notez que le réglage « Ultra » existe déjà : la PS5 Pro l’utilise pour le ray tracing, et les PS5, PS5 Pro et Xbox Series X pour les textures des véhicules. Sur les PC les plus puissants, il pourrait être appliqué partout.
Sur Xbox Series S, les sacrifices ne touchent pas que l’image. Selon le même tableau, la densité de piétons et de véhicules, l’intelligence artificielle et la qualité du moteur physique y passent en « Moyen », tout comme les textures et les cheveux. Les rues de Vice City y sont donc moins peuplées que sur les trois autres consoles.

articles.title: Así conecta ‘Blade Runner 2099’ con las películas, según sus protagonistas: «Los replicantes están en el poder»
articles.text:
Acaba de estrenarse en Amazon Prime Video su nuevo gran proyecto, Blade Runner 2099. Se trata de una serie de ciencia ficción que se ambienta en la legendaria franquicia creada por Ridley Scott hace casi 45 años. Esta vez, la saga da el salto al streaming con una historia de ocho episodios que promete seguir indagando en su complejo y fascinante universo.
Cincuenta años después de los sucesos de Blade Runner 2049, Los Ángeles ha renacido, aunque no a manos de la humanidad. Cora, una fugitiva que intenta dejar de huir de una vez por todas, adopta una última identidad: la de Blade Runner. Obligada a asociarse con Olwen, una replicante a la que le quedan pocos días de vida, da caza a un fugitivo que oculta una verdad capaz de hacer colapsar su frágil ciudad.
De cara al estreno de Blade Runner 2099, en Hipertextual hemos podido atender a la conferencia de prensa de sus dos protagonistas, Michelle Yeoh (Todo a la vez en todas partes) y Hunter Schafer (Euphoria). Y en ella nos han contado cómo será el mundo que los fans se encuentren en la serie. Porque, después de tantos años, ahora son los replicantes los que tienen el control y los humanos lo que deben esconderse.
Los replicantes de Blade Runner 2099
"Creo que al final de Blade Runner 2049 se empieza a vislumbrar el germen de una revolución o algo que se ha estado gestando. Y han pasado muchas cosas desde entonces. Los replicantes están en el poder y, no solo eso, sino que han mantenido el sistema al estilo de Blade Runner y, de hecho, lo han invertido por completo. Ahora son los humanos a quienes se persigue", explica Schafer.
"Mantienen a los humanos a raya. Cuando ganas una guerra, ¿cómo te aseguras de mantenerte en el poder?", se une Yeoh a su compañera de reparto. "Me encantan las preguntas que plantean esta serie e incluso las dos primeras películas: ¿qué es ser humano? ¿Qué es la humanidad? ¿Nacemos con humanidad o es algo que hemos aprendido con el tiempo y la experiencia de la vida?", se plantea a su vez.
"Los replicantes no nacieron con emociones. De hecho, no tenían alma. Fueron creados de carne y hueso a nuestra imagen y semejanza, pero más fuertes para poder hacer cosas que nosotros no haríamos o que físicamente no podríamos hacer", prosigue la veterana actriz.
"Pero cuando se les da tiempo y recuerdos... ¿les estamos dando esperanza? Porque lo que hacen los replicantes en 2099 también da esperanza a los humanos. Si eres bueno, si haces esto, podrías ir a un lugar mejor. Y eso es mentira, porque cuando Cora descubre que no hay nada ahí fuera, siente una gran sensación de traición. Esto es todo lo que tienes", sugiere, dejando entrever algunos detalles de por dónde discurre la trama y el componente filosófico de Blade Runner 2099.
Dos personajes muy distintos
Las dos protagonistas de Blade Runner 2099 son Cora, una joven humana que debe hacerse pasar por replicante y Olwen, una androide a la que el tiempo se le acaba. Se trata de dos mujeres totalmente antagónicas que se encuentran en un mundo en el que deben aliarse. Pero, en el fondo, ambas luchan sus propias guerras. "Cora es un personaje que, en cierto modo, ha perdido su identidad. ¿Cómo se interpreta a alguien que no sabe quién es?", revela Schafer sobre su papel.
"Y, además de eso, ¿cómo interpretas a alguien que no sabe quién es y que se hace pasar por otra persona durante gran parte de la serie? Sabía que iba a ser un gran reto y me daba miedo, lo cual es en parte por lo que quería hacerlo. Era una cuestión de encontrarlo y volver a ello constantemente", añade. "Cada vez que se volvía abrumador o me daba un poco de vértigo, tenía que recordar que ella simplemente actúa en modo de supervivencia y lo único que quiere es sobrevivir y mantener con vida a su hermano y a ella misma", cuenta sobre su personaje.
"Por mi parte, cuando conoces a Olwen por primera vez, te das cuenta de que es una replicante muy segura de sí misma. Es, como dirían, la replicante más dura que hay", menciona Yeoh acerca de su personaje de Blade Runner 2099. "No permite que la fecha de caducidad defina todo lo que ha hecho como Olwen, la Blade Runner, ni lo que ha conseguido. De hecho, ella misma lo dice: «He dado a luz a estrellas». Ya sabes, «he hecho todo lo que quería ver y hacer». Pero esa es la Olwen que quiere que los demás perciban", sugiere después.
"Se supone que no debes sentir empatía, que no debes tener este tipo de deseos porque eres una replicante. Así que hay que mantener eso dentro, mostrar control. Pero luego hay momentos... ¿Por qué estaría ella, en sus últimos días, tan decidida a completar una misión? Hay secretos. Secretos que no puede permitir que otros replicantes, otros humanos, vean, porque eso sería mostrar un lado terriblemente vulnerable de sí misma. Eso no solo la hundiría a ella, sino a todo el ecosistema. Todo el lugar es muy frágil en este momento porque los humanos quieren recuperar lo que hay allí y los replicantes quieren continuar, quizá ser más y evolucionar", concluye.
Blade Runner 2099 ya está disponible en Amazon Prime Video.

articles.title: Priyank Kharge targets Mangaluru with Rs 6,000 Cr regional growth push
articles.text:
Priyank Kharge targets Mangaluru with Rs 6,000 Cr regional growth push
Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge is urging investment in Mangaluru, with Dakshina Kannada contributing 5.3% of the state’s GDP. The Beyond Bengaluru strategy aims to unlock the region’s business and talent potential.
Bengaluru may be Karnataka’s best-known technology hub, but the state government wants companies to look further along the coast. Mangaluru, with its established educational institutions, skilled workforce and quality of life, is being positioned as another centre for economic growth.
At the inauguration of Deloitte’s 27th office in India, in Mangaluru, Karnataka IT and BT Minister Priyank Kharge called on industry leaders to invest in the region and help create opportunities closer to where talent already lives.
Kharge said Dakshina Kannada is Karnataka’s second-largest district contributor to the state’s GDP after Bengaluru, accounting for 5.3% of the total. He said the region’s economic strength and talent pool make it an important part of the state’s next phase of growth.
“Our objective through Beyond Bengaluru is to take opportunities to where talent already exists, rather than expecting talent to move to Bengaluru,” he said.
He also acknowledged Deloitte’s decision to establish an office in Mangaluru, thanking Romal Shetty and the company’s team for supporting the government’s regional development agenda.
Building growth beyond Bengaluru
The government’s Beyond Bengaluru strategy aims to develop multiple economic centres by building on the strengths of different regions.
Kharge pointed to a recent Karnataka Cabinet meeting held in Mangaluru for the first time in the city’s history. The meeting identified growth opportunities for the region, with approximately Rs 6,000 crore committed towards its development.
He also cited the Local Economy Acceleration Programme (LEAP), which focuses on identifying regional strengths, attracting investment and creating employment.
Mangaluru, he said, has an agile talent pool and some of the country’s leading educational institutions. Its quality of life could also help companies attract and retain employees.
As an example, he mentioned a Danish team from software firm EG that surfs at Sasihithlu beach in the morning before heading to work. Kharge said such advantages could help the city stand out as a business destination.
Developing more employment centres across Karnataka could also ease pressure on Bengaluru, which continues to attract migrants from across the country.
Connecting education with industry
Attracting companies is only one part of the plan. Priyank Kharge said industry and educational institutions must work together to ensure graduates have the skills required by employers.
He called on companies such as Deloitte to help shape curricula and prepare students for emerging job opportunities.
“Why should a student studying in Mangaluru not be equipped to work with a company like Deloitte?” he asked, describing this as an opportunity for industry and government to work together.
The Minister also suggested exploring a Centre of Excellence in Mangaluru, potentially focused on health sciences, given the region’s established healthcare ecosystem.
Startups and new opportunities
Priyank Kharge encouraged entrepreneurs from the region to apply to the state’s ELEVATE programme, which offers eligible startups equity-free grants of up to Rs 1 crore.
He also outlined Karnataka’s regulatory sandbox initiative, which allows startups working on public-sector challenges, including urban mobility, to test their solutions with the government. Successful pilots can then be scaled across the state and potentially taken to other states.
The programme has enrolled 16 startups so far, with the government aiming to increase participation to 100.
The government’s message to businesses was that Karnataka’s next phase of growth need not be concentrated in Bengaluru. By bringing investment, skills development and startup opportunities to cities such as Mangaluru, it hopes to build more regional economic centres across the state.

articles.title: ACET spinoff Ascension Capital announces $30-million first close of new early-stage fund
articles.text:
The early-stage startup landscape in Québec’s Eastern Townships now has deeper pockets and a new VC brand.
The news: The partners behind ACET Capital, the venture arm of Sherbrooke, Que.-based tech incubator ACET (Accelerator for the Creation of Technological Businesses), announced on Thursday an early-stage fund targeting up to $50 million CAD under the new entity Ascension Capital.
The fund has reached a first close of $30 million, backed by Fonds de solidarité FTQ and undisclosed private investors from the Estrie region. Investissement Québec, the provincial government’s investment arm, has committed up to $25 million if its investment is matched dollar-for-dollar by private investors.
Ascension Capital, led by managing partners Dominic Denis and Ghyslain Goulet, plans to back between 16 and 20 pre-seed and seed-stage startups with differentiated technologies across a broad range of sectors, including deep tech and AI.
From the source: “We’ve reached the stage where we can support startups in a way that’s in line with our ambitions,” Denis said in an interview, which BetaKit has translated from French. “We want young startups to become recognized international brands.”
The context: ACET Capital is the venture capital arm of the incubator-accelerator ACET, established in 2011 out of the Université de Sherbrooke. It has backed startups across several disciplines, including quantum, healthtech, manufacturing tech, AI, and cleantech—including risk-management software Trustii and battery-cooling tech startup Calogy Solutions.
ACET Capital’s previous funds have been smaller, at $4 million and $7.6 million, respectively, and will continue to operate. While Ascension Capital will have a pool of startups emerging from ACET programs as potential targets, it is also open to investing in non-ACET companies.
Final thought: Sherbrooke emerged as a hub for quantum and other deep tech in Québec, something the provincial government has invested in heavily through sectoral support and the establishment of a Quantum Innovation Zone. The bet has so far paid off, with homegrown upstarts like Nord Quantique reaching a unicorn valuation and becoming part of US and Canadian programs to build a useful quantum computer.

articles.title: Programmieren ja, Urteilsvermögen nein: Wo KI-Modelle an ihre Grenzen stoßen
articles.text:
Warum KI-Modelle mit diesem Update besser bewertet werden können – aber Fragen offen bleiben
Einige Fähigkeiten großer KI-Modelle verbessern sich weiterhin exponentiell – aber eben nicht alle. Bei Aufgaben, die Urteilsvermögen erfordern, schneiden sie beispielsweise nicht ganz so gut ab, wie beim Programmieren. Das ist ein Ergebnis eines neuen Berichts der gemeinnützigen Organisation Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), die an KI-Sicherheit arbeitet.
Doch das ist noch nicht einmal der spannendste Aspekt des Berichts. So liefert METR darin auch eine Aktualisierung einer sehr bekannten Zeithorizont-Grafik der Organisation, die häufig fehlinterpretiert wird. METR bewertet darin die KI-Modelle, indem die Organisation sie eine große Anzahl an Aufgaben ausführen lässt, die jeweils zuvor auch von Menschen erledigt werden konnten. Der Schwierigkeitsgrad jeder Aufgabe wurde daran gemessen, wie lange die menschlichen Tester:innen für deren Erledigung benötigten – und anschließend wurden die Modelle anhand des Zeitumfangs der Aufgaben bewertet, die sie bewältigen konnten. Die entsprechende Grafik zeigte, dass sich KI-Systeme in den vergangenen Jahren rasch verbesserten – alle vier Monate verdoppelte sich die Länge der Aufgaben, die Spitzenmodelle erfolgreich bewältigen konnten.
Die Schwierigkeit, die Ergebnisse von KI-Modellen zu überprüfen
Die aktualisierte Grafik deckt jetzt weitere Aufgaben mit ab: einige, für die Menschen schätzungsweise weitaus länger benötigen als für die aus der ursprünglichen Untersuchungsreihe, und andere, die offener gestaltet sind. Eine der derzeit größten Fragen im Bereich KI ist, inwieweit sich Fortschritte bei „überprüfbaren“ Tests auf Aufgaben übertragen lassen, bei denen Erfolg oder Misserfolg schwerer zu messen sind. Denn: Die Menschheit weiß, wie sie neuronalen Netzen beibringt, überprüfbare Aufgaben zu lösen. Forscher:innen lassen die Systeme eine Aufgabe viele Male versuchen, stärken dabei die Bereiche im neuronalen Netzwerk, die zum Erfolg beitrugen, und schwächen diejenigen, die zu Fehlschlägen führen. Daher sind KI-Systeme mittlerweile so gut in den Bereichen Programmierung und Mathematik – zwei Aufgabengebiete, in denen sich automatisch feststellen lässt, ob eine Lösung stimmt oder nicht.

articles.title: Trump doesn’t want US data centres built in Canada
articles.text:
US President Donald Trump seems to be unhappy that US hyperscalers want to build in Canada.
On Friday, Trump threatened to put “a tremendous tax” on US companies that build data centres outside of their home country. It’s not yet clear how serious the proposal was, or how he’d enforce it.
Trump’s threat could throw a wrench in Alberta’s plan to attract $100 billion in AI data-centre buildout, as well as the broader efforts to expand compute capacity across Canada. The largest developers are in the US; companies like Anthropic, Meta, and Microsoft have huge, multi-billion-dollar Canadian projects in the works. Many more have signed on to Canada’s responsible data centre development framework, signalling some intention to build in the country.
A spokesperson for Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told BetaKit in a statement that the province is aware of Trump’s threat but is waiting to see what happens. The spokesperson added that Alberta will keep working with the feds and its US partners “to make sure North America leads on AI, together.”
Aperture AI CEO Jaxson Khan, also a Munk School senior fellow and former federal policy advisor, said he’d be surprised if Trump’s comment had any major impact.
“I think this will blow over eventually after some further advocacy from the big tech giants themselves to the Trump administration,” Khan said.
Khan also pointed out that Trump just lost control of Congress in the midterm elections, where many data centre projects were also voted down. As the US sours on data centres, Trump’s threat appears to be an attempt to stop US companies from getting any funny ideas about looking for a friendlier development climate.
Alex Riehl, 
Ottawa Staff Writer

The stock market bump from Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia on Monday appears to be short-lived. Big tech firms, all three main US stock market indices, and the TSX are continuing last week’s slump. After its public-market-debut surge, Anthropic had been trading below its IPO price of $83 USD per share; however, it nearly recovered that price tag prior to market close on Wednesday.
Changes to Bill C-22
The Senate’s defence committee has been considering amendments to the Lawful Access Act this week after hearing some pretty major concerns from tech and civil advocates that the bill could increase surveillance and weaken encryption. Advocates were happy that the Senate strengthened the bill’s definition of systemic vulnerability but weren’t pleased that a motion to curb metadata retention failed.
Vocal C-22 critic and Tailscale CEO Avery Pennarun told BetaKit that the Senate has made “some meaningful improvements” to the Act, but said he is still disappointed that measures that compel some companies to collect more information than they normally would haven’t been addressed. Josh Tabish, of tech industry advocacy group Chamber of Progress, said it’s now a question of whether the Minister of Public Safety “takes the win,” or rejects the amendments to “pass his own version of the bill when it comes back to the House.”
You’re the show
Google has filed a patent for a product that would take user information and create a personalized, AI-generated TV channel filled with “shows” starring the user, as well as customized advertisements, according to 404 Media. Finally, you can be a Blade Runner. What was the moral of that again?

articles.title: Why Y Combinator is backing fewer African startups
articles.text:
Four years after African founders made up roughly one in 17 companies in a Y Combinator batch, the continent has become a footnote at Demo Day. The reasons say as much about how YC has changed as about African tech.
In early-2022, Y Combinator’s Winter batch included 24 African startups, 18 of them from Nigeria. For the first time, an African country ranked third in a YC cohort, behind only the United States (US) and India. Lagos founders talked about the accelerator as a rite of passage, and the Paystack exit to Stripe made the path look repeatable.
Indeed, Disrupt Africa wrote articles around that time about the “cult of Y Combinator”, and the rave reviews the programme received from founders that participated in it.
That moment did not last. By Winter 2023 the African count had fallen to three, and Winter 2024 again admitted just three. Africa’s share of a batch had shrunk from about six per cent at the peak to around one per cent by Winter 2024. A search of the YC website for African startups for the 12 batches since then returns the message “sorry, no matching companies found”.
The pullback, however, is not a single decision made in San Francisco. It is the product of three things moving at once – a YC that has changed what it wants, an African funding market that cooled faster than most, and a portfolio record that has made the case for Africa harder to argue.
The numbers: from 24, to a handful, to none
YC’s African intake rose fast in the remote era and fell faster when it ended. The accelerator went fully remote from Summer 2020, ballooned its batches, and African founders who could never have relocated to San Francisco for three months suddenly could apply from Lagos or Nairobi. The Winter 2021 batch had ten African startups; Winter 2022 had 24.
Then came the correction. YC cut its Summer 2022 cohort to 240 companies from 414, citing the downturn and a changed venture market, and only eight African startups made it. Winter 2023 admitted three. Winter 2024 admitted four again – Nigerian fintechs Cleva and Miden, Kenyan travel-tech startup Triply, and Zimbabwe’s Ocular AI, out of 260 companies picked from more than 27,000 applications. There have been none since.
Across 14 years the picture is lopsided. YC has backed roughly 100 African startups since Wave in 2012, about two per cent of a portfolio of more than 4,600 companies. Nigeria accounts for around 40 per cent of them, Egypt about 15 per cent, and Kenya about 14 per cent, and more than half are fintechs. In other words, the surge in 2021 and 2022 was the anomaly, not the decline.
YC changed first
The biggest reason fewer African startups get in is that YC now wants something different, and wants it in San Francisco. Three shifts matter most.
The first is a return to physical programmes. Summer 2022 opened with an in-person kickoff, the first since Winter 2020. The programme now runs mainly on YC’s San Francisco campus for three months. For a founder in Accra or Kigali, that means a US visa, a quarter away from customers and staff, and San Francisco rents paid from a pre-seed budget. The remote years removed those costs; the return to campus put them back.
In addition, the type of company YC accepts has changed. Recent batches are dominated by AI companies selling to other businesses. In Spring 2026, 62 per cent of the cohort was B2B, and the Summer 2026 batch was focused on infrastructure for AI agents, with consumer companies at about five per cent. African YC alumni were overwhelmingly fintech and consumer-facing marketplaces built around local market gaps. That profile now sits outside what YC is hunting for.
In the meantime, YC raising the size of its cheque has set a higher bar, especially for African ventures. Its standard deal is now US$500,000 – US$125,000 for seven per cent, plus a US$375,000 uncapped SAFE. Companies must also incorporate in Delaware. A larger cheque on an uncapped note is a bet on US-scale outcomes, which raises the bar for businesses whose ceiling is set by Nigerian or Kenyan purchasing power.
YC did move to four batches a year in 2025, with smaller cohorts and more application windows. That gives African founders more shots, but it has not yet shown up as a visible rebound in African admissions. As previously mentioned, there have been none in that time.
Africa’s own downturn
The African side of the story made YC’s retreat easier. Startup funding on the continent fell by 27.8 per cent to US$2.4 billion in 2023, and a further 53.5 per cent in 2024, to US$1.12 billion.
When it recovered in 2025, to US$1.6 billion over the course of the year – note, 2026 is likely to be similar to this – the money went mostly to large rounds. The recovery has been real, but it has not been a seed-stage recovery. Average Series A and B cheques grew, while investors backed fewer companies. For YC, whose model depends on a deep pool of follow-on seed and Series A investors, that matters. A Demo Day company needs someone to lead its next round, and fewer global funds were writing early cheques into Lagos or Nairobi.
Currency made it worse. The naira lost most of its value against the dollar after Nigeria’s 2023 reforms, and Egypt’s pound was devalued repeatedly. A startup earning in local currency but valued in dollars watched its revenue shrink in the metric YC investors care about. Nigeria, which supplied 18 of the 24 African companies at the 2022 peak, took the hardest hit.
The portfolio record has not helped either. Of roughly 100 African YC companies, the ones that returned real capital or reached meaningful scale are a short list – Paystack, Flutterwave, Wave, Nomba and Reliance Health. Most of the rest are subscale, or shut down. Paystack’s US$200 million sale to Stripe in 2020 remains the benchmark exit, but it is six years old. At least five YC-backed African startups are formally inactive in YC’s directory.
What fills the gap
Fewer YC slots cost African founders more than US$500,000. The YC badge worked as a signal that let a first-time founder in Lagos raise from US investors who had never heard of them. Briter Bridges counted about US$1.3 billion in follow-on funding raised by YC’s African portfolio by 2021. Local alternatives can match the cheque, but not yet the network.
They are trying. Iyin Aboyeji’s Future Africa launched Accelerate Africa, openly pitched as a home-grown answer to YC. It takes no equity on entry and may invest US$250,000 to US$500,000 after due diligence. Madica writes up to US$200,000 on a SAFE, Katapult Africa invests US$150,000 to US$500,000 in agri-, food- and climate-tech, and Antler runs residencies in Nairobi and Lagos. Google’s equity-free Africa programme drew nearly 2,600 applicants for 15 places in 2026.
The broader accelerator map is shrinking, though. Techstars closed its Lagos programme in late 2024 after two cohorts, and the Founders Factory Africa venture studio shut in 2025 after its Mastercard Foundation partnership ended. The founders YC turns away are competing for a smaller set of local seats.
There is a quieter shift too. A growing number of YC’s African alumni now invest or build locally, and YC has kept supporting its earlier bets. In 2025 it took part in follow-on rounds for Nigerian food-delivery startup Chowdeck’s Series A and Egyptian grocery company Breadfast. YC is still in Africa. It is just backing what it already owns rather than buying new tickets.
A question of fit
Underneath the cyclical story is a structural one. YC’s model rewards companies that grow fast and reach liquidity within a decade. That works for payments, which is why Africa’s YC winners are almost all fintech startups. It fits poorly with the sectors where the continent’s infrastructure gaps are largest, such as energy, agri-tech, e-health, logistics, and last-mile delivery, which need longer runways, heavier regulation and less obvious exits.
There are reasons the numbers could tick up. Four batches a year means four chances rather than two, and smaller cohorts of roughly 100 to 125 companies may favour founders who were crowded out of the old twice-yearly rush. African teams building AI tools for global business customers fit YC’s current thesis far better than the marketplace startups of 2021. And the African funding market has been recovering in 2025 and 2026, even if the money is skewing late-stage.
The Fall 2026 Demo Day on December 2 will be one test of whether any of that is landing. But the more interesting question may run the other way. With local capital deeper, local accelerators more credible, and a generation of YC alumni now writing cheques at home, Africa’s next Paystack may not need Y Combinator at all. Whether YC can adapt fast enough to find it first is YC’s problem, not Africa’s.

articles.title: What Happens to Your Returned Gadget? The Hidden Journey of Electronics Returns
articles.text:
You return a laptop that “just stopped working”. The shop scans the box, hands over a refund and you walk out feeling lighter. Two weeks later, where is that laptop?
Most of us never think about it. But what happens next decides whether the thing gets a second life or ends up in a skip bin. It also shapes the price you pay for new gear, how fair warranty decisions are, and how much e-waste Australia produces. Here’s the journey, step by step.
Why a returned electronic isn’t like a returned jumper
Behind every returned gadget is a process of paperwork, tracking and decisions that most shoppers never see
A jumper goes back on the rack. A laptop doesn’t. Someone has to confirm the serial number, check whether the fault is real, wipe your data, reset the firmware and decide if the battery is safe to ship. Skip any of those and the retailer either resells a dud or throws away a perfectly good machine.
That’s why businesses that sell tech at any scale often bring in dedicated electronics returns management services to handle the messy middle: RMA intake, inspection, functional testing and the call on what happens next. It’s a model that suits retailers, brands and integrators alike, because the work is repetitive, technical and easy to get wrong when it’s squeezed in between everything else a warehouse does.
The trouble is that returns don’t arrive labelled. A “faulty” phone might have a dead battery, a software glitch or a cracked screen from last Tuesday’s drop. Each one leads to a different outcome.
Your rights come first
Before any of that, there’s the law. Under the Australian Consumer Law guarantees, a major problem with a product entitles you to a repair, replacement or refund, and you get to choose the refund. Signs saying “no refunds” are unlawful. Changing your mind, on the other hand, isn’t covered unless the store’s own policy says so.
For the retailer, that puts pressure on record keeping. If you claim a defect, they need to show whether a technician found a genuine fault or “no fault found”. Clean notes and photos protect both sides.
There’s another wrinkle: a manufacturer’s warranty isn’t the final word on your rights. Australian Consumer Law can still protect you after that warranty expires, which is why extended warranties aren’t always worth the extra money. A retailer can’t automatically dismiss a legitimate fault just because the warranty period has ended.
The inspection bench: test, grade, decide
Once your gadget lands at the returns bench, it follows a fairly standard path. The serial number is logged. The device is reset and put through a functional test. Any damage gets photographed. Then comes the verdict, usually one of these:
- No fault found
- Genuine defect, covered by warranty
- Out of warranty
- Customer damage
- Approved credit or replacement
Working units then get a simple grade. Grade A looks like new. Grade B has light cosmetic wear. Grade C works fine but shows its age. Those grades drive the price, and the price drives whether anyone bothers to rescue the device at all.
Not every step is cheap. Testing takes a technician’s time, and a lithium battery that’s swollen or damaged needs careful handling. That cost is real, and it’s the reason some retailers are tempted to write returns off. It’s a bad habit.
Resell, refurbish or recycle?
Where the gadget goes next depends on what the bench found.
Working and barely touched? It may be sold as open-box stock. Faulty but fixable? It heads for repair and comes back as a refurbished unit, the kind of phone you now see on shelves at big Australian retailers. Beyond repair? Salvageable parts come out, and the rest goes to a certified recycler.
Reuse beats recycling almost every time. Keeping electronics in use for longer reduces the demand for new devices and the raw materials, energy and resources needed to manufacture them. A gadget that can be repaired and resold still has plenty of value, making refurbishment a better option than breaking it down for parts.
The problem stretches well beyond Australia. Globally, electronic waste is growing much faster than recycling efforts can keep up. According to Clean Up Australia, the world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, with that figure expected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030. Those numbers make a strong case for extending the life of electronics before they become waste.
Fair warning: refurbishing isn’t free, and not every model is worth the effort. Older, low-value devices often cost more to fix than they sell for. A good returns process makes that call device by device instead of defaulting to the bin.
The e-waste bit we can’t ignore
Australia generates about 500,000 tonnes of e-waste a year, according to the federal national waste report as covered by ABC News in February 2025. That’s roughly 20kg per person, against a global average of about 7kg. About half was recycled in 2022, and only 35 per cent of the valuable materials were recovered. The same report projects a rise of nearly 30 per cent, to 657,000 tonnes, by 2030.
Our own habits don’t help. Tech Guide has already looked at hoarding old devices, and TechCollect figures cited there show only 33 per cent of people take e-waste to a designated drop-off.
Returns sit upstream of all that. A working laptop that’s tested, graded and resold never becomes a statistic. One that’s written off as “too hard” does.
What to do next
If you’re a shopper, keep your receipt and packaging, back up and wipe your data, photograph the fault, and name the consumer guarantees if you’re knocked back. You’ll be surprised how often that settles it.
The same preparation matters if you’re selling a working device instead of returning a faulty one. Knowing what to check before buying or selling a smartphone can help you avoid losing personal data, overlooking a hidden fault or accepting less than the device is worth. A little preparation can make its next life much easier.
If you run an online store or sell tech for a living, treat returns as a proper flow, not an afterthought. Track failure modes so you can spot a dodgy batch early, and route working units back into resale quickly. That’s where most of the value, and most of the e-waste, is decided.
Where it all lands
Every returned gadget ends up somewhere, and the bench decides where. A few minutes of testing and an honest grade can turn a “faulty” laptop into someone else’s bargain, or into a pile of parts headed for landfill. It’s a choice, and it gets made long before most of us ask where our old gear went.

articles.title: PlayStation Plus : les 3 jeux offerts en décembre 2026
articles.text:
Nous sommes bientôt au mois de décembre et Sony a dévoilé, ce mercredi 25 novembre sur le PlayStation Blog, l’ultime fournée de jeux proposés aux abonnés PlayStation Plus en 2026. Une fois ajoutés à votre bibliothèque, les titres ne sont jouables qu’avec un abonnement actif.
L’abonnement PlayStation Plus est obligatoire pour jouer en ligne à la plupart des jeux sur PS4 et sur PS5. Il existe trois formules : Essential (9,99 € par mois), Extra (15,99 € par mois) et Premium (18,99 € par mois).
Les jeux dans le PS Plus en décembre 2026
Trois jeux seront offerts à partir du mardi 1er décembre avec toutes les formules de l’abonnement PlayStation Plus :
- Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3+4 (PS4, PS5)
- Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 (PS4, PS5)
- Amnesia: The Bunker (PS4)
Vous pourrez les ajouter à votre bibliothèque jusqu’au lundi 4 janvier.
Sony se montre moins généreux qu’à Noël dernier : en décembre 2025, les abonnés avaient eu droit à cinq jeux, contre trois habituellement. Cette année, la sélection de fin d’année s’en tient au rythme ordinaire.
Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3+4
Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 3 et Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater 4, sortis en 2001 et 2002, reviennent dans une compilation de remakes parue en juillet 2025, avec davantage de skateurs, de skateparks et de figures. L’éditeur de skatepark permet en prime de créer ses propres objectifs et de les partager avec des amis.
Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2
Dans le jeu de rôle et d’action Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, sorti en 2016, on crée son propre personnage et on explore Conton City pour remplir des missions en compagnie des héros emblématiques de la saga culte.
Amnesia: The Bunker
Comme son nom l’indique, Amnesia: The Bunker se déroule dans un bunker, un lieu particulièrement oppressant, théâtre d’une expérience flippante. Grâce à des éléments générés de manière aléatoire, chaque partie est différente et c’est au joueur, courageux, de s’adapter.

articles.title: Nexent Capital launches $1B fund focused on AI & data centres investments
articles.text:
Nexent Capital launches $1B fund focused on AI & data centres investments
The fund will deploy the capital in various modes such as private equity, credit and public equity.
Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, a financial services firm, has launched Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting $1 billion in capital commitments for investments in quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy. The fund can be expanded up to a $1.6 billion hard cap.
According to a company statement, the fund is structured as an Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM)-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund (QIF), which will serve as the master fund. A GIFT City-based, IFSCA-regulated Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) will act as its feeder.
Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the fund's ADGM-based manager, with the company progressing towards authorisation from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority (FSRA).
The statement said Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I will deploy capital across five areas: infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets; private credit and structured capital; special-situations M&A; growth equity and PIPEs; and liquid, public equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain.
The Fund has an anchor commitment of $20 million from the Tyagi family office and line of sight to an identified pipeline of quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy projects across North America and India, including data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform.
On the launch, Adesh Tyagi, Managing Partner, Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited, said, “AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure—power, land, and compute—that most capital isn’t positioned to finance at the scale or speed this moment demands. Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I is designed to meet that gap directly, giving institutional and family-office investors a disciplined way to back the infrastructure and energy assets that will underpin the next decade of AI growth.”
The statement said, the launch comes as global investors increasingly look to deploy capital into the physical infrastructure underpinning AI growth—power generation, data centers, and advanced energy systems — and as GIFT City and the Abu Dhabi Global Market continue to develop as complementary gateways for structuring cross-border alternative investment vehicles.

articles.title: Steam intègre une solution de paiement solution 100% européenne, mais il y a un mais
articles.text:
La solution de remboursement entre amis Wero, concurrent de sumeria (anciennement Lydia) et remplaçant de Paylib, est en train de passer un cap pour devenir un peu plus que ça. Alors qu’on attend encore le paiement en magasin aux alentours de la fin 2027, la plateforme s’invite sur Steam, le magasin en ligne numéro du jeu PC.
Un utilisateur allemand de Reddit a repéré la nouveauté, et la version française de Steam l’intègre d’ores et déjà dans les options de paiement, nous avons pu le vérifier par nous-mêmes.
Comment utiliser Wero pour payer sur Steam
Pour se lancer, rien de plus simple. Ils vous suffit de changer votre méthode de paiement. Dans les logos proposant les diverses méthodes, Wero s’est désormais invité. L’option est disponible à la fois sur PC et sur l’application Android.
Une fois Wero sélectionné, la suite des opérations peut être un peu désarçonnante. En effet, vous n’avez aucune information à remplir directement dans Steam, si c n’est l’adresse de facturation. C’est une fois l’achat validé que s’ouvre une nouvelle fenêtre vous redirigeant vers Nuvei, un partenaire de Wero (on y reviendra plus bas dans cet article).
Là, vous devez sélectionner votre banque, puis scanner un QR code avec votre smartphone ou votre tablette. Un processus un peu lourd donc, qui oblige tout de même à avoir deux appareils différents.
Quelles sont les banques compatibles ?
Toutes les banques ne sont pas encore disponibles. Il existe une liste bien précise que voici :
- Banque populaire
- Banque transatlantique
- BNP Paribas
- BRED Banque populaire
- bunq
- Caisse d’Epargne Grand Est Europe
- CIC
- Crédit Mutuel
- Hello bank! France
- La Banque Postale
- Monabanq
- SBE Banque populaire
- Société Générale (accès limité pour le moment)
Wero précise également que d’autres banques seront bientôt prises ne charge :
- Caisse d’Epargne
- Nickel
- Revolut
- Crédit Agricole
- Crédit Mutuel Arkéa
- LCL
- Banque Populaire
- N26
Un lancement pas si souverain que ça
Comme expliqué plus haut, Wero passe par Nuvei, partenaire privilégié de l’opération pour le déploiement de la solution de paiement un peu partout. Quel est le problème ? Vous passez par un partenaire nord-américain, basé au Canada. Cela n’est pas forcément un problème en soi, mais, étant donné que Wero se pense comme une alternative à l’américain PayPal, cette précision technique vient légèrement contrarier cette promesse d’un paiement souverain.

articles.title: Après une crise historique sans précédent, Microsoft a déclenché le Code Rouge
articles.text:
La panne mondiale qui a affecté Microsoft durant 24 heures a laissé des traces. En réponse, le géant américain lance son initiative Code Rouge.
Souvenez-vous. Les 12 et 13 novembre derniers, Microsoft expérimentait une des pires pannes de son histoire, qui touchait à la fois Outlook et Microsoft 365. Une panne mondiale qui avait affecté autant les entreprises que les services publics ou bien les hôpitaux. Autant dire que le géant américain ne veut pas voir l'événement se répéter, et commence à s'organiser en conséquence.
Microsoft lance l'initiative « Code Rouge » après la panne de la mi-novembre
Microsoft vient de lancer sa nouvelle initiative dite « Code Rouge », selon une information de Reuters. Celle-ci a pour ambition de revoir totalement la stratégie de prévention et de gestion des pannes majeures chez Microsoft, après les événements de mi-novembre qui ont représenté un véritable échec.
« Le niveau "Code Rouge" signifie qu’il s’agit de la tâche la plus prioritaire pour notre équipe » a expliqué dans un mémo interne le président de Microsoft 365 Core, Jason Henderson. Il faut dire qu'il y a sûrement du travail à faire de ce côté. Car dans une autre note, la vice-présidente de Microsoft en charge de M365 Core et de Work IQ, Amanda Silver, explique que les équipes d'intervention ont dû échanger plus de 11 000 messages sur près de 11 conversations Teams afin de gérer la panne.
Les agents IA pourront à l'avenir aider à répondre plus vite à l'urgence d'une panne
Ils ont ainsi eu beaucoup de mal, du fait de la dispersion des systèmes de suivi internes, a avoir une version cohérente permettant de juger les hypothèses et les décisions à prendre. Pour rappel, il a finalement été découvert que c'était un bug passé inaperçu pendant plus de trois mois qui était l'origine de la panne mondiale.
Cinq axes de travail ont ainsi été dégagés par Amanda Silver, dans le cadre de ce « Code Rouge ». L'objectif est pouvoir résoudre les futures pannes qui pourraient arriver en moins d'une heure. Des agents IA devront par ailleurs être déployés dans ces situations pour aider à une analyse plus rapide des données de la part des ingénieurs. Suffisant pour ne pas voir les déboires se répéter ?
Source : Reuters

articles.title: GTA 6 : les réglages graphiques cachés sur PS5, PS5 Pro et Xbox ont fuité
articles.text:
Sur console, GTA 6 n’affiche aucun menu graphique : le jeu de Rockstar, sorti le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series, tourne à 30 images par seconde partout, sans dire ce que chaque machine sacrifie.
Un dataminer surnommé Tex2, qui fouille les fichiers du jeu, a trouvé la liste de ces réglages console par console. Son message sur le forum GTAForums a été supprimé depuis, mais le site MP1st l’a recopié ce mercredi 25 novembre.
Black Friday : la TV Samsung Micro RGB 65″ R95H perd 1 000 € et s’affiche à 1 999 € au lieu de 2 999 €, du 21 au 30 novembre. Grâce à sa technologie Micro RGB, il délivre « un niveau de précision et de richesse colorimétrique inédit ».
Premier enseignement : la PS5 et la Xbox Series X utilisent exactement les mêmes réglages. Si la Xbox Series X tient mieux ses 30 images par seconde que la PS5, la différence vient donc du matériel.
La PS5 Pro seule avec des ombres en ray tracing
La PS5 Pro est la seule console à calculer les ombres en ray tracing, une technique qui simule le trajet de la lumière pour des ombres plus réalistes. Elle passe aussi l’éclairage global, c’est-à-dire la façon dont la lumière rebondit sur les surfaces, en « High » au lieu de « Medium ».

|---|---|---|---|
| Illumination globale ( globalIlluminationQuality) | Haut | Moyen | Moyen | 
| Qualité BVH ( bvhQuality) | Ultra | Haut | Faible |

| Échelle de flou de mouvement ( motionBlurScale) | 1.5 | Absent (par défaut) | Absent (par défaut) | 
Pourtant, elle reste bloquée à 30 images par seconde, et aucun mode sans ray tracing ne permet d’échanger ces effets contre de la fluidité. Rockstar l’a justifié par le processeur de la PS5 Pro, trop juste pour faire tourner la simulation du jeu plus vite. Et comme la PS5 et la Series X mélangent déjà réglages moyens et élevés, un mode 60 images par seconde obligerait à les baisser encore, avec une image nettement moins belle.
La Xbox Series S réduit aussi la foule dans les rues
La Xbox Series S, la moins puissante des quatre consoles, coupe plus large : textures, cheveux et eau perdent un cran. Surtout, la densité de piétons et de voitures passe de « High » à « Medium », comme la physique et le comportement des personnages.

articles.title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling
articles.text:
Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models, where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block.
However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs.
Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute.
This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer.
Reactor, a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post.
Improving throughput with NVFP4
NVIDIA RTX Blackwell has lower BF16 matmul throughput compared to the data center variants. While data center workloads are bounded by softmax (FlashAttention4 tries to solve this through pipelining and exp2 emulation), the NVIDIA RTX Blackwell is bounded by MMA on BF16 Attention. Due to higher TFLOP/s for NVFP4, throughput can be improved to achieve better performance.
Attention compute
The general attention computation and the two core matrix multiplications it involves are:
- Query-Key matrix multiplication (\(QK\)): The first matmul in attention, \(QKᵀ\), where \(Q\) contains query vectors and \(K\) contains key vectors. It computes the attention scores used by softmax.
- Attention-Weight Value matrix multiplication (\(PV\)): The second matmul in attention, \(PV\), where \(P\) contains softmax-derived attention weights and \(V\) contains value vectors. It combines the value vectors according to their attention weights to produce the output. In the tiled attention kernel discussed here, \(P\) contains unnormalized softmax weights, and final normalization is applied after the output has been accumulated across tiles (similar to FlashAttention).
How SageAttention3 accelerates attention using NVFP4
SageAttention3 is a native NVFP4 attention mechanism specifically designed for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell streaming multiprocessor (SM) 120. It performs both \(QK\) and \(PV\) using NVFP4. Its primary innovation came from performing two-level scaling for \(P\).
NVFP4 quantization generates two tensors: an NVFP4 data tensor and an FP8 scaling tensor. Because softmax outputs are bound to a narrow [0, 1] range, they can underutilize the NVFP4 dynamic range, resulting in accuracy degradation. Two-level scaling addresses this by first normalizing the values to fully utilize dynamic range before quantizing the result.
SageAttention3 cooperative thread array stable state design
The SageAttention3 cooperative thread array (CTA) design is as follows:
- The CTA uses four producer warps and eight consumer warps. For each N128 tile, consumers execute \(QK\), softmax and probability quantization, and \(PV\) in sequence.
- While consumers perform softmax, scaling, and quantization, tensor-core activity has gaps. Video 1 illustrates this sequential execution.
# Current SageAttention 3 CTA Execution (per N tile)
# CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer)
For each N tile:
    # 1. Producer Role: Data Loading
    # Q is loaded once per M tile
    AsyncLoad(Q)
    # K, V, Scale Factors, and delta_s use 3-stage async TMA pipeline
    AsyncLoad(K, V, Scale_Factors, delta_s)
    # 2. Consumer Role: Dependency Chain (Serial Execution)
    # 8 Consumer warps (256-thread MMA collective)
    # A. QK Computation
    Execute_QK_OMMA()
    Apply_delta_s_correction()
    # B. Softmax & Quantization
    Apply_Masking()
    Execute_Online_Softmax()
    Execute_NVFP4_Probability_Quantization()
    # C. PV Computation
    Execute_PV_OMMA()
    # Note: Execution is strictly serial per N tile
    # No overlapping or independent fragments in flight
The following observations can be drawn from this CTA design and the parallel thread execution (PTX) and instruction set architecture (ISA) for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs:
First, TMA Loads are bound to Shapes of 128×128, not utilizing the entire shape would mean underutilizing our GPU bandwidth.
Second, the NVIDIA Blackwell RTX OMMA operation remains constrained to m16, n8, k64 (where m and n represent LHS/RHS free dimensions, while k is the contraction axis), as specified by the PTX instruction mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X.m16n8k64.
To cover the full contraction dimension of k=128, two MMA instructions with k=64 must be issued. The current CTA design issues these instructions for \(QK\) in succession. Because MMA execution is synchronous, the issuing consumer warps wait for completion before proceeding to online softmax and intermediate quantization.
This means that the operations within the stable loop are sequentially pipelined. There is a large gap in MMA activity, as there is no compute scheduled on the tensor cores. The warps are busy computing the softmax, scaling, and quantization operations.
Video 1 shows the attention-kernel timeline, including sequential \(QK\) matrix multiplication, softmax, and \(PV\) matrix multiplication.
Register constraints
Producer warps use 3,072 registers, and consumer warps use 59,392 registers. The total of 62,464 registers occupies approximately 95.3% of the SM’s register capacity. This leaves little room to hold an additional score tile while processing the current tile.
Optimized CTA design
The design retains four producer warps, eight consumer warps, and complete N128 K/V tile loads. The change is in how consumers compute and store attention scores. Each N128 score tile is split into two N64 halves, and each occupies a separate register slot.
After one half has been exponentiated and quantized, its score registers are reused to compute the corresponding \(QK\) half of the next tile. This interleaves the next tile’s \(QK\) to work with the current tile’s remaining softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) operations.
The online-softmax state is still updated across the complete N128 score tile before either half is consumed.
Video 2 shows how this schedule fills gaps in tensor-core activity without allocating a second complete score tile.
The following pseudocode illustrates the optimized schedule, including the initial score computation, steady-state register reuse, and processing of the final tile.
Unlike the original design, which completes \(QK\), softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) sequentially for each N128 tile, the optimized design splits the score tile into two N64 register slots. When half is quantized, its score registers are reused for the next tile’s \(QK\) computation. This allows work from adjacent tiles to be interleaved without allocating a second complete score tile, while retaining the same four producer warps and eight consumer warps.
# Optimized CuTe DSL CTA Execution
# N64/N64 Cross-Block Ping-Pong
# CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer)
#
# All 8 consumer warps remain active.
# Each N128 score tile is represented by two N64 register slots:
#   ScoreSlot0 = columns [0:64]
#   ScoreSlot1 = columns [64:128]
# 1. Producer Role: Three-Stage Data Pipeline
# Q and its scale factors are loaded once per M128 query tile.
AsyncLoad(Q, Q_ScaleFactors)
# Producer warps continuously prefetch complete N128 K/V tiles.
# K and V retain separate three-stage pipelines.
for N_tile in traversal_order:
    AsyncPrefetch(
          K[N_tile],
          V[N_tile],
          K_ScaleFactors[N_tile],
          V_ScaleFactors[N_tile],
          delta_s[N_tile],
      )
# 2. Consumer Prologue: Produce the First Score Tile
CurrentTile = First_N_Tile()
# Compute one complete QK score tile as two symmetric N64 halves.
ScoreSlot0 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[CurrentTile, 0:64], delta_s[CurrentTile, 0:64],)
ScoreSlot1 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[CurrentTile, 64:128], delta_s[CurrentTile, 64:128],)
  # 3. Consumer Steady State: Cross-Block Ping-Pong
  while HasNextTile(CurrentTile):
      NextTile = Next_N_Tile(CurrentTile)
      # Calculate the maximum, online-softmax update, and output rescaling
      # jointly across the complete current N128 score tile.
      Update_Online_Softmax_State(ScoreSlot0, ScoreSlot1, OnlineMax, OnlineSum,)
      Rescale_Output_Accumulator(Output, OnlineMax)
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------
      # Process current N64 half 0.
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------
      # Convert the current score half into packed NVFP4 probabilities.
      Probability0 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot0)
      # ScoreSlot0 is now dead. Reuse those same registers for QK belonging
      # to the next N tile-no second complete score allocation is needed.
      ScoreSlot0 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[NextTile, 0:64], delta_s[NextTile, 0:64],)
      # Accumulate the current tile's first probability half into the output.
      Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability0, V[CurrentTile, 0:64],)
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------
      # Process current N64 half 1.
      # ---------------------------------------------------------------
      Probability1 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot1)
      # Reuse the second dead score slot for the next tile.
      ScoreSlot1 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[NextTile, 64:128], delta_s[NextTile, 64:128],)
      Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability1, V[CurrentTile, 64:128],)
      # ScoreSlot0 and ScoreSlot1 now contain the complete score for NextTile,
      # while PV for CurrentTile has finished.
      CurrentTile = NextTile
  # 4. Pipeline Drain: Consume the Final Score Tile
  # There is no following tile, so the final score slots are not overwritten
  # with another QK operation.
  Update_Online_Softmax_State(ScoreSlot0, ScoreSlot1, OnlineMax, OnlineSum,)
  Rescale_Output_Accumulator(Output, OnlineMax)
  Probability0 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot0)
  Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability0, V[CurrentTile, 0:64],)
  Probability1 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot1)
  Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability1, V[CurrentTile, 64:128],)
  # 5. Epilogue
  Output = Output / OnlineSum
  AsyncStore_BF16(Output)
NVFP4 attention kernel integration latency results
Reactor evaluated the optimized kernel on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU with 96 GB of memory (SM120), measuring its impact across four world-model workloads.
Attention kernel speedup
To isolate the scheduling optimization, the original and optimized NVFP4 kernels were compared using identical \(Q/K/V\) inputs, packed tensors, and log-sum-exp settings.
| Workload / mask | Original (ms) | Optimized (ms) | Speedup | 
|---|---|---|---|
| LongLive 7,040 / noncausal | 0.75052 | 0.63548 | 1.18x | 
| LongLive 7,040 / causal | 0.44992 | 0.37927 | 1.19x | 
| Synthetic 4,096 / noncausal | 0.28962 | 0.23190 | 1.25x | 
| Synthetic 4,096 / causal | 0.21199 | 0.16087 | 1.32x | 
| Synthetic 8,192 / noncausal | 1.00177 | 0.85648 | 1.17x | 
| Synthetic 8,192 / causal | 0.76466 | 0.46659 | 1.64x | 
| Synthetic 16,384 / noncausal | 3.80862 | 3.25377 | 1.17x | 
| Synthetic 16,384 / causal | 2.20630 | 1.78152 | 1.24x | 
All cases use batch size 1, 24 heads, head dimension 128, and equal query/key lengths. The 7,040-token input was captured from LongLive; the other inputs are synthetic. Core timing excludes Q/K/V quantization and output-stride restoration
Measurements used three fresh processes per implementation, alternating run order, active prewarming, and repeated CUDA-event timing blocks.
End-to-end model inference performance
Reactor integrated this NVFP4 attention kernel into its production serving infrastructure and used it to serve real customer traffic across several models. Table 2 shows the impact on end-to-end model inference latency on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
Latency was measured for the complete model path per video chunk, full generation, or action prediction. The table specifies which attention operations use NVFP4; other attention operations and model weights remain BF16. The terms idle and moving refer to camera scenarios with the same NVFP4 coverage.
For the video-chunk and action-prediction benchmarks, the BF16 baseline uses native cuDNN attention. Timings include quantization, layout conversion, and decoded CPU-frame or action output, but exclude model loading, warmup, networking, queueing, and client pacing.
| Model / scenario | Measured output | Attention using NVFP4 | BF16 E2E latency (s) | NVFP4 E2E latency (s) | Latency reduction | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LongLive | 32 frames 704 × 1280 | Self-attention + cached history | 5.13 | 4.79 | 6.70% | 
| Helios | 33 frames 384 × 640 | 11,280-token self-attention only | 5.94 | 5.84 | 1.70% | 
| Helios | 33 frames 384 × 640 | All self-attention calls | 5.94 | 5.87 | 1.11% | 
| OmniDreams – idle | 8 frames 704 × 1280 | Self-attention + cached history | 0.60 | 0.51 | 14.77% | 
| OmniDreams – moving | 8 frames 704 × 1280 | Self-attention + cached history | 0.60 | 0.51 | 14.95% | 
| Cosmos 3 Nano Policy Droid (pilot) | 32 × 8 action prediction | Dense generator attention only | 1.72 | 1.69 | 1.70% | 
| LongLive (long run) | 1,021 frames 32 chunks | Self-attention + cached history | 162.52 | 151.89 | 6.54% | 
| Helios (long run) | 1,056 frames 32 chunks | Largest self-attention calls only | 190.88 | 187.48 | 1.78% | 
| Helios (long run) | 1,056 frames 32 chunks | All supported self-attention | 190.88 | 188.36 | 1.32% | 
| OmniDreams – idle (long run) | 1,021 frames 128 chunks | Self-attention + cached history | 77.34 | 65.79 | 14.94% | 
| OmniDreams – moving (long run) | 1,021 frames 128 chunks | Self-attention + cached history | 77.77 | 65.95 | 15.20% | 
| OmniDreams – idle (long run) | 2,045 frames 256 chunks | Self-attention + cached history | 155.44 | 131.84 | 15.18% | 
| OmniDreams – moving (long run) | 2,045 frames 256 chunks | Self-attention + cached history | 155.92 | 132.00 | 15.34% | 
Long-run rows measure complete warmed generations through decoded CPU frames, excluding model loading and transport. LongLive and Helios report medians of three independent process runs per arm using eager execution; OmniDreams reports one process per arm/scenario. Latency reductions are calculated from unrounded measurements.
Get started accelerating NVFP4 attention
The scheduling and score-register reuse techniques described in this post improve NVFP4 attention performance on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell. This approach helps accelerate world model inference. The core optimization has been merged into the FlashInfer main branch.
To learn how Reactor integrated this kernel into production to serve real customer traffic, refer to Integrating NVFP4 Attention into Real-Time Models on Reactor.
Ready to get started accelerating NVFP4 attention?
- Clone the FlashInfer main branch with its submodules and follow the source installation guide.
- Integrate the SM120 NVFP4 attention API into supported attention layers in your model on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell, then compare end-to-end latency and output quality against your BF16 baseline.
Acknowledgments
We thank the Reactor team for sharing their measurements and supporting our evaluation of NVFP4 attention across world models.

articles.title: Röntgenlaser-Rekord: Forscher erzeugen Licht kleiner als ein Atom
articles.text:
Energie-Rekord bei Röntgenlasern erzielt: European XFEL in Hamburg übertrifft sich selbst
Erstmals konnten Forscher:innenteams des European XFEL und des DESY an der Forschungsanlage in Hamburg Röntgenlaserblitze mit einer Wellenlänge von etwa 0,04 Nanometern erzeugen und aufrechterhalten. Damit haben sie sich selbst übertroffen und ihren Rekord aus dem Jahr 2020 in den Schatten gestellt.
Laser-Meilenstein: Lichtwellen kleiner als ein Atom
Der European XFEL ist ein Röntgenlaser, der freie Elektronen (FEL, wobei das X für X-ray, also Röntgen steht) statt eines herkömmlichen Lasermediums nutzt. Um die Röntgenblitze zu erzeugen, bringt ein rund 1,7 Kilometer langer Linearbeschleuniger zunächst Elektronenpakete auf nahezu Lichtgeschwindigkeit. Die beschleunigten Elektronenpakete werden dann durch sogenannte Undulatoren auf einen Slalomkurs gezwungen. Das sind tonnenschwere Gerüste, in denen abwechselnd gepolte Magnete sitzen. Bei ihrem Slalomkurs senden die Elektronen Röntgenstrahlung aus; durch die Wechselwirkung der Strahlung mit den Elektronen selbst verstärkt sie sich zu extrem kurzen, intensiven Röntgenblitzen, die für Forschungsexperimente genutzt werden.
Der European XFEL ist eine riesige Maschine – und das nicht nur materiell: Ein Verbund von zwölf Staaten hat diese Anlage für rund 1,5 Milliarden Euro gebaut. Rund 600 Menschen arbeiten fest am XFEL. Am DESY, dem Deutschen Elektronensynchrotron, kümmern sich zusätzlich 250 Menschen um den Elektronen-Beschleuniger – dazu kommen die Gast-Wissenschaftler:innen, die an der Anlage ihre Experimente durchführen.
Die neue Bestmarke habe mit einer Photonenenergie von 30 Kiloelektronenvolt (keV) realisiert werden können, teilten die Forscher:innen mit. Im Jahr 2020 lagen die Parameter bei 0,05 Nanometern und 25 keV. Damit ist die erzeugte Wellenlänge deutlich kürzer als die typischen Abstände zwischen Atomen in Festkörpern. Fragt man nach dem Einsatzzweck solcher ultrakurzen Laserlichtblitze, verweisen die Forscher:innen darauf, jetzt dichte Materialien untersuchen zu können oder schnelle Veränderungen in Experimenten zu erfassen.
Das Team um Frank Brinker und Ye Chen, die den Bereich am Elektronenbeschleuniger in Hamburg leiten, hat über den Meilenstein am XFEL einen Forschungsartikel in der Fachzeitschrift Optica veröffentlicht. Die Arbeit ist somit der Beleg dafür, dass der erzeugte Röntgenstrahl stabil und nutzbar für Experimente ist. Anders Madsen, leitender Wissenschaftler am MID-Instrument am European XFEL und einer der Mitautor:innen der Veröffentlichung, sieht das als Alleinstellungsmerkmal unter den FEL-Anlagen weltweit.
In dem Paper beschreiben die Forscher:innen ihr erfolgreiches Setup: Es gelang dem Team, 800 Blitze pro Sekunde zu erzeugen und diese über eine Strecke von etwa einem Kilometer zu transportieren. Das geschieht in einer sogenannten Strahlführung. Darin schafften es knapp 60 Prozent des extremen Röntgenlichts bis ans Ende dieser Führung. Das ist auf mehrjährige Simulationen der Elektronenstrahldynamik und Beschleunigertests zurückzuführen. Dabei spielen Hohlräume aus Niob, die Energie auf die Elektronen übertragen, und die Undulatoren, also Magnetsysteme, eine entscheidende Rolle.
Röntgenlaserblitze, um Quantenmaterialien zu untersuchen
Die Forscher:innen freuen sich, damit nun den Bereich an möglichen Experimenten erweitern zu können. Sie sehen beispielsweise Untersuchungen von Funktionswerkstoffen, Katalysator- und Quantenmaterialien.
Der Röntgenlaser vom XFEL war erst Anfang dieses Jahres neu gestartet. Vorausgegangen war eine lange Phase von mehreren Monaten für Wartungsarbeiten und für zahlreiche Neuerungen an der Tunnelanlage und an den Experimentierstationen. Der Röntgenlaser selbst liegt größtenteils in Tunneln mindestens sechs Meter tief – stellenweise bis zu 38 Meter – unter der Erde. Insgesamt ist die Anlage 3,4 Kilometer lang und reicht vom DESY-Campus in Hamburg-Bahrenfeld bis in die schleswig-holsteinische Stadt Schenefeld (Kreis Pinneberg). Weltweit gibt es rund 20 solcher Freie-Elektronen-Laser-Anlagen, allerdings unterscheiden sie sich in der Optimierung auf bestimmte Bereiche. Während der European XFEL eine reine Forschungseinrichtung ist, arbeitet das US-Startup Xlight daran, einen FEL für die Chipproduktion zu nutzen.
~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Microsoft confirms authentication issues after November updates
articles.text:
Microsoft has confirmed that customers may experience authentication issues after installing November security updates that address a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability.
Tracked as CVE-2026-118737, this security flaw was found in the Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime and stems from a timing-dependent authentication weakness that unauthenticated attackers can exploit to remotely execute code without user interaction on unpatched systems.
Microsoft says the November security updates represent the first phase of NTLM message-signing improvements, which reduce exposure to relay attacks by ensuring authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing.
However, as Microsoft explained in an updated support document, the new security improvements introduced to address this vulnerability may also cause authentication failures on patched devices.
"Microsoft is aware of compatibility issues affecting some third-party apps and devices, including authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) solutions, and application packaging solutions that use NTLM authentication," it said.
"This issue can occur when such a proxy device does not correctly implement the NTLM protocol. For example, an affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field."
While a fix is not yet available, Microsoft said affected apps and devices return an NTLMSSP_CHALLENGE message with an empty "Target Info List" in network trace signatures or Target Machine fields with "Not Found" values in event logs.
As a temporary workaround, the company advised customers to go through the following procedure on affected systems:
- Set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm REG_DWORD registry value under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 to 1 (the value used for clients that do not offer SIGN)
- Check whether the affected device or application supports a configuration that uses Kerberos authentication or whether the vendor provides a software or firmware update compatible with the NTLM signing requirements introduced by CVE-2026-118737.
- If neither option is available, contact the device or software vendor to request an update that complies with the NTLM protocol requirements described in 3.1.5.1.2 Client Receives a CHALLENGE_MESSAGE from the Server.
However, Microsoft said the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm registry setting is a short-term solution and may be removed in the future.
"Updating the affected product or using a compatible authentication configuration is the recommended long-term resolution," it noted.
Since it addressed installation issues affecting the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft has also confirmed that this month's security updates are causing Windows activation failures and SQL Server performance issues.
The company is also investigating a known issue that may break printing documents with complex formatting for customers who have installed the latest Windows updates.
