articles.title: Teen helps find girl kidnapped over a year ago after meeting her in Among Us
articles.text:
What just happened? People who try to monitor or restrict communications often don't realize that online video games are also technically chat networks. This oversight usually emerges in discussions about online child safety, but in one recent case, an online friendship led to the rescue of a teenager who had been missing for more than 500 days.
A 39-year-old Oregon man is currently in jail awaiting trial on allegations that he kidnapped and sexually assaulted a teen who was reported missing last year. Police recovered the girl from the man's residence days after she began chatting with a Colorado teen and his mother in the online game Among Us.
While chatting with 16-year-old Landon Tresp in late October, Jenny (an alias), 17, admitted she had run away from home after years of abuse but was now being held against her will in an unknown location in Oregon. She had met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media last May. He told her he was disabled and offered her money for help getting to Oregon.
However, after Harmel picked up Jenny in Utah, he threw away her phone, kept her in the basement of his Oregon home, and forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed while keeping a knife (pictured) under his pillow. Jenny said he became aggressive and abusive and forced her to remove her braces with pliers so she couldn't be identified. She also said she had tried to escape before.
Harmel gave Jenny a phone that couldn't make calls but could access Wi-Fi, which is how she was able to play Among Us. After striking up a friendship with Tresp in the game in mid-October, more than a year after her disappearance, she eventually moved their conversations to Discord, revealed she was being held against her will, and shared links to news stories about her disappearance. She knew what town she was in, but not her exact location.
When Tresp told his mother, 41-year-old Khristina, on Halloween, she immediately jumped into action. The pair later told the BBC that Khristina asked Jenny over video chat to retrieve any documents in the house that might contain her captor's full name. The mom then searched tax and property records and matched photos of Harmel's property from Zillow with Jenny's description.
After contacting Jenny's mother on social media, Khristina received a call from the FBI almost immediately. On November 1, when Harmel next left the residence, Khristina used a video call to guide Jenny out of the building while receiving minute-by-minute updates from police.
Jenny later received medical treatment and remains in daily contact with the Tresps.

articles.title: ShinyHunters Claims Comeback, New Inception Group Rejects Alleged Ties
articles.text:
Someone claiming to represent ShinyHunters has announced the notorious cybercrime group’s alleged return. Separately, the operators of a new extortion campaign named Inception have denied having ties to ShinyHunters.
According to DataBreaches, the return of ShinyHunters was announced in a message posted on the Exploit cybercrime forum. The post came from an account linked to ShinyHunters since 2020.
The message included the address of the new leak site and a new PGP key to authenticate future communications. Its authors also noted that they will not be active on other cybercrime forums and disavowed several hackers who claimed to be members of ShinyHunters.
The post’s authors attempted to establish their identity using a crypto key known to be associated with ShinyHunters, but DataBreaches noted that the original PGP key had reportedly been leaked.
Other threat actors have sought to capitalize on the ShinyHunters name and reputation, and the possibility that the comeback message is the work of impostors cannot be ruled out.
The announcement follows the arrest of several individuals suspected of being involved in ShinyHunters attacks, including a Canada-based cybersecurity expert, a Jordanian national believed to be group leader Rey, as well as a suspect in the Netherlands.
New group Inception
The cybersecurity community has started tracking a new cybercrime group called Inception. Its leak site emerged earlier this month and lists several major US companies, including AMD, PepsiCo, Lucid Motors, Henry Schein, and Cigna Healthcare. The group has leaked hundreds of gigabytes of data allegedly stolen from these companies, but the data’s authenticity has not been independently verified.
According to research conducted by Okta, Inception may involve hackers previously associated with ShinyHunters. Okta has been tracking these hackers since March as O-UNC-053.
Okta says the cybercriminals’ phishing domain registrations dropped in September and October (around the time of the arrests), but activity picked up in November.
The company’s researchers previously saw organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 being listed on the ShinyHunters data leak site. After the ShinyHunters site went offline, they did not see O-UNC-053 victims being listed on any other website until November 16, when companies targeted by the group were named on the Inception website.
“We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the [data leak site] themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor,” Okta said.
Security researcher Dominic Alvieri has also suggested a possible connection between Inception and ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” Alvieri noted.
In a lengthy statement posted on its website, Inception denied having any connection to ShinyHunters.
“[Okta’s] evidence amounts to shared use of commodity services — domain registrars and CDN providers available to anyone — and overlapping targets. Neither constitutes operational linkage. We acknowledge that privately available tooling circulates among independent operators. Shared access to a service does not equate to shared identity,” the hackers wrote, adding, “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.”
ReversingLabs has also monitored Inception’s activities and reported this week that it has uncovered phishing domains suggesting that the cybercriminals may have also targeted companies such as Anthropic, Amazon, Adobe, Nintendo, Netflix, OpenAI, and Tesla. There is no indication that any of them were successfully compromised.
The security firm identified 21 confirmed phishing domains and another 41 associated with the campaign with high confidence.
Related: Last of Five Defendants Sentenced in US Scattered Spider Hacking Case
Related: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database

articles.title: Flipkart CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy to step down next week amid IPO uncertainty
articles.text:
Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above), who steered Flipkart through Walmart’s acquisition in 2018 and helped build it into one of India’s biggest e-commerce companies, is stepping down as chief executive next week after more than 11 years with the company.
On Wednesday, Flipkart said it would announce Krishnamurthy’s successor in the coming weeks, and Chief Product and Technology Officer Balaji Thiagarajan will lead the company until a replacement is found.
A Walmart spokesperson told TechCrunch that Krishnamurthy’s last day at Flipkart will be December 4.
Krishnamurthy joined Flipkart in 2015 from Tiger Global, one of the company’s early investors, and became its CEO in 2017. He remained at the helm after Walmart acquired a controlling stake in the company for $16 billion in 2018.
Under Krishnamurthy, Flipkart said its business grew more than five-fold. The company has more than 500 million registered users and over 1.4 million sellers, including those on Shopsy, its low-cost shopping platform. The company’s marketplace offers over 150 million products across more than 80 categories.
Flipkart has of late moved into newer segments, including quick-commerce through Flipkart Minutes and, more recently, food delivery through a venture called Eat-in by Minutes. The expansion is targeted at Indian consumers who are increasingly turning to quick-delivery services for everything from groceries to electronics.
Thiagarajan joined Flipkart in September last year to lead its product and technology teams. Before that, he had founded Kasu.ai, a Bay Area startup working on AI assistants for corporate finance. He also previously worked at Google, Microsoft, and Uber in senior engineering positions, per his LinkedIn profile.
Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid uncertainty around Flipkart’s IPO. In March, the company moved its headquarters from Singapore to India as part of its preparations to go public, but in May, Walmart reportedly told Flipkart to delay its IPO and focus on becoming profitable first.
Walmart declined to comment beyond its announcement when asked what prompted Krishnamurthy’s departure, and whether the leadership change would affect Flipkart’s IPO plans. Flipkart did not respond to a request for comment.
Founded in 2007 by Sachin and Binny Bansal as an online bookstore, much like its bigger rival Amazon, Flipkart eventually expanded into other categories. Under Krishnamurthy, it has grown into India’s largest online retailer by gross merchandise value, ahead of Amazon.
“Both Flipkart and Walmart are better because of Kalyan. We are grateful for his leadership, the governance he instilled and his many contributions to the company,” Chris Nicholas, president and CEO, Walmart International, said in a statement.

articles.title: Amadores usam IA para encontrar possíveis planetas em dados da NASA
articles.text:
Dois entusiastas da astronomia usaram ferramentas de inteligência artificial (IA) para procurar possíveis planetas fora do Sistema Solar em dados públicos de telescópios da NASA. Trabalhando de forma independente, eles analisaram observações de milhões de estrelas e identificaram sinais que agora serão examinados por pesquisadores.
Os casos foram apresentados pela OpenAI em publicação de seu blog de ciência. Kevin Bond, engenheiro da empresa, usou o Codex para desenvolver uma busca em dados do telescópio espacial Kepler. Já Ethan Byrd, fundador da startup Primitive, recorreu ao Astra para analisar observações de diferentes arquivos astronômicos.
Nenhum dos dois confirmou a existência de novo planeta. Os resultados são candidatos que precisam passar por verificações adicionais, mas mostram como ferramentas de IA podem ajudar pessoas fora da comunidade científica profissional a participar de pesquisas astronômicas.
IA analisou dados de milhares de estrelas
- Bond começou sua investigação com observações de aproximadamente 100 mil estrelas registradas pelo telescópio Kepler, missão da NASA que operou entre 2009 e 2018. Com o Codex, ele comparou métodos de análise já publicados, combinou essas técnicas em programa de busca e testou diferentes versões do código;
- O sistema procurava pequenas quedas recorrentes no brilho das estrelas. Na primeira análise, identificou mais de 200 sinais, incluindo dez associados a planetas que já haviam sido confirmados;
- Dois alvos chamaram a atenção. Um deles, identificado como KIC 5689121, é uma estrela relativamente fria, com aproximadamente metade do tamanho do Sol, localizada na constelação de Lira. O programa encontrou redução de brilho que se repete a cada 13,8 dias;
- Se o fenômeno for provocado por um planeta passando diante da estrela, o objeto teria diâmetro estimado em cerca de 2,4 vezes o da Terra;
- O segundo candidato, KIC 6691030, é uma estrela pouco brilhante no céu do hemisfério norte. Nesse caso, o sinal aparece a cada 4,8 dias e seria compatível com a passagem de um planeta menor que Netuno;
- Um astrônomo do Instituto SETI analisou os dados de maneira independente e identificou os mesmos dois sinais. Segundo a OpenAI, as verificações iniciais foram consideradas promissoras, mas a confirmação das causas das variações pode levar meses ou até anos.
Outro entusiasta analisou dados de 19 milhões de estrelas
A investigação de Ethan Byrd teve escala ainda maior. Ele usou o Astra para planejar duas buscas: uma ampla, voltada à identificação de possíveis exoplanetas, e outra concentrada em estrelas com regiões potencialmente habitáveis.
Para isso, pediu à ferramenta que revisasse métodos científicos publicados, desenvolvesse os programas de busca e realizasse verificações iniciais dos sinais encontrados.
A análise utilizou observações do telescópio TESS, da NASA, e de outros arquivos públicos. No primeiro processamento, a busca identificou 49 candidatos.
O sinal considerado mais promissor foi encaminhado a pesquisadores que trabalham com a missão TESS e aguarda análise mais detalhada. Outros dois candidatos ainda devem ser enviados para avaliação.
Leia mais:
- Como a OpenAI quer estabelecer limites para o avanço da IA no setor
- OpenAI e Anthropic têm medo de lançar suas IAs mais poderosas; entenda o motivo
- Meta integra Muse ao Instagram e prepara terreno para novas vendas
Como os astrônomos identificam um planeta distante?
Uma das técnicas mais comuns para encontrar exoplanetas é observar o brilho de uma estrela ao longo do tempo. Quando um planeta passa entre a estrela e a Terra, ele bloqueia pequena parte da luz que chega até nós.
Esse fenômeno é chamado de trânsito. Em gráfico que registra o brilho da estrela, aparece uma queda que pode se repetir em intervalos regulares, conforme o planeta completa suas órbitas.
O problema é que nem toda redução de brilho indica a presença de um planeta. Duas estrelas passando uma diante da outra, por exemplo, podem produzir efeito semelhante. Até mudanças de temperatura dentro de um telescópio podem interferir nos instrumentos e fazer uma estrela parecer menos brilhante.
Por isso, os candidatos precisam passar por outras verificações. Pesquisadores podem realizar novas observações e usar técnicas diferentes, como a medição da velocidade radial, que identifica pequenas oscilações no movimento de uma estrela provocadas pela atração gravitacional de um planeta.
A confirmação também envolve a análise dos resultados por outros cientistas e a publicação das evidências em uma revista científica revisada por pares.
Como participar da busca por exoplanetas
A participação de pessoas interessadas em astronomia não é novidade. Há anos, programas de ciência cidadã permitem que voluntários ajudem pesquisadores a examinar dados de telescópios e identificar fenômenos que merecem investigação.
A NASA mantém o projeto Exoplanet Watch, que permite solicitar dados e aprender a construir gráficos de variação do brilho das estrelas. A iniciativa também oferece orientações para quem tem acesso a um telescópio e deseja contribuir com observações.
Outros programas reúnem voluntários para acompanhar estrelas e registrar trânsitos de exoplanetas. Dessa forma, pessoas sem equipamentos próprios também podem colaborar com pesquisas científicas.
Os trabalhos de Bond e Byrd mostram como ferramentas de IA podem facilitar algumas etapas desse processo, desde a elaboração de programas até a triagem de grandes volumes de dados. Mas a tecnologia não substitui a validação científica: os sinais encontrados ainda precisam ser investigados para determinar se realmente indicam a presença de planetas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send
articles.text:
WhatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.
WhatsApp’s new scheduled messages let you choose the right time to send
You can schedule WhatsApp texts you might forget to send up to two weeks ahead of time.
If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too.
Meta:
To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.
Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.
Scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

articles.title: User passwords safe after 1Password security breach, company says
articles.text:
User data from 1Password has been compromised by hackers, but the company is assuring users that their passwords and recovery keys are safe.
The news: On Wednesday, 1Password announced it was subject to a breach on Nov. 19, when hackers gained access to the company’s backend system. That breach exposed the names, email addresses, and additional metadata of an unspecified number of users. Despite the attack, the Toronto-based cybersecurity software company said no passwords or recovery keys were exposed and said there is no need for users to update that information. 
From the source: “1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents,” the company wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. “Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.”
The context: 1Password uses a “vault system” that creates an encrypted container where users can control access to sensitive information like login details, credit card credentials, passkeys, and other documents. The company itself does not have access to the contents of user vaults, protecting them through dual-key encryption; access requires an account password and secret key that is not sent to or stored by 1Password servers.
1Password said the breach happened after an employee’s GitHub account was compromised and used by the attacker to introduce malware to the company’s source code. Aside from names and email addresses, the attacker downloaded records around account creation and sign-in times, public keys, user identifiers, and other metadata.
BetaKit reached out to 1Password for more detail on the incident and whether it reported the breach to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, but has not yet received a response.
RELATED: Why Canadian tech is standing against Bill C-22
Final thought: 1Password has since stated that the company has taken a number of remediation actions including disabling the impacted employee’s GitHub account, rotating credentials, lengthening recovery codes, and retaining independent cybersecurity experts to validate its efforts.
Still, this is another in a rash of global cybersecurity incidents as of late, affecting companies from Bell to Binance, that have set many on edge. 1Password’s unique point of trust—and the sheer volume of sensitive information it stewards—makes even the appearance of insecurity particularly impactful. Greg Osuri, founder of Silicon Valley’s Akash Network, said online that his trust in the company was diminished even if no passwords had been exposed.
Feature image courtesy of 1Password.

articles.title: Décollage d’Ariane 6 : que s’est-il passé avec l’incendie déclenché par la fusée et qui a approché une cuve d’hydrogène ?
articles.text:
Le Centre spatial guyanais, la base de lancement européenne de Kourou, est entouré en grande partie de savane. Lors du dixième vol d’Ariane 6, ce mardi 24 novembre, cette végétation a pris feu sous l’effet des flammes de la fusée. D’après BFMTV, l’incendie a parcouru environ cinq hectares, soit à peu près sept terrains de football. La mission s’est pourtant déroulée comme prévu : la fusée d’Arianespace a placé en orbite 36 satellites d’Amazon Leo, le réseau d’Internet par satellite d’Amazon.
Une cuve d’hydrogène sur le chemin du feu
Poussé par le vent, le feu a traversé une végétation que Péyi Guyane décrit comme très fragilisée par la sécheresse. La sécurité incendie du site est assurée par la Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris. Sur X, la brigade a expliqué que le feu menaçait « une cuve de propane et d’hydrogène liquide ». Selon France-Guyane, il a fallu six lances pour en venir à bout.
Le CNES, l’agence spatiale française qui gère la base, minimise l’incident, dans une déclaration adressée à Numerama. Pour elle, ces débuts de feu dans la savane près du pas de tir sont « un phénomène anticipé dont le risque est maîtrisé ». Elle explique qu’à chaque lancement, les pompiers arrivent les premiers sur le pas de tir pour nettoyer la zone et empêcher le feu de s’étendre. Ici, les flammes ont eu le temps de parcourir cinq hectares, jusqu’à une cuve d’hydrogène liquide. Personne n’a été blessé, et l’incendie n’a pas perturbé la mission.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
  November 14, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

articles.title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
articles.text:
The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Announced on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a DropGuard helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.
The headline is the stabilisation of !, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as panic!(), return or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing Result<T, !> to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes std::convert::Infallible an alias for !, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using Infallible now accept ! transparently.
To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from () to ! and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting issues on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.
The core of the long-awaited allocator_api is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with Vec and Box through the new Allocator trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.
On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:
This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:
- bool::toggle() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.bool.html#met...
- Box::map() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#m...
- str::trim_prefix(), str::trim_suffix, Path::trim_prefix()
The new global-min-publish-age setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"
On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:
You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,
and
you should immediately patch security advisories.
One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.
ImportStatic found on the beta that cargo install ignores the setting entirely and that an update could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.
Other notable additions include core::mem::DropGuard for running a closure on every exit path, std::mem::conjure_zst for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as bool::toggle, str::trim_prefix, str::trim_suffix and Box::map.
Upgrading uses rustup update stable; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.
Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

articles.title: I Played GTA 6 at "60 FPS"
articles.text:
One of the biggest issues with Grand Theft Auto 6 is that it runs at just 30 FPS on consoles. We recently explored why this is the case from some angles that aren't often discussed, and as a PC gamer used to playing games at frame rates above 60 FPS, I've found it a bit difficult to adjust to the game's relatively low frame rate. But over the weekend, I started seeing discussions online about a bizarre configuration that can be used to make GTA 6 run at 60 FPS, so to speak. Naturally, I was intrigued.
This configuration involves taking the 30 FPS GTA 6 output from a console like the PlayStation 5, routing it into a capture card connected to a separate PC, and then running 2x frame generation on that video input signal to produce a 60 FPS output. There are several applications that can be used to do this, but the one I've seen discussed most frequently is called Veyra.
Why this sounds like a terrible idea
When I first heard about this configuration, I thought it would be absolutely horrendous. And that's for a few reasons.
First, 30 to 60 FPS frame generation has generally been quite bad in my experience on PC. A game running at a low render rate tends to produce tons of visual artifacts when using frame generation, as the gap between frames is large, leaving the algorithm with more interpolation work to do. The shorter the gap between frames, the better frame generation tends to work, which is why I typically recommend a minimum render rate of 60 FPS.
Second, this type of frame generation doesn't have access to game data such as motion vectors or UI flags, so it's applying frame generation to the entire image every single time with little to no context. This makes the technique most similar to driver-based frame generation on PC, which delivers worse visual quality than frame generation integrated into games and is a feature I don't usually recommend.
Game data genuinely helps improve frame generation quality, especially when it comes to menus and UI elements, which will always be subject to interpolation with driver-based or video-based frame generation.
And third, one of the key reasons why 30 FPS sucks to play is the high levels of input lag relative to gaming at higher render rates. When you apply frame generation to a 30 FPS output, you increase latency due to the way frames are buffered, as well as the processing time of the frame generation algorithm itself. With this weird capture card method, you're adding even more latency on top of all that due to the time it takes for the capture card to process and display the incoming signal.
All of this makes the GTA 6 capture card method sound pretty bad: the potential for worse visual quality with tons of frame generation artifacts, and much higher input latency on top of what is already high latency from running at 30 FPS.
And yet, at least based on what I was seeing on social media, this technique was getting rave reviews, with some gamers saying it made GTA 6 "playable" for them. So I had to try it out.
Before getting into the setup process, it's worth touching on my personal experience playing GTA 6 at 30 FPS on the base PlayStation 5 as a predominantly PC gamer. I found it a bit harder than I expected to acclimatize to GTA 6 running at 30 FPS, with the biggest issue for me being the motion and display blur associated with running at a low frame rate...
With the default settings on a 4K OLED monitor, I found the game quite blurry during any sort of motion, an issue we discussed in our previous GTA 6 analysis.
Some of this was due to motion blur, which can be turned off or even increased in the settings. I found that turning off motion blur helped alleviate some of the blurriness, leaving me with display blur. But this also made the game choppier due to the low frame rate, and on an OLED monitor, you get another issue: judder.
As OLEDs have extremely fast response times, they're able to display each frame almost instantly. During panning motions, you get this juddering effect where objects quickly update their position and are then blurred somewhat by display persistence. On slower LCD monitors, this effect is reduced as response times are longer, effectively blurring away the judder to some degree.
I've seen some people suggest that turning up motion blur when using an OLED is better for reducing judder. In GTA 6, I found this made the game even blurrier and a bit nauseating due to the sheer amount of blur.
However, input latency wasn't a huge issue for me, mostly because GTA 6 is a fairly slow-paced game, with a lot of deliberate, slow, lifelike animations and a game engine that has never been optimized for fast inputs (looking at you, Red Dead Redemption 2).
It's obviously not as good as running PC games at a higher frame rate, but from an input latency perspective, I found the game playable. And when you engage with the world at a slower pace, avoiding huge camera pans or whips all the time, walking around, even driving at the speed limit, you don't end up seeing heaps of display blur all the time. The input latency is manageable enough, so in that sense, it is playable.
How to play GTA 6 at 60 FPS using Veyra
The good news for anyone wanting to try this 60 FPS conversion trick is that Veyra is a free and open-source application, so at least on the software side, there is no cost. You do, however, need a capture card connected to a reasonably capable PC.
When launching Veyra, select Capture Card. From here, you'll get a list of settings specific to capturing the game. Typically, you'll want to match the resolution to your monitor's resolution, in my case 4K, and then select either 30 or 60 FPS, depending on what your capture card supports. The most crucial setting is the pixel format: this should be set to NV12 if you plan on gaming in SDR, or P010 if you plan on gaming in HDR.
I own several different capture cards, including USB and PCIe models, and found that some combinations of resolution, frame rate, and pixel format aren't available simultaneously.
For example, on my Elgato 4K X over USB, capturing at 4K 60 FPS using P010 wasn't possible for whatever reason. I could only use NV12 at that resolution and frame rate, or drop down to 4K 30 FPS with P010. However, on an AVerMedia GC573 over PCIe, I could get everything working at the same time.
After selecting the pixel format, scroll down to the audio settings. Enable audio monitoring if you want the audio to route through your PC to whatever audio device you have connected.
Then, in the final section for format and picture, set the input color to HDR PQ if you want to use HDR. Otherwise, Auto is fine. I also used Auto for the other settings, although there is a minimum latency option that reduces buffering at the potential expense of dropped frames.
At this point, the capture card is configured, so you can hit Connect and Start. You should see the input from your console in the window, provided it's connected correctly to the HDMI IN port on the capture card. You don't need anything connected to the OUT port, as the output is routed through your graphics card to whatever display is connected to your PC.
However, at least on the PlayStation 5, you do need to disable HDCP in the console's settings. Head to Settings > System > HDMI > Enable HDCP and make sure this toggle is off.
It's also a good idea at this point to confirm everything is working as intended on the console side. Go to Screen and Video > Video Output and check the current video output signal. This should match the configuration you've selected in Veyra, and you'll want to confirm HDR is active if that's what you've set. If something doesn't look right, you may need to adjust either the console or Veyra settings.
The final major step is to enable frame generation. Using the tabs on the right, go to Frame Gen, enable the feature, and then under Frame Generation Method, choose NVIDIA VFG if you have an Nvidia GPU. I found VFG to work significantly better than the DLSS Frame Generation option, which produces way more artifacts. AMD GPU users should choose AMD FRC, though you can experiment with FSR FG as well.
I also chose to increase VFG quality to High, up from the default of Medium, and to enable strict frame pacing.
At the bottom of the settings, in the optical flow section, it's essential that you enable Remove duplicate frames and set it to 60 to 30 mode if you've configured the capture card to run at 60 FPS. As GTA 6 runs at just 30 FPS, there will be duplicate frames in a 60 FPS capture signal. You don't want those to be part of the frame generation process, otherwise it will look weird and run badly. I also enabled low latency mode but left the other settings at their defaults.
The last option you might want to consider is adjusting the audio delay if video and audio latency are mismatched. Veyra automatically applies some audio delay when enabling features like frame generation, but you can tweak this further in the settings.
Then, just click the full-screen button, and you're playing GTA 6 at "60 FPS" through a capture card and PC-based frame generation.
Further optimizations can be made in the GTA 6 settings themselves. I'd recommend turning off motion blur and setting both look and aim acceleration to the maximum. This makes inputs feel quicker and removes the game's motion blur from each frame, feeding the interpolation algorithm the cleanest image possible.
The surprisingly good 60 FPS experience
But is all this any good? Is GTA 6 actually more enjoyable to play through this weird system?
You might need some context for what I'm about to say. I don't like frame generation at low frame rates. I've tested frame generation extensively and consistently found 30 to 60 FPS to be a bad experience. I don't like that frame generation increases latency, I don't think it works particularly well without game integrations, and I'm highly sensitive to artifacts like flickering, boiling, and frame generation-related blending problems.
I typically only use it in some games to increase visual smoothness, especially when already rendering at a high frame rate in excess of 60 FPS. Despite all of this, despite my dislike of low frame rate frame generation on PC... I actually think this capture card method works.
I genuinely thought it would be terrible when I heard about it. I thought I would try it out and hate it, and maybe I'd even get a chance to poke fun at how bad it looks or works. But that's just not the case.
I can't quite believe how much I like the way this system enhances the GTA 6 experience. I'm actually a bit blown away.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
What sealed it for me was running both options at the same time and switching between them. On my monitor, I had my PC connected over DisplayPort, running GTA 6 through Veyra at 60 FPS. On the HDMI input, I had the native game presentation at 30 FPS, using the passthrough output from the capture card.
I far preferred playing the game through Veyra at 60 FPS rather than natively at 30 FPS. In fact, every time I went back to the 30 FPS option, I was a bit stunned at how choppy and blurry it looked. When using this system, you do need to temper your expectations, though. This does not make GTA 6 play like a normal 60 FPS game on PC. There are artifacts, and there is an input delay problem that you simply don't get with proper, native 60 FPS gaming.
However, given there is currently no option to play GTA 6 at anything other than 30 FPS, I see this as more of an enhanced 30 FPS experience. Specifically, it makes the game significantly less blurry and less juddery on an OLED monitor, which makes it more enjoyable in my opinion.
In our previous analysis of the issues with 30 FPS gaming, we explained how low frame rates increase display persistence blur on sample-and-hold displays, by far the most common display type today. This makes 30 FPS look extremely blurry during any sort of motion.
Going up to 60 FPS is a significant improvement in clarity. It's not crystal clear or anything, but it doesn't immediately look like a blurry mess under the slightest camera movement. Provided you're delivering 60 frames per second to the monitor that actually look somewhat decent and have good clarity themselves, running at 60 FPS is a huge boost to motion clarity. There are additional benefits to smoothness, as there are simply more frames being presented to you, reducing choppiness.
What impressed me the most about using Veyra in this way is that the quality of frame interpolation is surprisingly good. It's not flawless, but it's generally free of obvious artifacts in a way that I haven't experienced before with 30 to 60 FPS video interpolation.
I've played around five hours of GTA 6 using this method and haven't experienced any huge, game-breaking artifacts or massive full-screen blur or warbling issues, as is common with other techniques. It's much better than TV-based frame smoothing, for example, which doesn't do a great job of preserving clarity and tends to blend frames together in a horrible, smeared way.
Part of this appears to be down to how Nvidia VFG works, especially on the High setting. Veyra reports that this frame generation system takes around 10ms to perform interpolation, which is much longer than you'd typically see from DLSS Frame Generation in a game. In Veyra, using DLSS Frame Generation instead of VFG drops the processing time to under 3ms. Essentially, VFG takes over three times as long to compute, and it's specifically tuned for video input.
So with Veyra producing decent frame interpolation, you get a genuine reduction in display persistence blur from running at 60 FPS, which makes the entire game look clearer in motion. This significantly improves one of the biggest issues with GTA 6 at 30 FPS, and it's this benefit that keeps me using Veyra for my GTA 6 gaming.
Of course, there are issues. Frame interpolation is not perfect, so there are going to be artifacts at times. I found VFG on the High setting tended to do a decent job of keeping the UI intact without obvious warbling or flickering artifacts, and even in menus or on the map, it held up well enough.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
But there are limits. Occasionally, the frame generation system will produce artifacts on UI elements, such as the tracking markers on screen or when text animates in or out of the frame. It can also struggle with some types of movement, such as when complicated patterns or textures move or transform significantly between frames.
In a PC game, these artifacts would probably be a deal-breaker. You'd be better off lowering settings to get the game running above 60 FPS. This would reduce display blur in the same way as frame generation, but it would do so without interpolation artifacts and with even better motion quality. But with GTA 6, there's no "lowering the settings" option. So it's a question of whether the high levels of blur at 30 FPS or some artifacts from frame generation at 60 FPS make for a better experience. To me, 60 FPS with artifacts wins out whenever I try both options.
In-game artifacts are a bit worse when using Veyra's NVIDIA VFG option set to Medium. I found this mode struggled more with the UI and tended to produce warbling around text where VFG High would not. Medium is about twice as fast at generating frames and may be required on PCs with fewer resources.
I also found that the overall quality of each frame, even the real frames, is reduced slightly through the capture card method compared to sending the game natively to the display. There's a very faint line pattern that I'm noticing through Veyra. This might just be down to how the capture card actually captures each frame, I'm not entirely sure, but it's very slight and, again, not a deal-breaker compared to running at 30 FPS with increased blur.
Another factor worth considering when discussing frame generation artifacts is that GTA 6 already has quite a few visual artifacts of its own, especially when playing on the base PS5.
The upscaling method is awful in my opinion. It does a terrible job of reconstructing fine detail, it's quite blurry, and there are lots of sizzling and ghosting issues visible throughout the game. There is also a lot of noise due to the use of ray-traced lighting. The ray count in this game must be quite low, and the denoising solution doesn't appear to be particularly high quality, so many surfaces exhibit grain, pixelation, boiling, and so on in motion.
The overall visual fidelity is very impressive despite these artifacts and flaws, especially considering the relatively slow console hardware it's running on, so I fully understand why there are issues. It's not a PC game, and we can't expect a PC-like experience where these issues could be addressed with faster hardware.
But the good news is that, given there are already quite a few artifacts in the game, the frame generation artifacts introduced by Veyra don't stand out nearly as much as they otherwise might in a game with a cleaner, more artifact-free image. I find the sizzling due to upscaling much more noticeable during general gameplay than interpolation artifacts. And that sizzling is present no matter what. It's part of the native 30 FPS experience.
The cost of 60 FPS: Input latency
What about latency? This is the other major part of the equation, as running the game through a capture card and then applying frame generation will obviously increase latency. I tested this, and at least on my setup, the overall latency increase was around 35ms. This is made up of around 25ms of capture latency and around 10ms of frame generation latency.
Note that this is measured to the first point of change on screen, which in the case of frame generation will be an interpolated frame. Measuring latency with frame generation is always a bit different, so keep in mind there's another 17ms to account for if we're measuring real-frame-to-real-frame latency at 60 FPS.
At face value, this sounds like a noticeable latency increase. And it would be absolutely disastrous for PC gaming, where at decent frame rates in single-player titles, you typically see somewhere between 30 and 40ms of latency. Using a capture card and running frame generation would therefore roughly double the latency of a typical PC game, making it a pretty stupid solution that would feel awful.
The funny thing about GTA 6, though, is that this game has extremely high input latency to begin with.
On my monitor, running the game natively over HDMI without Veyra at all, I recorded approximately 160ms of input lag for most actions I attempted. This means the normal 30 FPS experience is pretty sluggish to begin with. I found getting used to the shooting mechanics quite difficult as a result, but once you get used to it, it's playable.
On top of this, GTA 6 is just a slow game in general. Actions are accompanied by lifelike animations that take time, there's lots of slower-paced gameplay, and it isn't really a game where you feel like you have instant control over the characters.
With Veyra frame generation added on top, latency in my configuration was around 190 to 200ms. That's a lot of lag, but relative to the 160ms baseline, the increase isn't that bad. We're already in the "really bad input lag" zone, so adding another 30-40ms isn't necessarily a deal-breaker. It amounts to roughly a 20-25% increase, which is not trivial, but it's not a doubling of latency like you'd see if the game was running with just 30-40ms of native latency.
I can tell that frame generation is adding a bit of latency when playing GTA 6, but it's not a deal-breaker for me because the game already has high latency. I was already having to adapt to the high-latency experience at 30 FPS, so it's much the same thing at 60 FPS with Veyra. After a while, I didn't really notice the difference, though it took some time to dial in the faster skills in the game, like driving and shooting.
As with everything else we've discussed, this comes down to a trade-off. Is GTA 6 a better experience at 30 FPS with heavy display blur and 160ms of latency, or is it better at 60 FPS with less display blur, somewhat more artifacts, and up to 200ms of latency?
To me, the reduction in blur from playing at 60 FPS is more than enough to offset the increases in artifacts and latency, so I prefer playing GTA 6 using the Veyra frame generation method. This is not going to be a low-latency, artifact-free experience no matter which path I choose, so I'm basically willing to concede some latency in a quest to fix display blur. Other gamers who are more latency-sensitive will disagree, and the Veyra method will be an even worse experience for them.
Is it worth the trouble?
Would I recommend gamers use Veyra to play Grand Theft Auto 6? As I've said, I prefer playing the game this way, and when switching back and forth between native 30 FPS and 60 FPS via Veyra, I consistently prefer the latter. However, I don't expect that will apply to everyone, especially those who prioritize latency above everything else.
If you don't mind the display blur and lack of visual smoothness but are concerned about the latency side of things, you should probably stay away from Veyra.
If you happen to own a capture card already and a PC that's capable of running Veyra (which should be most gaming PCs), I think it's worth giving it a try just to see which option you prefer. It's also easy to set up a quick comparison for yourself, with one display input connected to your PC running Veyra, and another connected to the HDMI passthrough from the console. That way, you can switch back and forth and decide for yourself which way you want to play.
If you don't own a capture card, I'm on the fence as to whether I'd recommend investing in one specifically to play GTA 6 this way. A high-quality PCIe capture card capable of 4K with HDR will set you back over $150, which is an investment compared to simply waiting for the game to come to PC. And there's no guarantee you'll even like playing through Veyra.
With that said, there are USB capture cards and models that are only capable of 1080p that are much cheaper, provided you don't need the game running at the highest resolution.
If you do want to buy a higher-end capture card, I'd recommend one from AVerMedia. I've tried a number of capture cards from different brands, and AVerMedia's have been by far the most reliable in my experience. I've used the GC573 for all my Veyra testing here and regularly use a GC553G2 for capturing footage for Hardware Unboxed videos. Unfortunately, my experience with Elgato cards hasn't been nearly as positive.
Ultimately, Veyra isn't a substitute for running GTA 6 at a native 60 FPS, and I still stand by my usual recommendations when it comes to frame generation on PC. But in this particular scenario, where there is no option to increase the game's render rate, the trade-offs make surprisingly good sense. I went into this experiment expecting to find yet another example of why frame generation at 30 FPS is a terrible idea. Instead, I ended up finding my preferred way to play GTA 6, at least until the PC version arrives.

articles.title: US Treasury’s FinCEN Disconnects Systems Following Cyber Incident
articles.text:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the US Treasury Department’s financial intelligence unit, has disconnected some of its systems while investigating a cyber incident.
“FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline,” the agency said in a notice on the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System website.
The website is operational, but some FinCEN services may be temporarily unavailable, and the agency has extended the deadlines for qualifying filers affected by the disruption.
“FinCEN is granting temporary, limited exceptive relief in response to a service disruption that is hindering filers’ ability to adhere to reporting obligations,” the agency said in a November 24 order (PDF).
The agency has not shared further details on the nature of the incident and made no mention of a potential data breach, but said it was working to return all systems to normal.
It is unclear who was behind the attack and if any data was accessed or stolen. SecurityWeek has emailed FinCEN for additional information and will update this article if the agency responds.
FinCEN disclosed the incident amid a wave of cyberattacks and outages impacting US government agencies, including the CIA, which had an unclassified system breached.
The Department of Defense’s National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence were also affected by the open source intelligence system breach, The New York Times reported on Tuesday.
Last week, the National Security Agency temporarily took offline an internal network used to communicate classified information, and the FBI is looking into an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database.
