articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
  November 12, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler, Eduardo Fernández. Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: Plagiarism Checker Turnitin Investigating Cyberattack
articles.text:
Education technology platform Turnitin has disclosed a cyberattack involving certain customer-facing systems.
A subsidiary of Advance Publications, Turnitin provides plagiarism checking solutions used by thousands of education and research institutions worldwide.
“We are writing to let you know that we recently identified unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing Turnitin systems,” CEO Chris Caren revealed in a November 23 letter on the company’s website.
The company immediately initiated its incident response plan, notified the relevant authorities, and launched an investigation with support from external cyber experts.
“We can confirm our systems are fully operational and safe to use and that these customer-facing systems do not collect government identification credentials or institutional financial information,” Caren said.
The company continues to monitor the affected customer-facing systems while its investigation into the nature and scope of the incident continues.
Customer-facing Turnitin systems include the submission portal for students, a grading interface for instructors, integration APIs for institutions, and reporting dashboards. The company did not say if any or which of these systems was breached.
Caren did not say if any data was accessed or how many customers might have been affected, but the University of Colorado Boulder said on Tuesday it was in touch with the company to understand if any CU Boulder information was compromised.
“At this time, we have no indication that student or instructor information, assignments, or other CU Boulder data was exposed. Since Turnitin is primarily accessed via a Canvas integration, OIT has added additional monitoring to ensure Canvas has not been impacted,” the university’s Office of Information Technology said.
SecurityWeek has emailed Turnitin for additional information on the incident and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Elon Musk promete doar ações da SpaceX a crianças dos EUA
articles.text:
A SpaceX anunciou que vai doar ações da companhia a crianças estadunidenses inscritas nas chamadas Trump Accounts, contas de investimento criadas pelo governo de Donald Trump. O CEO da empresa, Elon Musk, também prometeu contribuir pessoalmente com uma ação para cada beneficiário, igualando a doação corporativa.
Em comunicado divulgado nesta quarta-feira (25), a SpaceX afirmou que pretende distribuir uma ação de sua classe A para cada conta ativa do programa. Musk fará uma doação equivalente, o que significa que cada beneficiário poderá receber duas ações da companhia.
A empresa justificou a iniciativa como forma de permitir que a próxima geração de estadunidenses participe dos resultados de seus projetos. “A SpaceX está construindo a infraestrutura do futuro e trabalhando para tornar a vida multiplanetária. Acreditamos que a propriedade da empresa que desenvolve esses sistemas deve se estender à próxima geração de americanos, para benefício deles no longo prazo”, declarou a companhia.
Ainda não está claro quantas contas são consideradas ativas. A Casa Branca informou em outubro que quase 70 milhões de Trump Accounts haviam sido criadas, incluindo mais de 60 milhões por meio de inscrição automática.
Como funcionam as Trump Accounts?
- As Trump Accounts, também chamadas de contas 530A, são destinadas a crianças estadunidenses com menos de 18 anos que tenham número de Seguro Social;
- O programa permite que pais, responsáveis, avós e outras pessoas contribuam com até US$ 5 mil (R$ 29,1 mil) por ano para cada beneficiário, em valores após a incidência de impostos. O limite anual será corrigido pela inflação a partir de 2028;
- Crianças nascidas entre 2025 e 2028 também podem receber um depósito único de US$ 1 mil (R$ 5.822,40) do Tesouro estadunidense. Outros recursos podem ser disponibilizados conforme critérios específicos;
- Para que familiares, amigos e empregadores façam contribuições, a conta precisa ser reivindicada por um responsável. Crianças inscritas automaticamente, porém, podem receber doações filantrópicas, mesmo que nenhum adulto tenha concluído essa etapa;
- Desde o lançamento do programa, em 4 de julho, familiares e amigos já contribuíram com mais de US$ 1 bilhão (R$ 5,8 bilhões). O total depositado nas contas ultrapassa US$ 9 bilhões (R$ 52,4 bilhões), segundo informações divulgadas anteriormente pela CNBC.
Leia mais:
- Anthropic e SpaceX impuseram regras incomuns e irritaram bancos no IPO
- SpaceX é processada nos EUA por imagens sexuais geradas pelo Grok
- SpaceX recebe autorização para lançar um milhão de satélites de IA
SpaceX já havia anunciado outras doações
A iniciativa anunciada agora se soma a uma contribuição anterior de Gwynne Shotwell, presidente e diretora de operações da SpaceX. Ela havia se comprometido a doar pessoalmente mais de duas milhões de ações da companhia para as Trump Accounts. Os beneficiários elegíveis devem receber esses papéis em dezembro.
Em outubro, Musk também publicou no X que pretendia doar uma ação da SpaceX a cada criança dos Estados Unidos no ano seguinte.
As doações de ações foram permitidas por regras temporárias publicadas pelo Departamento do Tesouro no fim de setembro. A mudança abriu espaço para que as contas recebessem participações em empresas, além de contribuições em dinheiro.
A modalidade pode beneficiar quem doa, pois permite evitar o pagamento de impostos sobre ganhos de capital que seriam cobrados caso ações valorizadas fossem vendidas. Para as famílias, porém, existem restrições: em geral, os papéis recebidos não podem ser vendidos antes de cinco anos ou do fim do ano em que o beneficiário completa 17 anos, valendo o que ocorrer primeiro.
A regra também significa que parte do patrimônio acumulado pelas crianças poderá ficar vinculada ao desempenho de empresas específicas.
SpaceX negocia possível fusão com a Tesla
O anúncio ocorre enquanto a SpaceX negocia uma possível fusão com a Tesla, montadora de veículos elétricos também controlada por Musk.
As duas companhias criaram comitês especiais para conduzir as conversas e contrataram assessores para avaliar possível operação de grande porte. Enquanto as negociações avançam, as ações da SpaceX enfrentam pressão sobre seus preços.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.
Bruno Capozzi é jornalista, mestre em Ciências Sociais e editor executivo do OD.

articles.title: 1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
articles.text:
1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident. It’s unclear how many users are affected.
1Password breach leaked customer names and emails, but not passwords
1Password says the security breach didn’t compromise its vaults, but didn’t mention how many customers were affected.
The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.
It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.
The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.

articles.title: Voyager 1 ist einen Lichttag entfernt, sendet aber keine Daten mehr: Wie die Nasa das Problem lösen will
articles.text:
Ein Lichttag entfernt, aber keine Daten mehr: Nasa untersucht Panne bei Voyager 1
Am 18. November 2026 hatte Voyager 1 einen historischen Meilenstein erreicht. Als erstes menschengemachtes Objekt ist die Sonde einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern.
Antenne der Nasa empfing nur leeres Signal von Voyager 1
Doch kurz bevor Voyager 1 diese Marke erreicht hatte, gab es ein Problem. Die 1977 gestartete Sonde schickte keine wissenschaftlichen oder technischen Daten mehr an die Erde.
Eine Antenne des Deep Space Network der Nasa bei der australischen Hauptstadt Canberra empfing nur ein Trägersignal ohne Inhalt. Dieses Signal bestätigte immerhin, dass die Voyager die Rekordentfernung von einem Lichttag erreicht hat.
Nasa hat Bordcomputer in Verdacht
Ingenieur:innen der Nasa untersuchen laut einer Mitteilung der US-Raumfahrtbehörde, was zu der Panne geführt haben könnte. Da das Trägersignal funktioniert, liegt der Ausfall wohl nicht an der Antenne oder der Sendetechnik von Voyager 1.
Die Nasa vermutet vielmehr, dass ein Bordcomputer ausgefallen ist, der Daten der Messinstrumente der Sonde erfasst. Der Rechner wandelt diese Informationen zudem in ein richtiges Format um, damit sie zur Erde übertragen werden können.
Vor drei Jahren hatte Voyager 1 dasselbe Problem
Bereits im November 2023 war ein vergleichbares Problem aufgetreten. Auch vor ziemlich genau drei Jahren schickte Voyager 1 keine wissenschaftlichen Daten, obwohl ansonsten alles zu funktionieren schien.
Erst im Frühjahr 2024 konnte die Nasa herausfinden, wo der Fehler lag. Einer von drei Bordcomputern hatte einen Defekt, das sogenannte Flight Data Substytem (FDS). Es ist verantwortlich dafür, die wissenschaftlichen Daten für den Transport zur Erde zu verpacken.
So löste die Nasa die Panne von 2023
Ein einziger Chip des FDS, der für die Speicherung eines Teils des Arbeitsspeichers zuständig ist, hatte den Dienst quittiert. Er beinhaltete auch einen Teil des Softwarecodes des FDS.
Die Nasa konnte den Chip natürlich nicht reparieren. Deshalb versuchte das Team der Raumfahrtbehörde, den Code an andere Teile des FDS zu schicken. Da er in vollständiger Form zu groß war, teilten sie ihn in Abschnitte und integrierten diese in verschiedene Stellen des Systems. Mit Erfolg. Nach fünf Monaten Funkstille konnte die Nasa wieder Kontakt mit Voyager 1 aufnehmen.
Zusammenhang mit Aussetzer von Voyager 1 im Oktober 2026?
Die Weltraumagentur prüft derzeit, welche Lektion sie aus dem Vorfall von 2023 ziehen kann. Außerdem untersuchen die Ingenieur:innen, ob es einen Zusammenhang mit einem weiteren Aussetzer von Voyager 1 aus dem Oktober 2026 gibt.
Am 18. Oktober 2026 blieb die Sonde bei einem Kontaktversuch komplett stumm. Zwei Tage später hatte sich das Problem von selbst gelöst. Später konnte die Nasa den Grund für die Funkstille herausfinden. Eine Gruppe von Triebwerken der Voyager 1 war unerwartet offline gegangen. Das System schaltete deshalb automatisch eine Backup-Gruppe3 hinzu. Um diesen Wechsel fehlerfrei durchzuführen, begibt sich das System in einen abgesicherten Modus und pausiert bis zur Umsetzung alle anderen Funktionen.
Wirklich beeindruckend, dass der Mensch 1977 Technik ins Weltall geschickt hat, welche knapp 50Jahre lange Fliegt und Funktioniert.
Tatsächlich beeindruckent welche Unfassbare Entfernung.
Und auf der Erde schafft man es Nicht, dass mein Fernseher 3 Jahre bei Normal Nutzung nicht Kaputt geht, oder das Wahlen ohne Probleme Ablaufen!

articles.title: The machine shop of the 21st century
articles.text:
This article appears in The BetaKit Guide to Alberta’s Silicon City. Learn more about Edmonton semiconductor innovation here.
The University of Alberta (U of A)’s Electrical and Computer Engineering Research Facility (ECERF) sits on a tree-lined street in Edmonton’s university district. The large, concrete building looms over the modest, mid-century bungalows that dot the rest of the neighbourhood. But inside the ECERF, people are working on something very, very small.
“We like to think of ourselves as the machine shop of the 21st century.”
The ECERF is home to the university’s nanoFAB centre: an open-access training and collaboration hub that serves as a kind of maker space for nanotechnology that allows private companies, researchers, and academics to develop and produce their own semiconductor chips.
And while the chips that come out of the nanoFAB are tiny—sometimes unfathomably so—its influence on the Canadian semiconductor industry is anything but small.
Semiconductor chips, named for the semiconductive properties of materials like silicon that comprise them, are the minute electrical components that underpin virtually all of modern computing and electronics. Think of semiconductors as the electronic brain of a device, controlling the flow of electricity to process, store, or move information digitally. Today, you can find them in everything from the high-end, AI-enabling GPUs and CPUs powering frontier AI to the LED lights at your office or the computer controlling your car’s engine.
Big things start small
The nanoFAB was founded in 1999 to fill the gap left when the U of A’s previous nanotechnology initiative, the Alberta Microelectronics Centre, spun out of the university into a private, for-profit company called Micralyne. The organization had been created by the university in the early 1980s to build regional expertise in semiconductor fabrication and micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) development.
“That unit used to provide a lot of research support on campus,” nanoFAB director Eric Flaim said. “When the spin-out occurred, they took all of the assets and the people, and it left a gap in research capability.”
Flaim’s been with nanoFAB since 2008. Over his tenure, he witnessed the transformation from a small lab to a 25,000-square-foot space with more than $135 million in specialized equipment. Initially focused on academic research, the lab space is now home to over 75 private-sector employees who use it as part of the nanoFAB’s growing number of partnerships with industrial and commercial clients.
“A large portion of our user base is from Edmonton, but we have industrial clients coast-to-coast, from Victoria to St. John’s,” Flaim said.
Working at a tiny scale
Edmonton’s nanoFAB doesn’t make the kind of semiconductor chips you might have read about in lengthy think pieces on Taiwanese supply chains that power your cellphone. Instead, the facility aims to be a resource for companies or developers working on more niche products.
“We’re not … making memory cards or CPUs or the kinds of things that go into consumer-level products and are often commoditized,” Flaim said.
Instead, the NanoFAB builds chips like industrial sensors for oil and gas operations, quantum computing qubits, and MEMS used in tools like gyroscopes, microphones, and nanoscopic mirrors.
Building the semiconductor chips for those tools involves manufacturing on silicon disks known as wafers. Fabrication requires complex processes like lithography and plasma etching to clear away unwanted materials and transfer the nanoscopic transistors, circuits, and other components onto the semiconductor. That requires equipment capable of working at truly small scales; the nanoFAB can fabricate devices as minuscule as one to 10 micrometres (0.0001% of a metre). For context, a single red blood cell measures about eight micrometres, while a human strand of hair comes in at 50 to 100 micrometres.
That scale makes sense when you consider that individual semiconductors can be as small as two millimetres, or about the width of a grain of rice. A single six-inch wafer can thereby produce upwards of 4,000 semiconductors.
And that’s where the nanoFAB’s equipment—like the Raith Voyager electron beam lithography system, which can cost between $1.5 and $2.5 million USD—comes in.
“We like to think of ourselves as the machine shop of the 21st century,” says Flaim. “We’re providing the advanced toolsets and capabilities that allow people to build devices utilized in a wide variety of different verticals.”
It’s here that Alberta’s nanoFAB differs from its two largest peers: Ottawa’s Canadian Photonics Fabrication Centre (CPFC) and the MiQro Innovation Collaborative Centre (C2MI) near Bromont, Que. While CPFC operates largely as a fee-for-service foundry, creating chips to the specifications of clients, and C2MI specializes in non-profit and academic research, Edmonton’s nanoFAB acts more like a maker space you might find at a library, putting its tools and resources into the hands of individuals and companies that might not otherwise be able to access or afford them.
“What we’re trying to do is empower researchers and companies to build new hardware and devices, new technologies,” Flaim said. “Our model is trying to support direct access and use … we try not to set ourselves up as a contract manufacturer or a foundry.”
That’s attracted a lot of attention from the private sector, according to Flaim, who said the nanoFAB model allows intellectual property to stay directly in the hands of companies.
“We’ve found a niche where companies are interested in hiring their own people, having them trained on the equipment, and then having those people work here in a normal nine-to-five capacity,” Flaim added.
A difference of 100 millimetres
Flaim’s focus at the nanoFAB circa 2026 is growing the private partnerships the lab has built over the past 25 years and leveraging both interest and potential investment to expand its capabilities. Presently, the nanoFAB can fabricate semiconductors on wafers up to 150 millimetres, but staff are actively pursuing the equipment upgrades needed to work with 200-millimetre wafers. If successful, the nanoFAB would become the only place in Western Canada, and one of just two nationwide, capable of fabricating at that size.
While it might be nice to think of the nanoFAB as a potential player in the global semiconductor arms race playing out in Taiwan, Japan, the US, and China, the truth is that Edmonton’s unlikely to compete any time soon, even if the federal government is showing increased interest (more on that later).
Most of the semiconductor manufacturing making headlines today—like at the now world-famous Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)—happens at the 300-millimetre size.
“What we’re trying to do is empower researchers and companies to build new hardware and devices, new technologies.”
Eric Flaim, nanoFAB
“Internationally, when we hear people talking about TSMC, global foundries, or chip shortages for GPUs, what they’re talking about is wafer processing at the 300-millimetre level. It’s state-of-the-art processing,” Flaim said.
A difference of 100 millimetres doesn’t sound like a lot, but it does cost a lot. At the 300-millimetre level, facilities are almost always fully automated and often the size of several football fields.
“Wafers are transported in boxes that no human has touched, going from robot to robot before being fed into a machine that does all of the lithography, deposition, and etching,” Flaim said.
The price tag for that kind of automation? Flaim says it’s in the tens of billions. That’s the largest reason he doesn’t see the nanoFAB taking on that kind of scale any time soon.
Despite its more modest goals, the nanoFAB has been recognized for its strategic value here at home. As recently as last spring, the lab received federal and provincial funding in the tens of millions to expand its equipment and fabrication capabilities.
“There’s recognition that you want to have some domestic manufacturing capability in these strategic areas,” Flaim said. “There’s a recognition on the defence side that if you’re going to buy airplanes from Saab or Lockheed Martin, you want those companies spending money domestically. If those companies want to invest domestically, you need to have the capabilities to invest in.”
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy nanoFAB.

articles.title: Q&A: Why nanotech research is booming in Alberta
articles.text:
This article appears in The BetaKit Guide to Alberta’s Silicon City. Learn more about Edmonton semiconductor innovation here.
Nanotechnology first became a hot commodity in the early aughts. Heralded as the next revolution, it was common to see pop-culture visions of a future where nanobots would scour our bloodstreams for cancer cells and skyscrapers would self-assemble. The tech attracted billions in federal and VC dollars, with both US Presidents Bill Clinton and George Bush making hefty investments in the field.
Nanotech’s high profile has dissipated since then, but the technology hasn’t. Today, nanotech is more prevalent than ever, underpinning everything from the semiconductor chips powering AI to vaccines and even sunscreen.
The sector also continues to garner interest from government, business, and academia. To find out what that renewed interest means for the future of nanotech, and Canada’s place as a potential leader, BetaKit sat down with Dr. Andrew Myles, the director of research and development at the Quantum and Nanotechnology Research Centre (NANO) in Edmonton.
The following interview has been edited for both clarity and length. 
Many people might not really know what nanotechnology means. Can you define it for our readers?
Nanotechnology is any technology that exploits features on the nano scale; between one and 100 nanometres is usually the common definition. The way I like to explain it is: one nanometer compared to one millimetre is the same as one millimetre compared to one kilometre. So that gives you an idea of perspective.
Once you get down to these small particles, you have unique features, like an extremely high surface area of any material that is reduced to a nanoparticle, and you can exploit that kind of feature in any technology that would benefit from high surface area. It’s very applicable to biology and medicine because our bodies have DNA, proteins, and all of these enzymes that have little nooks and crannies in them at the nano scale. So for the medical side, for solar cells, for batteries, these types of technologies can all benefit from nanotechnology.
What’s the coolest thing being researched at NANO right now?
One thing that really motivates us here now is remote environmental sensing. We work a lot in the North and with Indigenous communities doing environmental sensing research and looking at detecting toxins in water, for instance, but also networking that information. So we have different sensors networking through and collecting that data and looking at those advances of not only the technology but also that digital technology component.
Seeing the technology and what it can do for these communities, I think that’s probably one of the most exciting things we’ve seen in the last little while.
What’s one thing you think people should know about nanotech today?
Nanotech can be applied across industry sectors and is often incorporated in more conventional applications than you may imagine. When you talk about nanotechnology being in things like tennis rackets or lubricants or bandages, people are kind of surprised. But it’s already deployed to a large extent, and there are a lot of benefits already. So it’s not as out of reach as some people may think. It’s a fantastic area to explore because it has a lot of interesting science still going on, but a lot of excellent applications already in place.
Biomedicine is extremely active in this space. I would remind you of the COVID-19 vaccine that was based on lipid nanoparticle technology developed in Canada. This is the beginning. Now this is being explored for all kinds of different biomedicines.
Why do you think Alberta has become an institutional home for nanotech and R&D in Canada? What makes the province so appealing to the industry?
It’s a combination of a couple of things. One is that Alberta’s always had this entrepreneurial, get-‘er-done spirit. I would also say that our universities are fantastic. There are a lot of universities in Alberta; they’re all strong; they all interact; there’s connections and engagement; people graduating with high-tech degrees, getting jobs, and bringing that expertise into companies.
What does Canada need to do to become a leader in nanotech, or to maintain its edge?
We like to look at demonstrating technologies to industry and really trying to move industry and our academic base closer together. I think you’re seeing that across the country in many universities. Places like the University of Alberta’s NanoFAB have many companies every single day, side by side with people at the university working on actual new products. It’s extremely exciting.
I feel like Canada’s move towards really funding and sponsoring technology development and science is very promising. Now it’s up to us as scientists to make sure that we deliver that value to our industries.
If Canada becomes a leader in nanotechnology, how does that benefit the country?
I think it’s all part of moving to a knowledge-based economy and having high-tech as a major pillar. It bolsters all of our industries. The concept of nanotechnology applied across sectors can be beneficial all over the place. It also just gets more conventional, maybe risk-averse companies to sort of step out and look at some options for how they could improve.
And, certainly, global competitiveness is a driver. But it also just strengthens industry locally. It strengthens our position, our major sectors. If we have more of these technologies introduced into our major resource sectors, it strengthens them and bolsters them even more than we already do.
What do you think the future of nanotech looks like, both here in Alberta and more broadly?
I see a lot of more conventional industries adopting nanotechnologies, and in the future you’re going to start seeing nano elements within lots of different technologies. Also, more specifically, connected sensing. So being connected through the Internet of Things and the use of AI to get real-time, remote, and complex data analyzed for us through sensing systems. I mentioned nanomedicine earlier, and with the success of lipid nanoparticle technology, I do expect to see more of that in the future as well.
Feature image courtesy Andrew Myles.

articles.title: Google Messages pourrait adopter une des meilleures fonctions d’iMessage
articles.text:
Après avoir changé sa manière de répondre aux messages, Google Messages s’attaque aux conversations. Suivre plusieurs sujets en même temps dans une conversation n’est pas toujours évident. En effet, Google Messages se contente aujourd’hui d’accrocher un aperçu du message initial au-dessus de chaque réponse. Si cette méthode est suffisante pour une réponse isolée, elle devient vite brouillonne pour une longue discussion. Mais en fouillant dans le code de la dernière version de l’application, on remarque un nouveau fil de discussion plus structuré, aussi bien dans les conversations privées que dans les messages RCS.
Suivre plus facilement les fils de discussions sur Google Messages
Sur l’interface de test qu’ont réussi à débloquer nos confrères d’Android Authority, on peut observer que les conversations sont mieux organisées, et donc tout de suite plus lisibles, grâce à des connecteurs graphiques très précis. Une ligne verticale sur la gauche relie désormais le message de départ à sa réponse. Dès qu’une conversation s’allonge ou compte au moins deux réponses, cette même ligne intègre une boucle pour marquer visuellement le fil de discussion actif. Cela fonctionne aussi bien pour les messages texte que pour les émojis ou les photos.
Source : Android Authority
Avec cette mise en page, les membres d’une conversation à plusieurs pourraient donc basculer d’un sujet à un autre sans mélanger les réponses. On note également que tout l’historique d’un sous-échange reste attaché à son point d’origine, ce qui permet de remonter le fil si nécessaire.
Lire une conversation sans distraction
Si de nouveaux messages sans rapport viennent s’intercaler dans une discussion, l’application affiche un compteur sous le message initial. En appuyant dessus, une fenêtre dédiée s’ouvre et floute l’arrière-plan de la conversation générale. Cela permet d’isoler les messages rattachés au fil de discussion que vous avez choisis et ainsi de rattraper une conversation que vous avez manquée sans devoir tout faire défiler.
Source : Android Authority
Pour répondre dans ce « sous-espace », une zone de saisie dédiée « Répondre dans le fil » s’affiche au bas de l’écran. Pour sortir de ce mode, il faut simplement toucher la zone floutée ou appuyer sur la croix située en haut à gauche. La fonctionnalité n’est toujours pas déployée sur Google Messages, mais semble malgré tout bien avancée. Reste maintenant à voir quand Google se décidera à la déployer.

articles.title: 29 millions de morceaux supprimés : Tidal bannit la musique générée par IA
articles.text:
Les plates-formes de diffusion de musique en streaming ont un gros problème. Avec l’explosion de l’IA, elles ont vu au cours des derniers mois leurs catalogues gonfler anormalement avec l’arrivée de millions de nouveaux titres provenant d’artistes inconnus.
Et pour cause, ces morceaux ne sont pas le fruit de créations humaines, mais d’intelligences artificielles. Il faut dire qu’avec la progression fulgurante de l’IA notamment en ce qui concerne la génération de musique, la tentation de faire fortune en diffusant des morceaux générés par IA sur les plates-formes de streaming est très tentante. Et ce d’autant plus que la plupart du temps, les auditeurs sont incapables de distinguer une chanson IA d’un vrai morceau.
Si certains services comme Deezer ont mis en place des outils pour détecter ces morceaux IA, dans la majorité des cas, les plates-formes se contentent simplement de les identifier en les étiquetant en tant que tels.
De son côté, Tidal vient de tirer le signal d’alarme. Après avoir démonétisé les morceaux générés par IA il y a quelques mois, l’entreprise passe à la vitesse supérieure.
Tidal retire 29 millions de morceaux IA de son catalogue
Au cours des trois derniers mois, Tidal indique avoir reçu 43 % de morceaux entièrement générés par intelligence artificielle. Une statistique inquiétante qui pousse l’entreprise à prendre des mesures draconiennes pour endiguer le problème.
 We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit. @Tidal will continue to make decisions that support real artists first. 🤘
— rsa (@rsa) November 24, 2026
Robert Anderson, un responsable de Tidal, vient ainsi d’annoncer dans un billet publié sur X / Twitter que la plate-forme allait tout simplement supprimer tous les morceaux IA de son catalogue. Leur suppression, qui doit commencer à compter du 9 décembre prochain, s’étalera jusqu’à la fin de l’année, avec environ 80 à 85 000 morceaux supprimés quotidiennement. Au total, la plate-forme va écumer son catalogue de quelque 29 millions de titres n’ayant pas été produits par des humains.
« Nous pensons que cela résonnera auprès des artistes comme des auditeurs, car 96 % de toutes les chansons générées par IA n’obtiennent aucune lecture. » a par ailleurs expliqué Robert Anderson.
Tidal, qui se félicite de cette décision, revendique être la première plate-forme de streaming à prendre ce problème à bras le corps et encourage les autres plates-formes à suivre son mouvement pour soutenir « les vrais artistes ».

articles.title: Trump admite perdoar CEO da Nvidia e pede que ele não fique em silêncio no Congresso
articles.text:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou que considera conceder um indulto presidencial a Jensen Huang, CEO da Nvidia, caso o executivo enfrente problemas judiciais. Em entrevista ao New York Post, o republicano também aconselhou o empresário a não recorrer à Quinta Emenda da Constituição estadunidense durante os depoimentos que deverá prestar ao Congresso na próxima semana.
“É sempre uma opção, eu acho, mas não acredito que será necessário”, declarou Trump ao ser questionado sobre a possibilidade de perdoar Huang por eventuais crimes federais.
O presidente disse acreditar que o executivo não precisará invocar o direito de permanecer em silêncio para evitar produzir provas contra si mesmo. Segundo Trump, Huang deve contar a verdade aos parlamentares, embora tenha reconhecido que a decisão final precisa considerar a orientação dos advogados do empresário.
O CEO da Nvidia deverá participar de duas sessões no Congresso: uma entrevista com integrantes do Comitê de Relações Exteriores da Câmara dos Representantes, em 1º de dezembro, e uma audiência no Comitê Bancário do Senado, dois dias depois.
Os parlamentares querem questioná-lo sobre possíveis violações das restrições estadunidenses à exportação de chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) para a China e eventuais riscos à segurança nacional. A investigação também ganhou repercussão após a divulgação de informações sobre relacionamentos pessoais do executivo.
Trump diz que interferiu para manter Huang no comando da Nvidia
- Durante a entrevista, Trump voltou a falar sobre sua participação no retorno de Huang à liderança da fabricante. O presidente afirmou que pressionou o conselho de administração da Nvidia para que o executivo fosse reconduzido ao cargo após breve saída;
- Segundo o republicano, a permanência de Huang é importante para a competitividade estadunidense no setor de IA. Ele argumentou que a escolha de um substituto inadequado poderia prejudicar os interesses dos Estados Unidos, especialmente diante da concorrência chinesa;
- Trump também afirmou que não se aprofundou nos detalhes dos relacionamentos extraconjugais admitidos por Huang antes de seu retorno à empresa. Um dos casos envolve Alice Huang, empresária sem parentesco com o executivo e apontada como possível espiã ligada a Pequim;
- O presidente disse que, pelo que sabia, não havia outras mulheres com ligações suspeitas com o governo chinês envolvidas com o CEO. Ele também afirmou não saber exatamente quantos relacionamentos Huang havia admitido;
- Em tom de brincadeira, Trump comentou que se concentrou mais nos negócios relacionados aos chips do que na vida sexual do executivo.
Leia mais:
- Retorno de Huang à Nvidia pode ter feito Trump lucrar US$ 15 milhões
- De volta à Nvidia, Jensen Huang fala de terapia, nega influência de Trump e descarta plano de sucessão
- Registros ligam empresas de Alice Huang a negócios de IA na China
Governo estadunidense pode adquirir participação na Nvidia
Outro assunto abordado na conversa foi a possibilidade de o governo dos Estados Unidos adquirir participação acionária na Nvidia.
Trump afirmou que já considerou a ideia, embora não tenha apresentado uma proposta à companhia. Como referência, citou o acordo envolvendo a Intel, no qual o governo estadunidense adquiriu participação equivalente a 10% da empresa.
“Eu pensei nisso. Disse: ‘Sabe, talvez eu devesse fazer isso’. Mas não mencionei neste momento. Provavelmente ainda não é tarde”, afirmou.
O presidente também comentou o desempenho das ações da Nvidia durante a entrevista. Ele acompanhou as cotações da companhia e destacou recuperação dos papéis após queda registrada anteriormente.
Trump considera a fabricante estratégica para manter a liderança estadunidense em IA. A relação próxima com Huang e a preocupação com o futuro da empresa ajudam a explicar a intervenção do presidente para garantir o retorno do executivo ao cargo.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Rackspace forced to shut down Spot cloud platform following security breach
articles.text:
Rackspace forced to shut down Spot cloud platform following security breach
Users are paying their respects on Reddit
- Attackers used stolen credentials to access Rackspace Spot, exposing Kubernetes secrets, API tokens, and other sensitive cloud resources
- Rackspace revoked affected credentials, advised customers to rotate secrets, and investigate cluster activity for potential compromise
- The company later announced it would discontinue the Rackspace Spot platform, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their workloads
Rackspace has recently announced it is shutting down its cloud platform, Rackspace Spot, allegedly after cybercriminals broke in and stole user information.
In the early hours of November 17 2026, a threat actor used stolen login credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot. The company learned about the intrusion a day later from a customer report, and later confirmed that multiple customers had been affected.
During the intrusion, the unidentified attackers created pods in people’s clusters, read Kubernetes secrets, and listed nodes and volumes.
What happened?
“With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user’s clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held,” Rackspace told the affected customers in a data breach notice emailed at the time.
Kubernetes Secrets can hold sensitive information, including database passwords, API keys, or authentication credentials. If threat actors managed to access these, they could use them to compromise other services, or systems connected to affected clusters. This is, among other things, why Rackspace urged its users to rotate their credentials, even if no data leak was confirmed.
To tackle the intrusion, Rackspace revoked affected Spot tokens and sessions, removed the pods the attackers created, and rotated the platform and storage keys involved.
The company urged its customers to reissue their Spot API tokens and replace any Spot refresh tokens stored in automation. It also told them to download fresh kubeconfigs for their cloudspaces, rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets, and review access logs from November 17 onward.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Pulling the plug
A few days after the incident, the company apparently decided it was time to sunset the whole operation. In an email notice seen by BleepingComputer, the company gave its customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data.
"Following a review of the situation, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the Rackspace Spot service. This decision is being made to provide a clear path forward for customers," the company said in the notice.
Customers have until December 8, 2026, 5PM Central Time, to move their data, after which all remaining workloads will be terminated.
The announcement did not sit well with Rackspace’s customers. Its cloud computing platform was a relatively inexpensive way to access cloud servers, virtual machines, and managed Kubernetes infrastructure. Its unique selling proposition was to offer lower cloud computing costs through a bidding system, rather than traditional fixed pricing. The company advertised savings of up to 90% compared to conventional, on-demand computing resources, with the caveat being that users must design their workloads to tolerate possible interruptions.
And tolerate them, they did. Reddit is filled with disappointed users, some of which are even urging the company to reconsider.
“I bet the vast majority of spot users would gladly pay a bit more for the service to keep it running,” one user said. “It's incomparable to anything out there right now. For the average Joe it's not the service, but for those of us who can handle our own clusters and workarounds the quirks, it's by far the best option out there.”
“Don't take this down!!!”
Others were more at peace with their fate, thanking Rackspace for the affordable compute and saying, “it was good while it lasted.” Rackspace has not commented on the calls to keep going, so we don’t know if they’re willing to reconsider.
As of November 25, 2026, no threat actors claimed responsibility for the attack on Rackspace, so we don’t know if this was ransomware or a nation-state attack. Furthermore, the data stolen in the incident doesn’t appear to have surfaced anywhere on the dark web, either for sale or for free.

articles.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
articles.text:
Unlike most smartphones, the Fairphone 6 Plus is designed for home repair, with easily replaceable parts that could help extend its lifespan well into the future. That makes its midrange price point easier to justify, especially now that it’s dropped to a new low of $552.49 (about $98 off) at Amazon as part of the retailer’s ongoing Black Friday sale.
The Fairphone 6 Plus is modular, repairable, and $100 off right now
You can replace everything from the cameras to the battery, potentially saving future you hundreds in repair costs.
The 6.3-inch Fairphone 6 Plus features 12 user-replaceable parts, including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and cameras, all of which you can swap out with the included screwdriver. Replacement parts are relatively affordable, too; a new battery costs $39.99, which helps offset its middling battery life and lack of wireless charging. It also comes with a five-year warranty and up to six Android OS upgrades, making it a good option if you want a phone you can keep using for years.
Although repairability is its marquee feature, the 6 Plus is also a solid midrange Android device. Fairphone prioritizes ethically sourced materials, making it a strong choice for environmentally conscious buyers who don’t want to sacrifice performance. Its Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor handles everyday tasks well, and its cameras take decent photos, though they’re not quite on par with those of pricier phones.
What’s more, it offers a clean, bloatware-free Android experience and modular back panels, which you can swap for optional accessories like a card holder or crossbody strap. Our own Allison Johnson particularly liked the phone’s dedicated switch for turning on customizable focus modes called Moments, which can simplify your homescreen and limit access to distracting apps — something we could all use a little less of.

articles.title: Q&A: Edmonton’s mayor on the city’s thriving deep tech scene
articles.text:
This article appears in The BetaKit Guide to Alberta’s Silicon City. Learn more about Edmonton semiconductor innovation here.
Less dependent on the boom-and-bust cycle of oil and gas than Calgary or its rural counterparts, Alberta’s capital city has traditionally featured a more diverse economic makeup than its peers. It’s home to skilled tradespeople and industrial manufacturing, a robust arts and culture sector, and, perhaps most notably, a world-class academic ecosystem that boasts eight postsecondary institutes and the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii).
“I’m a firm believer in the importance and the value of government in a lot of spaces”
In recent years, the city’s tech and startup community has come together to undertake the difficult work of commercializing that world-class research, endeavouring to turn decades of knowledge into an economic engine. The result is a growing deep tech sector that’s quickly gained prominence within Alberta.
BetaKit wanted to find out why so much deep tech is deciding to call Edmonton home, and what the sector’s interest in the city means for Edmonton and Alberta’s economic future. We sat down with Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack to find out, and discuss what the city can do to make sure deep tech succeeds.
The following interview has been edited for both length and clarity.
How and why has Edmonton, and Alberta, become a hub for deep tech? 
A few things have contributed to this. One is the strength of our postsecondary system and the talent that gets created here. We have eight postsecondaries, with anywhere from about 110,000 to 130,000 students, and they complement one another. That means you get different types of talent coming out of each group. That coalition has produced a lot of incredible talent. It’s also helped to create groups like Amii, which has attracted immense talent as well. These world-leading talents are able to say, “Hey, I come to Edmonton and I have this pipeline coming out of post-secondary.”
The other piece, which might not sound connected, is that Edmonton is also the most affordable major city in Canada. If you are somebody who is starting out in your career, you can maybe take on that job or research position that might not make a tonne of money at the start, but because of our cost of living, it gives you the opportunity to get started, build that foundation that allows you to grow into something bigger. If you’re taking a risk—and risk is significant in this space—this is the best place to take that risk.
How important is Edmonton’s tech sector to the city’s economy?
Really important. Alberta is known for being an oil and gas economy, and certainly Edmonton has been a part of that. But if you look at the last 10 or 20 years, the proportion of Edmonton’s economy that is tied to the natural resource sector is much lower than many other cities in Alberta. For us, that means we’re not as reliant on the boom-and-bust cycle, and so we can branch out into other sectors. There’s more we can do to support growth in that tech and deep tech space, but I think there’s a really strong foundation.
You mention there are things you think Edmonton can be doing better. What are they?
The one thing that Edmonton has been lacking is making sure we’re also putting in financial resources as a city. A lot of cities say they care about these sectors, and then might not invest the resources—the financial resources—to further expand on that, and I would say Edmonton’s been guilty of that.
In the City’s upcoming draft budget, there is a service package that is recommended to be funded called the Edmonton Advantage, which looks to start investing more resources into the overall economy and actually trying to encourage more businesses to start up here, higher job creation, and business growth in a way that we really haven’t done in my 13 years on council.
We don’t want to be the only ones doing this. We know this space, this deep tech space, needs support from many other investors, and it needs a strong ecosystem. I don’t think we’re looking to replace the ecosystem; it is growing, but we want to make sure we’re supplementing that work.
Amii has been an anchor for the deep tech community here. Now it’s been tapped to lead a national AI literacy program. What opportunities does that open up for Alberta in the global conversation? Does it elevate the City and province’s profile on the broader tech landscape?
I would say yes. It helps with that, being able to say, “Hey, the federal government has acknowledged the need to support this work, and has said the best group to do that in the country is right here in Edmonton,” will hold a lot of weight. When you have Amii going across the world to share that message, people will see that, hear that, and understand that, and see the opportunity that comes with that, as well.
One of the things we hear within the deep tech community is the challenge that comes with trying to commercialize a lot of this research. Is there anything Edmonton could do better to connect these post-secondary institutes with the startup community?
I’m a firm believer in the importance and the value of government in a lot of spaces, but this is an area that moves so quickly, and it is hard for us to take the lead in any of this work.
I do think our role is creating an environment where more investors see this as a viable solution. That can mean something as simple as the city being maybe the first customer for some of these projects as a proof of concept to allow that commercialization to become more defined or to more easily attract investors. This doesn’t just need to be city governance. I’m talking about the broader city, the business community, the post-secondary community—all of these spaces can benefit from the work of deep tech. Have they set themselves up in a way that allows us to test out the talents that these folks have to help improve the work that we’re doing?
Can you leave us with one thing you think we could all do a better job of cheerleading when it comes to deep tech in Alberta?
The broader question is, does the average person know about this? And I don’t think they do. I’ll be the first to acknowledge that I still feel like I don’t even fully appreciate just how good we are in this space. I hear it more and more: “Oh wow, this is bigger than we give it credit for.” We have a lot of Edmontonians who I don’t even think know what that means, let alone how we succeed in this space. This community is one that can sometimes still feel a little daunting. So, how do we simplify that?
Feature image courtesy Andrew Knack.

articles.title: Automotive Power, Charging, Load-Control Solutions at electronica
articles.text:
Vehicle electrical architectures are consolidating into fewer, more capable domain controllers, and each step in that direction raises the demands placed on the power and driver ICs around them. Supply rails must be sequenced and monitored to meet functional safety targets, cabin charging ports are expected to deliver laptop-class power from a 12 V system, and body loads once switched by relays now require diagnostics and programmable current limits.
At electronica in Munich, Southchip addressed these requirements with an automotive electronics exhibit organized around three application areas: intelligent cockpit, intelligent driving, and intelligent powertrain. The booth featured evaluation hardware for four product families: power management ICs (PMICs), USB and wireless charging, ambient lighting, and high-side drivers (HSDs). All of Southchip’s automotive products are AEC-Q100 qualified, and the company has the capability to meet the ASIL-D functional safety level, reflecting its position that quality and reliability come first.
Intelligent Cockpit: Charging and Ambient Lighting
Charging is the area in which Southchip established its reputation. The company’s USB and wireless charging solutions are well recognized by customers in the consumer electronics market, where the company has a strong, proven track record. Southchip now applies that experience to the vehicle cabin, where occupants expect phones, tablets, and laptops to charge as quickly as they do at a desk.
For high-power USB Type-C ports, Southchip demonstrated an EPR 240 W charging solution that pairs the SC8708Q, an 80 V automotive-grade buck-boost controller, with the SC2006Q automotive-grade protocol IC. The design supports 240 W Extended Power Range fast charging in a dual-port configuration. Where board area and component count carry more weight, the SC87580Q integrates the charging function in a single chip. It delivers up to 100 W with only one external MOSFET, reaches a peak efficiency of up to 97%, supports multiple mainstream charging protocols, and can be paralleled for dual PD-port applications. A complete USB module built on the SC8741Q and SC2021Q extended the concept with DisplayPort input and output, allowing a phone to charge while mirroring its screen to the head unit, or VR/AR glasses to charge while receiving video from it.
For wireless charging, the SC50080Q driver IC is compliant with the WPC Qi standard and supports up to 50 W under the Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) and up to 80 W under CPP. High-precision current sensing, foreign object detection, multichannel demodulation outputs, and UVLO, OVP, OCP, and OTP protection are integrated on-chip.
Ambient lighting was represented by the SC90039, a 30-channel ambient light driver MCU that integrates a 32-bit processor, a 2 A buck converter, and a LIN transceiver. Its 30 independent constant-current channels each drive up to 60 mA, with two-channel time-division multiplexing. The device is AEC-Q100 Grade 1 qualified and ASIL-B compliant, and it is supported by visual development tools for light-effect design and system debugging.
Intelligent Driving: Automotive PMIC Portfolio
ADAS domain controllers, cameras, and radar modules each impose distinct requirements on rail count, input range, and supervision. Southchip addresses them with more than ten automotive PMIC variants offering four to nine output channels and input-voltage coverage from 2.7 V to 60 V across the lineup. Spread-spectrum operation and wettable-flank packages are standard across the range, and the domain-control devices add watchdog and FCCU or ERR pin monitoring.
The SC62595Q is an ASIL-D MCU PMIC for ADAS domain control. It integrates seven power rails with more than 100 configurable power and logic functions on a single chip and accepts inputs from 3 V to 60 V. For the SoC side of the controller, the ASIL-D SC6209Q operates from a 2.7 V to 5.5 V input and integrates four 6 A synchronous buck converters and two 400 mA LDOs. Fixed-frequency constant-on-time control provides fast transient response, and multi-page one-time programmable memory with four user pages, selected through a PRESET pin, lets a single part number serve several rail configurations.
For millimeter-wave radar modules, the SC6207Q radar PMIC provides multiple rails from inputs up to 36 V. Its high efficiency reduces self-heating and the associated thermal noise, which supports precise and uniform radar imaging. At the sensor edge, where camera modules leave little board area for power conversion, the SC6206AQ camera PMIC stands out for its footprint: its QFN-18 package is notably smaller than comparable camera PMICs currently on the market. Within that compact package, the device integrates three buck converters and one LDO, operates from 4 V to 19 V, and is ASIL-B capable, with 1% undervoltage and overvoltage monitors and 1.5% output-voltage accuracy. Southchip complemented these devices with the SCP25501 serializer and SCP25502 deserializer, a MIPI A-PHY compliant link that carries camera video at up to 4 Gbps with 1.25 µs of latency.
Intelligent Powertrain: High-Side Drivers and Protection
Southchip’s high-side driver portfolio comprises over 20 part numbers in single-, dual-, and quad-channel configurations. Load-current classes extend from 1 A to 30 A, with on-resistance from 1.2 mΩ at the high-current end to 100 mΩ and above for low-current loads, so designers can match the switch to the load rather than oversizing it.
The SC77101Q single-channel driver offers an adjustable current limit with high monitoring accuracy, along with diagnostic and protection functions that report faults in real time. The four-channel SC77450CQ combines 50 mΩ on-resistance, a 4 V to 28 V input range, 0.5 µA standby current, and 40 V load-dump capability, built on a vertically integrated process.
Two further devices round out the powertrain display. The SC77010Q eFuse supports inputs from 4.5 V to 70 V, covering 12 V, 24 V, and 48 V systems, and provides diagnostics and high-precision current sensing for intelligent control of external FET loads. The SC77870HQ full-bridge driver operates from 4.5 V to 35 V and delivers up to 12 A for domain controller, chassis, and valve applications, with strong transient thermal performance under software-controlled current-limit stall conditions.
Quality, Reliability, and Functional Safety
Across all three application areas, Southchip treats quality and reliability as its top priorities. All of its automotive products are AEC-Q100 qualified, and the company’s development capability extends to ASIL-D. Functional safety classifications are assigned per device, from QM and ASIL-B for camera and lighting functions to ASIL-D for the PMICs that supply ADAS domain controllers. Integrated voltage monitoring, watchdog supervision, current sensing, and fault diagnostics carry the same priorities from the PMICs through to the load switches.
Conclusion
Southchip’s presence at electronica demonstrated a portfolio that spans cabin charging and lighting, safety-rated power management for ADAS, and protected load control for body and powertrain systems. To support European automotive customers, Southchip maintains a dedicated local team in Europe, enabling fast response and hands-on technical support from evaluation through production.

PCIe SVC; co-packaged optics; liquid-cooled data center model; LUT-GEMM; automotive traceability.
Cadence’s Igor Krause examines PCIe’s Streamlined Virtual Channel Extended Capability, which aims to address limitations of the traditional PCIe ordering model in modern multi-host fabrics by introducing a standardized approach for TC-to-VC assignment.
