articles.text:
El mundo no se pone de acuerdo sobre los robots asesinos: “Pueden acelerar una escalada de la violencia”
Naciones Unidas ha sido incapaz de impulsar el control o prohibición de las armas autónomas, que ya han matado en algunos escenarios bélicos y cuya proliferación podría cambiar la naturaleza de la guerra
El lado oscuro de la inteligencia artificial (IA) ha entrado este año con fuerza en la conversación pública. ¿Provocará una “posible extinción”, como declaró un ingeniero de Anthropic? ¿Se volverá “incontrolable”, asumirá una agenda propia? Mientras los focos se centran en este debate, pese a no haber indicio científico alguno de que pueda suceder algo así, se está desarrollando una negociación para afrontar un problema mucho más inmediato: qué hacer con las armas autónomas, es decir, las que seleccionan y atacan a sus objetivos sin intervención humana. El resultado es, hasta ahora, un fracaso: los países no se ponen de acuerdo en prohibir este tipo de armamento.
El último revés llegó el pasado fin de semana, cuando la ONU no consiguió dar el pistoletazo de salida de unas negociaciones que pudieran acabar en un tratado vinculante sobre el uso de armas autónomas, también conocidas como robots asesinos. Rusia fue quien bloqueó esa opción, aunque otros países, como EE UU, Japón, Corea del Sur, Alemania, Francia o Reino Unido, también se mostraron contrarios a firmar un acuerdo vinculante.
La reunión, que se desarrollaba en el marco de la Convención sobre ciertas armas convencionales (CAC) de Naciones Unidas, necesitaba el consenso para abrir la puerta a un posible tratado sobre armas autónomas. Un solo voto podía frenarlo todo. Y así fue, pese a que la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas aprobó el mes pasado una resolución, apoyada por 163 de los 195 países con derecho a voto, en la que se solicita al organismo a negociar un instrumento internacional para controlar este tipo de armas.
“No cabe duda de que la IA se ha desplegado de forma muy prominente en el campo de batalla, especialmente en las guerras de Medio Oriente, tanto en Gaza como en Irán, y en Ucrania. La carrera armamentista está en pleno apogeo”, dice a EL PAÍS Cordula Droege, responsable legal del Comité Internacional de la Cruz Roja (CICR). La jurista intervino hace ahora un año en el Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas precisamente para alertar de la necesidad de alcanzar un acuerdo para limitar la proliferación de este tipo de armas.
Ningún estado afirma abiertamente tener operativas armas autónomas, más allá de sistemas antimisiles que se disparan automáticamente cuando el sistema detecta la presencia de un proyectil. Sin embargo, tal y como apunta Droege, se han encontrado drones no tripulados, capaces de operar y disparar por sí mismos, en varios escenarios bélicos. En las trincheras de Ucrania, soldados rusos y ucranios han muerto ejecutados por sistemas totalmente autónomos, según publicó el New York Times. Se sabe que las grandes potencias militares invierten en este tipo de sistemas para conseguir que sus drones sigan funcionando en caso de que haya interferencias.
Para Droege, la proliferación de robots asesinos plantea serios problemas inmediatos. “Las armas con escasa o nula intervención humana corren el riesgo de causar una escalada de la violencia mucho más rápida porque los humanos no podrán detenerlas a tiempo”, señala. Al desplegarse para actuar con gran velocidad y a gran escala, añade, pueden multiplicar las violaciones del Derecho Internacional Humanitario que ya ocurren en los conflictos, como por ejemplo no distinguir entre combatientes y civiles.
Cruzar la línea roja moral
Y luego está el aspecto moral. “Atacar a seres humanos basándose en datos y sensores, sin agencia humana y sin respetar la dignidad de las víctimas, sería cruzar una línea roja que hasta ahora es tabú”.
Una de las ideas o mitos que rodean la aplicación de IA a las cuestiones públicas, también a la guerra, es la neutralidad o imparcialidad, el hecho de que sus decisiones no sean sesgadas. Nada más lejos de la realidad: múltiples estudios han demostrado que los algoritmos incorporan los sesgos de quienes los programan y los de los datos con los que se entrena el sistema. En el caso de los robots asesinos, esos sesgos pueden redundar en muertes.
También se suele atribuir a la IA una eficiencia superior a la humana. En el ámbito militar, ya se ha comprobado la invalidez del argumento. El algoritmo Lavender, por ejemplo, usado por el ejército de Israel para seleccionar las víctimas de sus bombardeos en los primeros meses de su invasión de Gaza, consideraba lícito que murieran hasta 100 personas de forma colateral siempre que se matara al objetivo principal. Así, se documentó que para acabar con algunos altos cargos de Hamás o Yihad Islámica se bombardearon por la noche (para asegurarse de que estuvieran en casa) varios bloques de viviendas (el edificio en el que vivían y los aledaños), matando así también a familiares y vecinos.
Más tecnología no significa menos bajas. “Los conflictos actuales cuentan con el armamento más sofisticado, pero no dejan de ser brutales ni evitan generar más muertes, lesiones y destrucción masiva”, apunta Droege. “Buen ejemplo de ello es lo que ocurre en Sudán, donde el aumento del uso de drones por las partes en conflicto ha puesto en grave peligro a los civiles en barrios residenciales, e incluso el propio equipo del CICR ha sufrido incidentes de seguridad”.
¿Es posible prohibirlas?
La incorporación de la IA a las fuerzas armadas es una de las banderas que ha enarbolado el presidente de EE UU, Donald Trump, desde que volvió a la Casa Blanca. Hasta el punto de cerrar contratos con empresas comerciales, como OpenAI o Google, lo que provocó quejas entre sus empleados, o de castigar a otras, como Anthropic, por no plegarse a ceder al Pentágono sus algoritmos.
¿Qué pasará a partir de ahora? Pese a que se le haya dado carpetazo a su negociación, ¿sigue siendo posible algún tipo de acuerdo internacional para controlar este armamento? “Creemos que la puerta no está completamente cerrada, continuaremos trabajando para conseguirlo”, asegura Droege. “Entre el 80% y el 90% de los ciudadanos, según varias encuestas, así como la industria y la comunidad científica, exigen que la IA y estas armas sean reguladas. Falta ver dónde está la valentía política de los gobiernos para responder a este llamamiento”, concluye.
“La historia demuestra que los tratados internacionales pueden prohibir o restringir con éxito las armas más inaceptables, desde las biológicas y químicas hasta las minas antipersona y las municiones en racimo”, dijo hace dos semanas su jefa, la presidenta del CICR, Mirjana Spoljaric. “No se puede permitir que las armas autónomas se desarrollen y proliferen sin normas internacionales ni un control humano efectivo. Las generaciones futuras juzgarán si los líderes actuaron para evitar un mundo en el que las máquinas maten a seres humanos de forma autónoma”.

articles.title: Il est désormais possible de se connecter à FranceConnect avec l'application carte Vitale
articles.text:
Une nouvelle méthode rejoint les six existantes pour vous connecter à FranceConnect. L'application carte Vitale est désormais de la partie, pour près de 4 millions d'utilisateurs.
L'application carte Vitale rejoint la liste des fournisseurs d'identité de FranceConnect. Elle permet depuis peu de se connecter à plus de 1 800 services publics en ligne, grâce à une double authentification sur smartphone. L'objectif : simplifier les démarches des usagers.
Un moyen d'identification supplémentaire
Pour accéder à une démarche en ligne via FranceConnect, il fallait jusqu'ici utiliser l'un des comptes ou identités numériques déjà reconnus par le dispositif : impots.gouv, compte ameli, France identité, MSA, Trustme ou l'INLP. L'application carte Vitale s'ajoute à cette liste. Elle concerne les 3,8 millions d'assurés qui l'ont téléchargée et activée.
Le parcours se déroule en trois étapes. L'usager choisit « FranceConnect » sur le site de la démarche qu'il souhaite effectuer, sélectionne l'application carte Vitale parmi les fournisseurs d'identité proposés, puis valide la connexion sur son téléphone.
Cette validation repose sur deux éléments : le smartphone sur lequel l'application a été activée, et l'identification par biométrie ou par mot de passe. Une personne qui ne disposerait que de l'un des deux ne pourrait pas se connecter à la place de l'usager.
Parmi les services accessibles par cette méthode figurent le portail des Allocations familiales (CAF), le portail Ameli, les sites de l'Agence nationale des titres sécurisés (ANTS) et info-retraite.fr.
Deux modes d'utilisation
L'application peut servir à s'identifier de deux manières, complémentaires.
Via FranceConnect, cette option s'adresse aux usagers qui veulent accéder aux services en ligne compatibles. Seules les données d'identité civile sont alors transmises.
Par accès direct, les fournisseurs de services peuvent intégrer le bouton « M'identifier avec mon appli carte Vitale » dans leur propre parcours d'identification. Cette option concerne en particulier les secteurs de la santé, du social et du médico-social : prise de rendez-vous en ligne, pré-admission en ligne dans les établissements de santé, téléconsultation, etc. Selon les données demandées et autorisées, il est possible de transmettre l'identité civile, l'Identité Nationale de Santé (INS) et des informations relatives à l'assurance maladie obligatoire. Les informations sur l'assurance maladie complémentaire sont prévues par la suite.
Ce second mode répond notamment aux besoins des acteurs du numérique en santé dont les démarches exigent une vérification d'identité renforcée. Les premiers services pourront intégrer la fonctionnalité au fur et à mesure que les fournisseurs concernés y seront autorisés.
Source : Gouvernement

articles.title: GTA 6 fait flamber les ventes de PS5 d’occasion, et les escrocs de Vinted en profitent
articles.text:
L’arnaque revient à chaque pénurie de consoles. Pris de court par les ruptures de stock chez les revendeurs officiels avec la sortie de GTA 6, le 19 novembre 2026, de nombreux joueurs se rabattent dans l’urgence sur les plateformes de seconde main pour mettre la main sur une PlayStation 5. C’est précisément sur cette fébrilité que misent des vendeurs malintentionnés sur Vinted : les signalements d’annonces piégées s’enchaînent depuis plusieurs jours sur le réseau social X.
À première vue, ces offres ont tout de l’aubaine rêvée : des visuels propres, un boîtier sous blister ou posé sur une table de salon, et un tarif nettement inférieur aux prix habituels du marché. L’acheteur pressé, persuadé de devancer des dizaines d’autres intéressés, valide le paiement en quelques secondes sans se méfier. Ce n’est qu’au moment de récupérer un colis anormalement léger en point relais que le piège se referme sur l’acheteur : à l’intérieur de l’enveloppe ne se trouve aucune console, mais une simple feuille A4 sur laquelle a été imprimée la photo de la PS5.
Une mention de photo PS5 noyée dans les tags, pour tromper l’acheteur et la plateforme Vinted
Si cette méthode avait déjà fait des victimes lors du lancement de la PS5 en 2020, ou plus récemment autour de la Nintendo Switch 2, sa version actuelle pousse le vice encore plus loin. Auparavant, les fraudeurs se contentaient généralement de glisser une phrase ambiguë tout en bas de la description, espérant qu’elle passerait inaperçue. Désormais, plusieurs annonces repérées par les internautes sur X dissimulent la mention « c’est une photo » ou « photo uniquement » directement au milieu d’une longue liste de hashtags en fin de texte.
Sur l’interface mobile de Vinted, où les descriptions longues sont tronquées et nécessitent un clic supplémentaire pour être déployées en entier, cette précision devient totalement invisible pour un acheteur qui parcourt rapidement l’annonce. L’objectif derrière cette ruse est double : tromper la vigilance du client tout en se constituant un alibi technique face au service client de la plateforme.
Car une fois le colis ouvert, obtenir gain de cause relève souvent du parcours du combattant. Les politiques de protection des plateformes d’occasion couvrent en priorité les colis perdus, endommagés ou non conformes à l’annonce. En prétendant avoir indiqué la nature réelle de l’objet dans le texte, même de façon dissimulée, l’escroc tente de bloquer le remboursement automatique en soutenant que l’acheteur a reçu exactement ce qui était écrit.
Face à la multiplication de ces signalements en pleine fièvre GTA 6, la règle d’or reste donc la même : fuir les tarifs trop beaux pour être vrais et systématiquement lire l’intégralité d’une annonce, jusqu’au dernier tag, avant de dégainer sa carte bancaire.

articles.title: Un moteur de GTI dans un SUV électrique : voici le Volkswagen ID. Cross R-Line, mais attention au prix
articles.text:
Dans son marasme actuel, Volkswagen peut toutefois se raccrocher à un succès : les débuts tonitruants de sa nouvelle gamme de citadines électriques, à savoir l’ID. Polo, l’ID. Cross, et les cousines Skoda Epiq et Cupra Raval.
    Pour aller plus loin
« C’est impossible à faire » : comment Volkswagen a réussi à produire 4 citadines électriques à 25 000 € en Europe
            
Maintenant que toute la gamme est lancée, place à plus de diversité. Volkswagen annonce ainsi l’arrivée d’une version R-Line sur l’ID. Cross, de quoi offrir plus de caractère au petit SUV électrique… mais aussi le moteur de l’ID. Polo GTI dans les mois à venir.
Une petite batterie encore sage…
Sur la petite batterie de 37 kWh, l’ID. Cross R-Line n’ira pas plus loin qu’une présentation plus affûtée. Pare-choc spécifiques aux feux de jours verticaux, jantes de 19 pouces, monogrammes dédiés, sièges sport à la sellerie spécifique : tout est là pour le show.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
La liste d’équipements s’allonge, avec l’arrivée en série de l’ouverture et démarrage sans clé, des phares matriciels ou de la caméra de recul. La base technique reste pour autant identique, avec un moteur de 99 kW (135 ch) et une batterie LFP de 37 kWh offrant 314 km d’autonomie selon le cycle WLTP.
Les commandes sont déjà ouvertes, et cet ID. Cross R-Line vous coûtera 38 450 euros minimum. Certes, il faudra retrancher le coup de pouce CEE (nouveau nom du bonus écologique) de 3 535 euros minimum, mais cela commence à faire (très) cher pour une voiture du quotidien.
…et une grosse batterie qui se prend pour une GTI
En revanche, la grande batterie de 52 kWh est beaucoup plus intéressante : certes, l’accastillage est repris, mais les ingénieurs Volkswagen se sont amusés à y intégrer le moteur de… l’ID. Polo GTI.
Nous voilà donc face à un ID. Cross de 166 kW (226 ch) et 290 Nm de couple, capable de passer de 0 à 100 km/h en 6,9 secondes et d’atteindre les 175 km/h en vitesse de pointe.
Pas question pour autant d’arborer le mythique badge GTI (privilège réservé aux voitures basses, comme l’ID. Polo et l’ID.3 Neo), mais notons tout de même quelques évolutions du châssis pour canaliser la puissance et améliorer le comportement.
    Pour aller plus loin
La Volkswagen GTI la plus puissante de l’histoire est une voiture électrique à propulsion : voici l’ID.3 GTI
            
Ainsi, la suspension perd 15 mm et devient adaptative, tandis qu’un différentiel électronique permettra de mieux réguler la cavalerie, qui continue de passer uniquement sur les roues avant. Toujours pour une histoire de motricité, un mode de conduite « Traction » fait son apparition pour les chaussées glissantes.
La batterie de 52 kWh est reprise, mais l’autonomie n’y perd pas (trop) de plumes avec 428 kilomètres WLTP en une charge. C’est même… deux kilomètres de plus que le reste de la gamme.
Les commandes ouvriront mi-mars 2027, à des tarifs qu’on imagine déjà haut perchés, et forcément plus haut que les 41 650 euros demandés par l’ID. Cross Style, l’actuel haut de gamme.

articles.title: Instagram rechaza que use el micrófono de celulares para escuchar conversaciones y dar publicidad
articles.text:
El responsable de Instagram, Adam Mosseri, explicó por qué un producto mencionado entre amigos puede aparecer después en la pantalla, sin que la aplicación tenga que grabar las conversaciones.
El director de Instagram, Adam Mosseri, negó que la plataforma utilice el micrófono de los celulares para escuchar conversaciones privadas y seleccionar anuncios con base en lo que dicen los usuarios. El ejecutivo respondió a una de las dudas más frecuentes sobre las redes sociales de Meta y explicó por qué algunas personas encuentran publicidad relacionada con asuntos de los que hablaron poco antes.
Además, dijo que realizar esa práctica representaría una vulneración grave de la privacidad de los usuarios.
El directivo señaló que recibe esta pregunta constantemente, debido a una experiencia que muchas personas aseguran haber vivido: conversan sobre un producto, una película, un artista o un tema específico y, poco después, encuentran publicaciones o anuncios relacionados en Instagram o Facebook.
Para Mosseri, esta coincidencia tiene explicaciones vinculadas con la forma en que las personas perciben la publicidad y con los sistemas que utiliza Meta para mostrar contenido relevante. La compañía sostiene que no necesita escuchar las conversaciones para anticipar qué anuncios podrían interesar a cada usuario.
Por qué Instagram niega que escuche las conversaciones
Uno de los argumentos que presentó Mosseri es que el uso constante del micrófono dejaría señales visibles en el funcionamiento del celular. Según explicó, si Instagram estuviera grabando conversaciones de manera permanente, el consumo de batería podría aumentar y aparecería el indicador luminoso que informa cuando el micrófono está activo.
En los dispositivos compatibles, ese aviso permite identificar cuándo una aplicación utiliza el micrófono o la cámara. Por ello, el responsable de Instagram considera que una actividad de escucha permanente sería difícil de mantener sin que los usuarios detectaran algún indicio.
El ejecutivo también afirmó que utilizar esos recursos para obtener información privada supondría una violación de la privacidad. Su declaración busca responder a las sospechas que circulan desde hace años sobre el funcionamiento de las plataformas digitales y sus sistemas de publicidad personalizada.
Sin embargo, la explicación de Mosseri no significa que Instagram carezca de mecanismos para recopilar información sobre los intereses de sus usuarios. La plataforma utiliza diferentes señales de actividad para determinar qué publicaciones, recomendaciones y anuncios pueden resultar relevantes.
Tres razones por las que aparecen anuncios sobre temas de conversación
Mosseri presentó tres explicaciones para entender por qué una persona puede hablar de un asunto y encontrar publicidad relacionada poco después.
La primera tiene que ver con la atención. Es posible que el usuario ya haya visto varias veces un anuncio en Instagram, pero no le haya prestado suficiente atención. Después de conversar sobre ese producto o servicio, comienza a reconocerlo con mayor facilidad cuando vuelve a aparecer en la pantalla.
La segunda explicación está relacionada con la percepción. Cuando alguien habla sobre un tema, este permanece más presente en su memoria. Por esa razón, puede identificarlo con mayor rapidez en publicaciones, anuncios o situaciones cotidianas que antes habría pasado por alto.
La tercera razón está vinculada con los datos que utiliza Meta para personalizar la publicidad. Mosseri explicó que la plataforma puede aprovechar información sobre el usuario, sus amigos y personas con características o intereses similares para seleccionar anuncios.
Esto significa que una conversación puede coincidir con una publicidad debido a patrones de comportamiento compartidos. Por ejemplo, si una persona interactúa con contenidos relacionados con un producto o mantiene vínculos con usuarios interesados en él, los sistemas publicitarios pueden considerar que también podría resultarle atractivo.
Cómo utiliza Meta los datos para mostrar publicidad
Las plataformas de Meta cuentan con sistemas que analizan diferentes señales para organizar el contenido que aparece en sus servicios. Entre ellas se encuentran las interacciones con publicaciones, las páginas visitadas, las cuentas seguidas y los intereses que pueden inferirse a partir de la actividad digital.
Estos mecanismos permiten construir perfiles publicitarios y seleccionar anuncios según la probabilidad de que llamen la atención de una persona. También explican por qué dos usuarios pueden recibir publicidad diferente aunque utilicen la misma aplicación.
La aclaración de Mosseri no elimina las preguntas sobre la privacidad y el uso de información personal en Instagram. La discusión también incluye qué datos recopilan las plataformas, cómo los relacionan con la actividad de terceros y qué opciones tienen los usuarios para limitar la personalización.
Por ahora, el responsable de Instagram mantiene que la compañía no necesita activar el micrófono para conocer los intereses de las personas. La publicidad personalizada se basa en información sobre la actividad digital y las conexiones entre usuarios, una práctica que puede generar coincidencias que parecen indicar que las aplicaciones escuchan conversaciones privadas.

articles.title: VU Venture Partners launches India VC accelerator, investment platform
articles.text:
VU Venture Partners launches India VC accelerator, investment platform
VU Venture Partners is bringing its venture-capital accelerator and startup investment platform to India, targeting early-stage companies while training prospective investors through Venture University.
US-based VU Venture Partners is bringing its venture-capital investor accelerator to India and plans to evaluate investments of $100,000 to $1 million in local startups. It said it will focus on seed and Series A, early funding rounds for young companies, combining investor training with access to its global investment network.
The programme will be delivered through Venture University, which VU said it established in 2018. Its first Indian cohort is scheduled to begin on April 5, 2027, with up to 25 participants accepted each quarter.
The 11-week course includes a 40-hour venture-capital masterclass and is followed by an apprenticeship of around three to 12 months alongside VU Venture Partners. Participants join one of nine sector teams, help assess investments and share in their cohort portfolio’s profits. VU said they may help select between seven and 28 investments over one to four cohorts.
The firm noted earlier cohorts collectively invested more than $80 million in over 125 companies, including SpaceX and OpenAI.
Founder and General Partner J. Skyler Fernandes said the programme was intended to provide practical experience. “Venture University equips individuals with practical knowledge, skills and investment experience, helping them build a track record,” he said.
For startups, VU noted it will use its global fund and a syndicate of more than 8,000 accredited investors, a network that co-invests in individual deals, to assess Indian companies. Its stated interests include AI, robotics, space and defence, advanced computing, healthcare, fintech and industrials.
The company said it has already invested in diagnostics and IVF provider Redcliffe Labs and hostel operator goSTOPS.
Anaina Malik, a partner on VU’s India team, said the firm wanted to connect founders with networks as well as capital. “India has a deep and diverse founder ecosystem, and we see an opportunity to connect ambitious Indian companies with the expertise and networks that can help them scale,” she said.
The launch comes as India’s private-capital market expands but becomes more selective. EY and the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association reported $60.7 billion in combined private-equity and venture-capital investment across 1,475 deals in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, investment totalled $17.1 billion, including $4.8 billion in startup deals.
Yet a Grant Thornton Bharat and IVCA report said domestic venture fundraising doubled to $5.4 billion in 2025 while seed funding fell 37% in the first nine months of 2026, pointing to tougher conditions for younger companies and emerging fund managers.
Other investors are also moving into specialist technology. Earlier this week, CortexSpark Ventures announced a Rs 1,000 crore deep-tech fund focused on areas including space, defence, robotics and AI.
Government schemes are intended to widen funding options. The Rs 10,000 crore Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 channels capital through registered alternative investment funds, pooled vehicles that invest in startups, rather than investing directly.
The separate Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation scheme is designed to provide longer-term finance for areas including deep technology, AI, robotics and space.

articles.title: Ce smartphone Samsung noté 4,5/5 perd 230,11 € à l'occasion du Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le smartphone Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra 256 Go à 859,99 € (-21%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra passe à 859,99 € chez Boulanger.com, soit une baisse d'environ 21 % et 230,11 € d'économie. Samsung a conçu le Galaxy S25 Ultra pour incarner le sommet de sa gamme de smartphones, aussi bien sur le plan matériel que logiciel. Par rapport au Galaxy S24 Ultra, ce modèle gagne encore en puissance et en autonomie. L'appareil avait pleinement convaincu notre laboratoire lors de ses essais.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra descend à 859,99 € chez Boulanger.com, soit environ 21 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (1 090,10 €). Cela représente une économie de 230,11 €.
Affichage lumineux et performances de premier ordre
Ce smartphone intègre une dalle de 6,9 pouces affichant une définition de 3120 x 1440 pixels, particulièrement lumineuse pour garantir une lisibilité sans faille en extérieur. articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
  November 11, 2026
- Source:
  ETH Zurich
- Summary:
  Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: MTN’s proposed Telkom takeover comes with a competition cost
articles.text:
South Africa’s telecoms industry may be heading for a major restructuring, with MTN, Africa’s largest mobile network operator, and Telkom, a major telecommunications provider, revisiting acquisition talks four years after previous negotiations collapsed. A deal could combine two major mobile businesses and one of the country’s largest fibre networks.
While a larger operator could pool infrastructure, reduce duplicated investment and strengthen its capacity to finance expensive next-generation networks, absorbing Telkom would also remove an independent infrastructure competitor. This could potentially weaken competition and limit choices for smaller operators, internet service providers and consumers.
The talks’ outcome will determine how smaller operators negotiate network access, whether internet service providers retain competitive wholesale options and, ultimately, whether consumers continue benefiting from affordable connectivity. 
Consolidation may strengthen network operators’ balance sheets, but without meaningful regulatory safeguards, it could also concentrate control over the infrastructure on which much of the digital economy depends.
The economics of getting bigger
MTN Group chief executive officer (CEO) Ralph Mupita has consistently argued that South Africa has too many mobile network operators competing for a limited pool of industry profits. In a 2023 interview with McKinsey, a global management consulting firm, he explained why the group believes consolidation is necessary.
“Most markets still have four or more operators licensed to operate and provide full infrastructure and services to their customers,” Mupita said, asserting that the capital required to maintain independent networks makes returns difficult to sustain. He added that some markets would move towards two operators, while others would settle at three.
Mupita’s argument reflects the economics of telecommunications. Building and maintaining mobile networks requires substantial investment in spectrum, base stations, fibre backhaul, electricity and technology upgrades. Operators must continually spend to improve coverage and capacity while competing to attract and retain subscribers.
Combining MTN and Telkom could therefore o eliminate duplicated infrastructure spending, improve network utilisation and direct more capital towards 5G and fibre expansion. MTN would also gain access to Telkom’s established fixed-line and enterprise businesses.
Consolidation also has potential consumer benefits. A larger operator could spread investment across more subscribers, reduce duplicated infrastructure costs and make network expansion into underserved areas more viable.
If these efficiencies translate to lower costs, better network quality and more affordable services, consumers could benefit. Fewer operators do not necessarily mean weaker competition, particularly where fibre providers, internet service providers (ISPs) and mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs) offer alternatives to traditional mobile networks.
For instance, Telkom’s group revenue increased 2% to R22.5 billion ($1.3 billion), according to its latest interim results. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose 5.8% to R6.4 billion ($377 million).
Its mobile business generated R13.3 billion ($764 million) in revenue, with mobile data subscribers increasing 13.6% to 21 million. Openserve, Telkom’s fibre business, meanwhile, recorded 15.1% growth in connected homes to 870,856.
“The next phase of Telkom’s transformation is not simply about proving that our business can withstand a changing market. It is about demonstrating that we can consistently convert our customer relationships, infrastructure and capabilities into sustainable earnings, cash generation and long-term value,” Telkom chief executive (CEO) Serame Taukobong said in a statement on November 17.
Telkom’s growth makes it an attractive acquisition target beyond its infrastructure assets. Its expanding mobile subscriber base would give MTN additional scale, while Openserve’s fibre footprint would strengthen its fixed broadband offering.
MTN would gain established revenue streams, a growing mobile competitor and an established wholesale fibre network, making the deal both a growth opportunity and a potential competition concern.
The regulatory test
The concern is who controls rivals’ networks. Cell C, an independent South African mobile operator, no longer operates its own radio access network, relying on roaming arrangements with MTN and Vodacom. Many MVNOs depend on host networks, letting banks, retailers and other brands sell mobile services without building infrastructure.
But their competitiveness depends on wholesale prices, coverage and service terms set by network owners. If MTN absorbs Telkom, smaller operators could face a larger supplier that also competes for their customers. Internet service providers buying wholesale fibre could face similar risks with fewer independent networks.
Following its Data Services Market Inquiry, whose final report was released in December 2019, the Competition Commission secured settlements with MTN and Vodacom in 2020. These included substantial reductions in prepaid data prices, daily free data and zero-rated access to educational and government services. The Commission subsequently estimated that the interventions saved consumers approximately R4 billion ($230 million) in the first year. Its recommendations also contributed to Openserve wholesale fibre price reductions and measures supporting MVNO competition.
Any transaction would face scrutiny from the Competition Commission and Tribunal. The Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), the country’s telecommunications regulator, would consider licencing and spectrum implications. The state and Public Investment Corporation, South Africa’s largest asset manager, which together own 51.6% of Telkom, are pivotal shareholders.
Regulators will need to weigh the potential investment benefits against the risk of weaker competition, particularly in mobile and wholesale broadband markets. The deal’s impact will depend on whether consumers and smaller operators benefit or face greater dependence on a combined business controlling more essential network infrastructure.
Ultimately, businesses and consumers will feel the real test. A stronger operator may benefit the industry, but not if consumers end up paying for it through weaker competition.

articles.title: À cause de GTA 6, la PS5 est en rupture de stock un peu partout
articles.text:
Ce jeudi 19 novembre avait une saveur particulière pour des dizaines de millions de joueurs à travers le monde : GTA VI était enfin là après 13 ans d’attente. Mais pour y jouer, il faut s’équiper : choisir entre Xbox et PlayStation. Si vous penchez du côté de Sony, c’est compliqué : les PlayStation 5 deviennent de plus en plus difficiles à trouver.
En 4 jours, 39 millions de joueurs ont lancé GTA VI sur PlayStation 5 : Sony est bien content
Sony a publié un billet de blog ce 23 novembre pour revenir sur la sortie de GTA VI sur ses consoles et les quelques jours qui ont suivi (week-end compris). Le fabricant de consoles revendique plus de 39 millions de joueurs uniques sur ses différentes PlayStation 5. Le jeu a également battu le record du nombre de joueurs simultanés sur un jeu PlayStation, toutes catégories de jeu confondues.
En quatre jours, ces 39 millions de joueurs ont déjà cumulé 689 millions d’heures sur le jeu et chaque joueur y a passé en moyenne 17,4 heures, ce qui fait plus de quatre heures par jour. Sony est content pour les joueurs, mais aussi pour son portefeuille, puisque l’entreprise a enregistré « le plus grand nombre de nouvelles consoles PS5 connectées en une seule journée » (hors périodes de fêtes de fin d’année). Un succès qu’elle doit évidemment à Rockstar Games, puisque depuis la sortie de son jeu « GTA VI a été le premier jeu testé sur 70% des nouvelles PS5 », précise Sony.
Difficile de trouver une PS5 en vente : c’est la pénurie
Si certains joueurs s’étaient préparés à l’arrivée de GTA VI depuis des semaines, des mois, voire des années, ce n’était pas le cas de tous. Depuis quelques semaines, beaucoup cherchent à acquérir une PS5, mais tous n’y arrivent pas. Neuves ou d’occasion, les PlayStation 5 (et 5 Pro) sont difficiles à trouver. En témoigne ce reportage de BFM ce mardi où un propriétaire de magasin d’occasion n’a plus de PlayStation 5. Et dès que quelqu’un en vend une, elle n’a pas le temps d’être mise en rayon qu’elle est déjà vendue.
La console la plus impactée par ces ruptures de stocks semble être la PlayStation 5 Pro ; la PS5 Standard et la Digital Edition subissent de fortes tensions, mais elles sont moindres. Et c’est normal : les joueurs qui veulent profiter de GTA VI dans les meilleures conditions privilégient le modèle Pro (qui rend le jeu un peu plus beau visuellement). Les pénuries sont loin de se limiter à la France : un peu partout dans le monde, il est devenu plus difficile d’en trouver, ou alors les délais de livraison se sont allongés.
Autre problème : certains commerçants ou vendeurs particuliers y voient du profit à faire. Chez certains revendeurs tiers, la PS5 Pro s’est affichée à plus de 1 000, voire 1 400 euros, alors que le prix officiel de la console est de 899,99 euros. Du côté des vendeurs particuliers, certains se sont mis à l’arnaque : sur Vinted, ils mettent en vente la console à un prix intéressant. Mais tout en bas de la description de l’annonce, ils précisent qu’ils vendent une image de la console et non la console en elle-même !

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Unpatched Flaw in Defunct Idunno AntiCsrf Library
articles.text:
Threat actors are exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in the open source anti-CSRF library Idunno AntiCsrf for remote code execution (RCE), security researchers warn.
AntiCsrf is a legacy ASP.NET module for WebForms applications that has no active maintainer and is no longer actively supported. The most recent version, 0.9.1 Beta, was released in December 2008.
Tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.3), the exploited security defect is described as an insecure deserialization bug in the processing of HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms endpoints.
“Exploitation requires only a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token. Active exploitation in the wild has been observed,” Google Cloud’s Mandiant warned on November 18.
The flaw allows an attacker to supply any non-empty value in the CSRF cookie along with a Base64-encoded gadget chain to gain RCE in the context of the IIS worker process, Mandiant notes.
According to preemptive cybersecurity firm WatchTowr, the issue exists because AntiCsrf does not perform sufficient checks on data from incoming form submissions before reconstructing it into program objects.
“The vulnerable check runs before the application’s own page logic, so it can affect many pages on an affected site, not just ones that use a login form. A successful attack gives the attacker control over the process that runs the website, which can lead to full compromise of the server,” WatchTowr says.
On Tuesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-131914 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, urging federal agencies to address it within three days.
As no official patch is available for the vulnerability, all organizations relying on the 18-year-old AntiCsrf to validate anti-CSRF tokens on form submissions should immediately discontinue the module and transition to an actively supported solution.
“WatchTowr Intel detected exploit probes across our honeypots that used creative .NET compiled gadget payloads to confirm if a given system is vulnerable. We validated the exploit and confirmed that, if the host was vulnerable, the server would be tricked into redirecting to a unique URL that would discreetly confirm control of the web server to the attacker,” WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek.
“There is no patch, and likely there won’t be one. Defenders should audit ASP.NET products to identify ones packaging the Idunno.AntiCSRF library and review their audit logs for signs of exploitation. Where possible, the library should be replaced in affected applications. Where that’s not possible, apply WAF rules until alternative workarounds are identified,” Ganchev added.

articles.title: ‘There are toys out there that could be harmful to your children’: New York just banned AI toys from being made and sold for five years — with parents told to play with children in a way that ‘stretches their imagination’
articles.text:
‘There are toys out there that could be harmful to your children’: New York just banned AI toys from being made and sold for five years — with parents told to play with children in a way that ‘stretches their imagination’
New York says no to AI toys ahead of the holiday season
- New York has enacted a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of AI-powered toys
- The ban comes ahead of the holiday season, with parents warned that many AI toys currently operate with minimal safety guardrails
- Numerous studies have found AI toys to be highly data-invasive, with some even encouraging children to find dangerous items
At a beloved Harlem toy store in New York, Governor Kathy Hochul announced a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of AI toys, citing the potential harms that they can have on children.
Given that numerous AI toys have been found to be requesting dangerous levels of device access, such as location, microphone, and camera access, and others encouraging children to find dangerous objects such as matches and knives, many experts have called for greater regulation on putting the technology in children's toys.
Outside of the obvious risks in collecting data on children and AI toys hallucinating, Hochul also encouraged parents to actively engage in how their children play rather than resorting to tech to keep them entertained, especially during the holiday season.
No more AI toys in New York
“Parents, as you're out there buying gifts for the kids for the holiday season, I wanted you to hear this loud and clear. This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” Hochul said.
To enforce the new ruling, companies found to have violated the new rules could face hefty fines of up to $15,000 per day, with Hochul adding that regulations need to keep pace with technology in order to keep it safe.
The announcement was made at Grandma's Place, a toy store opened in the late 1990s by retired schoolteacher Dawn Harris-Martine. “A good toy for a child is the one that stretches their imagination,” Harris-Martine said, adding that parents need to be present with their children during play.
“Do not put an iPad in your child's hands and go off and let them sit there and play with it themselves, she said. “It's really necessary when a three-year-old can sit and listen to a teddy bear telling them to do strange things—it's not a good thing.”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"We as the parents, and the children, we want these toys to be fun," said Muna Heaven, a Harlem mother and member of Mothers Against Media Addiction. "But we also have a baseline expectation that they will be safe."
The ban comes alongside numerous child safety groups calling on huge retailers such as Amazon and eBay to pause the sale of AI toys until they can be proven to be safe.
AI toy concerns accompany wider worries surrounding the effect of AI and other technology on children, especially how they learn and interact with the world around them.
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in some schools and has encouraged New Yorkers to push back against the “reckless adoption” of AI. This has already caused issues with how Google search is deployed for education in New York.
Studies have found that students are increasingly turning to AI to help with schoolwork, with 96% of college students using the technology to help stay on top of their education. Some countries have taken drastic measures, with Norway banning AI from being used to educate those below the age of 13 to allow basic reading, writing, and math skills to develop.
For better or for worse, how AI affects the way children learn and play will likely take years to be fully understood.

articles.title: Art of play in the age of AI
articles.text:
Art of play in the age of AI
Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here’s what we can learn through that process as developers.
As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.
In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!
For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.
The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.
Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!! #GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5
— Connie Xu (@conniecodes) October 28, 2026
you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge! repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY
— Rishab Kumar (@rishabincloud) October 27, 2026
Coding needs room for play
According to the Octoverse report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.
With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!
AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.
As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.
You don’t need a big idea to start
What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!
At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.
Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.
AI with oversight
AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.
In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.
Be kind, keep maintainers in mind
It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a lot to the maintenance burden.
Efforts need to be made by all of us, like the one shared here, to help ease burdens for maintainers.
As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”
Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:
- Read the contribution guidelines
- Check existing issues
- Understand what the project needs
Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.
Now it’s your turn
We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does. Give it a go on our virtual badge, and try tinkering on it yourself.
Then get your hands on your own badge. We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

articles.title: The loneliest peptide party in New York
articles.text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
The loneliest peptide party in New York
The peptide curious are looking for answers, and finding dubious products instead.
On a rainy fall evening, an experimental art venue in Chelsea Market had a small line out the door. There are always lines in New York City. Viral food trends, gallery exhibitions, pop-ups, and parties. The folks in line looked like your average joe, ready for a Friday night on the town. You wouldn’t look twice — except, perhaps, for a man with a wizard beard and a laser sword strapped to his back.
Inside, the man with a laser sword stood in the middle of the cavernous bottom floor of a two-story warehouse strewn with large bean bags. On the wall were psychedelic projections of jellyfish, shrimp, and other sea creatures. A bizarre choice, considering peptides won’t induce any trippy vision quests, and not a single person was getting groovy. The industrial beams had posters with QR codes that you could scan to get samples of Afterglow, a new type of peptide product. According to seemingly discarded pamphlets around the venue, Afterglow isn’t a standard injectable or oral peptide. The company makes strips that dissolve under the tongue. The “Afterglow Peptide Field Guide” also described what each sample does, dosing recommendations, and potential side effects. At the upstairs bar, bartenders mixed custom cocktails called Afterburn — complete with bioluminescent veggie nectar — and Margatrutide. (For the record, a bioluminescent veggie nectar cocktail tastes as awful as you think.)
Welcome to a peptide launch party.
Peptide parties are old news in San Francisco, but they’re somewhat more novel in New York City. Milling around the edges of the venue were various reporters and photographers. We were all trying to get a sense of why anyone had bothered to come out. Not that many did. Despite the venue’s size, the main floor had plenty of empty space.
One person I spoke to was a fencer with sore joints. They’d heard that one of the peptides might help with recovery. Another had a father in the wellness industry and had heard vague things about how effective peptides could be. One woman, staring at a projected jellyfish, merely shrugged. Her friend was more into “wellness stuff” and she had no plans, so, why not check out a party? A man, staring into his bag of Afterglow samples, was mostly interested in weight loss but scared about the safety of gray market products. A few feet away, another man was furiously reading the Afterglow pamphlet. “I like to know what I put in my body,” he said.
The only problem was he didn’t remember which sample he had tried.
A common refrain: Well, this beats doing research online. This, at least, was a social event where you could theoretically connect with other people. And there were clusters of strangers speaking to each other. Mostly, near the bar. Everywhere else, people stared awkwardly on their phones, their eyes occasionally roaming the room without meeting anyone else’s gaze for more than a second or two. After a while, they’d disappear into the back room and reappear with a goody bag full of peptide samples.
After 90 minutes, I decided to leave. For the umpteenth time that evening, I’d walked up to someone, asked about peptides, and got a noncommittal “I really don’t know anything — I just came to learn more.” (When asked if they had, they invariably shrugged and pointed to the goody bag.) It was clear that the only peptide evangelists here were likely associated with the launch. The whole thing, to me, seemed as if someone had tried to draw a cool party from memory. The last thing I saw was a person draped in a ghost sheet sitting alone in the corner.
As it turned out, the man with the laser sword was a performance artist who’d been invited to attend. Out of journalistic integrity, I asked if he had ever tried peptides. He told me he was more interested in the unifying energy of the universe. When I got up to leave, he waved and said, “Giggles.”
If I were peptide curious, the Afterglow launch party was a pretty awful way to learn anything about these substances. To be fair, Afterglow’s Partiful invitation mostly described this event as “an environment great for aura farming” and the “hard launch of [its] first of many experiments in culture.” Nevertheless, as part of the press, I did walk away with a smattering of Afterglow’s products. In total, I got packets of what Afterglow calls Charge (NAD+), Rejuvenate (glutathione), Wolverine Blend (BPC-157 / TB-500), Strength Blend (CJC-1295 / Ipamorelin), Glow Blend (GHK-Cu / BPC-157 / TB-500), Connect (PT-141), GLP-2 (tirzepatide), and GLP-3 (retatrutide). Or at least that’s what the packaging says. There’s no way to truly verify gray market peptides for safety or efficacy because they’re unregulated products.
First of all, last I checked, GLP-1 medications do not upgrade like iPhone models. Afterglow’s pamphlet correctly lists that your body has “three hormone switches”: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. The accompanying descriptors of what each does are broadly correct, though lacking in nuance. For example, there is a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 2, but it’s not tirzepatide. The “real” GLP-2 is a hormone related to intestinal health. Tirzepatide is still considered a GLP-1 medication that’s a dual agonist because it works on two hormones (GLP-1 and GIP.) The GLP-2 moniker is a misnomer popularized by ill-informed influencers. The same goes for retatrutide, which, as of this writing, is still an unapproved GLP-1 medication that works on three hormones (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon) and is therefore a triple agonist. There is no such thing as GLP-3.
For all the samples, there were no instructions regarding dosing on the packaging — just another QR code leading to Afterglow’s product page. Those pages happen to contain instructions for how to use the strips, and the amount of product within the strips. There are disclaimers about how little studied the compounds are, but nothing about interactions, side effects, or what to expect while taking. Just a throwaway line to talk to your doctor.
All that information, you’d have to find on the pamphlet given at the party. (Ironically, some “important cautions” on the pamphlet state to avoid taking samples with alcohol, at a party where the booze was flowing.) Provided you didn’t throw it out. One would hope that information is on a box if you were to buy directly from the seller. But for all intents and purposes, what I just described is what a clueless partygoer would have to go on.
If everything in that pamphlet were 100 percent factual, perhaps a conscientious partygoer could feel reassured. On that front, I have bad news. The pamphlet calls PT-141 an “FDA-approved peptide that boosts sexual desire for both men and women.”
PT-141, also known as bremelanotide or Vyleesi, is FDA approved. But only for premenopausal women suffering from hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It is not approved for post-menopausal women, men, or for general sexual performance enhancement.
Another concern: How does one evaluate a sublingual peptide strip? Specifically, is this delivery method even scientifically proven effective in humans? Spoiler: It’s not! A collapsible FAQ menu on Afterglow’s site states, “We don’t know yet. Nobody has published how much of most peptides reaches the blood from a strip compared with an injection. We’re funding studies to measure exactly that, and we’ll share what we find.”
As for why you’d want to even try a sublingual strip? Afterglow’s website suggests it’s more convenient than injections or pills. No refrigeration, no needles, and no need for learning how to reconstitute a drug. Just pop a strip under the tongue and go.
And good luck trying to find reputable sources of information on your own. Afterglow says it’s funding its own research, but its site has no reviewable documentation just yet. A Google search brings up a questionable AI overview, a handful of links from dubious med spas, a couple of dead links, and one PubMed study in mice. Most of the links also primarily discuss the difference between oral peptides in pill form and injectables — so not terribly relevant here.
I’d consider it fair game if I were confident that anyone at the party I went to did their due diligence. As it stands, I talked with over a dozen people who were mostly there for vibes, booze, and freebies.
Not all peptide parties are created equal. Some happen on WWII cargo ships, complete with panel discussions about peptide supply chains. Another “peptide 101” talk I attended in New York happened at the back of a bitcoin bar. There, most attendees also knew very little about peptides, but at least they got treated to a PowerPoint presentation about the basics. There was a dubious demonstration of how to inject oneself that would’ve probably made any pharmacist or doctor scream. But at the very least, peptides were defined and attendees could ask questions. (The answers to those questions were on the right track with regard to the dangers of the gray market. They were less reliable about scientific rigor and why “anecdotal evidence” is not the same as clinical evidence of safety.)
But a striking, recurring theme is just how much is unknown. These substances aren’t well-studied in humans, so there’s not much evidence as to long-term benefits or side effects. The peptide curious know shocking little about the substances they’re supposedly interested in. Likewise, it’s incredibly difficult to get reliable, unbiased data on gray market interest or usage, though there have been attempts to quantify this surging demand in recent months. Case in point, telehealth provider Hims & Hers just conducted a consumer survey of roughly 2,000 American adults. Of those surveyed, 68 percent said they had little to no knowledge about peptides. Less than 18 percent were even able to identify that peptides are chains of amino acids. Even so, 40 percent said they were interested or very interested in trying injectable prescription treatments — including peptides — if offered by a telehealth service.
Even so, peptides are everywhere. The word appears in copious ads for skincare creams, weight loss drugs, and supplements. Looksmaxxers, influencers, and celebrities like Gwyneth Paltrow and Joe Rogan talk about them in podcasts, documentaries, and social media as if they’re miracle shortcuts. Hims & Hers has even announced it’s launching a service called Peptide Plus — nevermind that the vast majority of what it’ll offer are not actual peptides.
In this kind of environment, of course more people will become peptide curious. Which makes it even more concerning that the most readily available information sources are not medical or scientific experts well-versed on the topic at hand. There are dubious links online summarized into less-than-critical AI overviews. There are pamphlets handed out at weird parties, where there’s more booze and schmooze than education. Influencers branding themselves as experts as they flash crudely summarized studies in a bar back room. Industry panels that are inaccessible to the average consumer, full of jargon and assumed knowledge of the science at hand.
It’s clear something needs to be done until general knowledge improves. Until then, the parties will continue.

articles.title: Du jamais-vu depuis 2013 : voici Ladybird, le navigateur qui ne dépend pas de Google, Apple ou Mozilla
articles.text:
L’alpha est arrivée le 23 novembre, en image disque pour macOS et en paquets Flatpak, Ubuntu ou Fedora côté Linux. Jusqu’ici, essayer Ladybird imposait de compiler soi-même son code source. Le canal est désormais continu, mis à jour automatiquement, et l’avertissement ne cache rien : « C’est une alpha, certains sites ne fonctionneront pas et il plantera parfois ».
Un web à trois moteurs, tous branchés sur la publicité
Chrome, Edge, Opera et consorts reposent sur Blink, Safari sur WebKit, Firefox sur Gecko. Le dernier moteur indépendant à avoir pesé s’est éteint en 2013, quand Opera a abandonné son Presto pour rejoindre la base de Chrome, un chemin que Microsoft a suivi en 2020 avec Edge.
Les trois moteurs sont open source. Blink et WebKit appartiennent pourtant à des géants de la publicité et du matériel, et l’essentiel des revenus de Mozilla provient d’un accord de recherche signé avec Google. « Ils sont tous financés par l’empire publicitaire de Google », résumait dès 2024 Chris Wanstrath, le cofondateur de GitHub qui a doté le projet d’un million de dollars. Ces mêmes acteurs siègent d’ailleurs aux consortiums qui écrivent les standards du web.
Ladybird, lancé en 2022 dans le sillage du système expérimental SerenityOS, n’emprunte pas une ligne de code à Blink, WebKit ou Gecko. Andreas Kling, son fondateur, est un ancien développeur WebKit passé par Apple et Nokia. La fondation à but non lucratif qu’il a montée avec Chris Wanstrath vit des dons et du mécénat d’entreprises comme Shopify, Cloudflare ou Proton VPN. Aucun accord de moteur de recherche par défaut n’est prévu.
Lire aussi : Proton recrute pour bâtir l’anti-Chrome que ses fans réclament depuis des années
Pourquoi treize ans sans nouveau venu
Un moteur de rendu doit parler toutes les langues du web : HTML, CSS, JavaScript et des centaines d’interfaces de programmation. Le W3C et le WHATWG, les consortiums qui tiennent ces standards, les amendent en continu, et suivre la cadence exige des ingénieurs à plein temps.
La conformité se mesure, et Ladybird s’y plie : le navigateur validait plus de 2 millions de sous-tests Web Platform Tests au printemps. Son score à l’exercice de vitesse Speedometer 2 est passé d’environ 47 à 64 au seul mois d’août. Le projet a aussi commencé, en février, à réécrire des pans entiers du code en Rust, moteur JavaScript en premier, pour limiter les bugs de mémoire propres au C++.
Aucune promesse n’est faite sur la sécurité, et les chercheurs sont même invités à malmener le logiciel : « Nous voulons que les passionnés de sécurité le piratent ! ». Les développeurs web disposent des protocoles WebDriver et des outils de développement de Firefox pour tester leurs sites. Windows devra patienter, faute d’installateur natif à ce stade.
La feuille de route vise une bêta en 2027 et une version stable en 2028, le temps de passer du jouet pour curieux au navigateur du quotidien. D’ici là, macOS et Linux peuvent déjà afficher un web rendu sans les lunettes de Google, d’Apple ou de Mozilla. Le projet entend prouver que le web reste une plateforme ouverte, où un moteur payé par des dons plutôt que par la publicité a droit de cité.

articles.title: Real Ventures returns with sixth fund and a refreshed accelerator program
articles.text:
Annual general meetings for venture funds don’t typically feature a musical performance.
“We’re looking to help you build the conditions for commercial success, but not at the expense of the purpose that you’re about.”
John Stokes, Real Ventures
But Montréal’s Real Ventures has never played by the rules. At the firm’s AGM in September, partner Katy Yam serenaded attendees (including portfolio companies and limited partners) with a karaoke rendition of the Broadway hit Defying Gravity. The moment felt significant; after a fundraising hiatus, Defying Gravity was the theme of Real’s AGM, highlighting a unique, against-the-grain vision the firm was putting forward for its first new fundraise since 2017.
Real Ventures announced the first close of its sixth pre-seed fund on Wednesday, along with the relaunch of its flagship accelerator program, FounderFuel. The fund, officially called Antifragile Fund I, has announced a first close of $45 million, anchored by the Government of Québec and several returning LPs, like Desjardins Capital, Fonds de solidarité FTQ, Teralys Capital (through the La Caisse-backed Fonds québécois d’amorçage Teralys), and BDC Capital (through its Black Entrepreneurs Fund). Targeting a $60-million total, the fund represents a remarkable comeback for a firm that paused fundraising in 2022 following a number of key departures, and whose future was uncertain amid a venture market downturn.
The comeback accompanies an evolution of the fund’s ethos and approach, according to managing partner John Stokes. The partners are looking to find and nurture founders “daring to question the systems we all depend on,” from sectors like energy and healthcare to civic infrastructure, he said in an interview.
Part of that means resisting the pull toward maximizing shareholder value over all else, including company values and mission. Some principles come from the book Incorruptible: Why Good Companies Go Bad and How Great Companies Stay Great, by American entrepreneur and author Eric Ries, which Real handed out to attendees at its AGM. In an era where corporate profits often seem to trump all other considerations, Real is making a bet on alternative ways of building startups where purpose and profit can stay on the same track.
“We’re looking to help you build the conditions for commercial success, but not at the expense of the purpose that you’re about,” Stokes said.
RELATED: Real Ventures launches revamped fellowship program for founder well-being
The first eight companies Real selects for FounderFuel, its Montréal-based, five-month accelerator program, will get to try out this approach. Though Real had run the program for years up until 2023, backing startups like BenchSci and Transit, this is the first time that it will make FounderFuel core to its fund thesis.
The idea is to invest $500,000 CAD into each cohort company at the pre-seed stage, reserving follow-on capital as well. In some cases, Real will consider investment opportunities outside of the accelerator cohort. Stokes and Montréal-based partners Sam Haffar and Katy Yam will all act as investment partners and be “hands-on” in the FounderFuel program. Stokes said Real is open to backing companies across Canada but expects FounderFuel participants to be in Montréal for the program’s duration.
“If you look at the fast pace of technological evolution…it has become even more difficult to be an entrepreneur,” Beatrice Couture, principal at Teralys Capital, said in an interview. “What Real figured out over the years is that founders who don’t have the resilience and capacity to grow with their company might break.”
Resilience is a familiar notion for today’s Real Ventures team. Co-founded in 2007 by Stokes, JS Cournoyer, and Alan MacIntosh before Canada’s venture capital (VC) industry took off, it notched some early successes. Real went on to back notable startups like League, Mejuri, and Sonder, establishing itself as one of Canada’s top pre-seed investors.
In 2022, following the 2021 VC boom and subsequent bust, as well as leadership shake-ups, Real paused raising its sixth fund. Toronto-based managing partner Janet Bannister stepped back from her role and later left to launch her own founder-focused early-stage firm, Staircase Ventures. BetaKit reported at the time that investors weren’t pleased with Real’s fund performance, and that having leadership outside Québec hadn’t helped.
Stokes said the major market headwinds coincided with a shift among LPs about the right balance between a fund’s value and how much capital it returned—a fine line that he acknowledged Real didn’t walk that well. “We were clearly going through a transition as we moved from the founding team of Real to those that would take it on to the next level, and we were doing that at a time when there were a lot of challenges,” Stokes said. Since then, he added, Real has had “amazing support” from its LPs.
Indeed, several of its investors have now returned. The AI boom has wrought returns in the intervening years, from portfolio companies like AI chipmaker Tenstorrent and physical AI scaleup Vention, which, respectively, have returned the entire value and half the value of Real’s third $89-million fund. Real has also earned industry honours for top deals, such as its support of live event commerce platform atVenu.
RELATED: Real Ventures partners with Panache, Inovia to relaunch FounderFuel accelerator
And despite a recent change in provincial government, the Québec government is participating as a key investor through Investissement Québec. Its support of Real Ventures (up to $30 million) was part of a broader announcement to back three local funds, including AQC Capital’s third fund, which is receiving up to $50 million, and ACET Capital’s fourth fund at up to $25 million.
Stéphane Paquet, Québec’s Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy, said in a French statement that the investment will help local entrepreneurs “transform their innovations into commercial successes” and share Québec’s expertise with the world.
Having Real and FounderFuel back in the ecosystem is an exciting prospect, according to Couture. “They have shown over the years that they are able to find these outlier companies before anyone else,” she said. “I hope that they will do it again this time.”
Feature image courtesy Real Ventures.

articles.title: Del ‘smartphone’ al hogar conectado, tecnología para aprovechar el Black Friday
articles.text: La campaña Todo Days de Orange ofrece, hasta el 30 de noviembre, una amplia selección de dispositivos de tecnología y pequeños electrodomésticos con descuentos. Tres de cada cuatro españoles (concretamente, un 76%) tienen previsto hacer alguna compra en los próximos días aprovechando los descuentos del Black Friday, según revela una encuesta de la Organización de Consumidores y Usuarios. El sondeo de la OCU, realizado entre más de dos mil personas de entre 18 y 74 años, revela que los dispositivos de electrónica (elegidos por el 39% de los encuestados) y los pequeños electrodomésticos (23%) ocupan el segundo y tercer lugar, respectivamente, en intención de compra para el Black Friday 2026, solo superados por las prendas de vestir, el calzado y los complementos de moda.
